item.title: Nano Letters: Layer-Number-Controlled Symmetry Breaking and Surface-State Transport in Rhombohedral Graphene Multilayers
item.description:
Bosai Lyu, Jian Zheng, Kai Liu, Yulu Ren, Size Wu, Yating Sha, Shuhan Liu, Youngju Park, et al.
Rhombohedral multilayer graphene hosts layer-polarized flat bands, providing an intriguing platform for correlated and topological states; however, how layer number governs symmetry breaking and surface screening remains elusive. Here, we prepare rhombohedral graphene multilayers and systematically conduct electrical transport measurements. We uncover an unconventional layer dependence of phase transitions: the critical displacement field Dc for the layer-antiferromagnetic-to-semimetal transitions remains nearly constant across tetralayer to hexalayer graphene, whereas Dc for the semimetal-to-layer-polarized-insulator transition increases with layer number, defying unscreened Coulomb interaction models. In hexalayer graphene, surface-state-dominated transport emerges with Landau levels and resistive peaks predominantly controlled by adjacent gates, revealing strong interlayer screening. High magnetic fields further reveal valley-layer-locked Landau levels and dissipative states associated with interlayer backscattering, highlighting the presence of decoupled surface states. Our findings establish the layer number as a key tuning knob for engineering correlated and topological phases in rhombohedral graphene multilayers.

item.title: JACS: Unifying Polar and Hydrophobic Models of Ice Recognition by Antifreeze Glycoproteins
item.description:
Alejandro Villacampa, Julio Zabalza, Alba Nin-Hill, Akari Yamauchi, Alicia Asín, Andrés G. Santana, Mattia Ghirardello, Ismael Compañón, et al.
Antifreeze glycoproteins (AFGPs) enable polar organisms to survive at subzero temperatures by inhibiting ice growth through selective association with specific crystallographic planes. However, the molecular basis of this interaction and its remarkable selectivity remain incompletely understood, and both polar and hydrophobic binding models have been proposed. Here, we combine the synthesis of AFGP variants with high-resolution NMR spectroscopy, antifreeze activity measurements, and molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the molecular determinants of ice recognition. Minimally perturbative chemical modifications, including site-specific deuteration and fluorination, were used to probe the contributions of nonpolar and polar interactions while preserving the characteristic AFGP conformation. The combined structure–activity relationships and computational analyses support an integrative binding model that provides a unified and parsimonious interpretation of the experimental observations. Within this framework, our experimental evidence is consistent with the view that dispersive interactions involving peptide and carbohydrate methyl groups favor productive association with the ice surface, whereas carbohydrate hydroxyl groups, together with sugar- and backbone-associated water molecules, contribute polar interactions that promote selective and persistent binding. This model reconciles key aspects of previously proposed polar and hydrophobic descriptions and provides a molecular rationale for the characteristic plane selectivity of AFGPs and the conservation of specific sequence motifs. More broadly, our results highlight minimally perturbative isotopic substitution and fluorinated molecular editing as useful chemical strategies for probing weak dispersive contributions to complex molecular recognition processes while preserving native molecular architecture.

item.title: ACS Nano: Engineered Peptide Nanoparticle Targeting Both Bacterial Load Reduction and Bone Repair for the Treatment of Bone Infections
item.description:
Yimeng Lu, Ti Zhang, Xiabing Han, Yaqi Cui, Dan He, Ming Yan, Xiaozhu Wang, Cheng Wang, et al.
Bone infection is a common and serious complication in orthopedic surgery. Conventional antibiotic strategies frequently induce antibiotic resistance, leading to the persistence of bone infections. In this study, an engineered peptide nanoparticle named C8-IK21 was designed based on the coiled-coil motif. Specifically, C8-IK21 effectively targeted bacterial cell membranes, further exacerbating bacterial death through lipid peroxidation. At safe doses, local administration of C8-IK21 demonstrated high efficacy in treating S. aureus-infected cortical bone defects in mice. No detectable resistance emerged under the tested experimental conditions. Additionally, C8-IK21 exhibited anti-inflammatory activity. Furthermore, C8-IK21 could enter cells by binding to ADAM9, activating the ERK signaling pathway to regulate osteoblast differentiation. Meanwhile, C8-IK21 reduced the expression of ITGB1 via ADAM9, thereby inhibiting osteoclast differentiation and function. Moreover, the pro-osteogenic effect of C8-IK21 was validated in organoids. In conclusion, C8-IK21 represents a promising therapeutic approach for the treatment of refractory bacterial infections and bone homeostasis disorders.

item.title: ACS Nano: ZnO–Te Anti-Ambipolar Switch Integration with Complementary Field-Effect Transistors Enabling a Pull-Middle Architecture for Standard Ternary Inverters
item.description:
Jun-Hyeok Choi, Hyeon-Seok Shin, Byeong Gwan Kim, Minjae Kim, Jae Hyeon Jun, Jun Yeong Hong, Chan Bin Lee, Useok Choi, et al.
We demonstrate a pull-middle architecture for standard ternary inverters (STIs) operating at 77 K, enabled by the cointegration of a ZnO–Te antiambipolar switch (AAS) and vertically stacked ZnO/Te complementary field-effect transistors (CFETs) using a BEOL-compatible low-temperature process (≤150 °C). Operation at 77 K not only isolates the intrinsic pull-middle switching mechanism by suppressing thermally activated off-currents but also establishes the architecture’s immediate viability for extreme-environment computing, such as radiation-hardened space data centers and cryogenic aerospace systems. In this architecture, the ZnO–Te AAS acts as an independent pull-middle device connected to an explicit Vdd/2 node, while the ZnO and Te FETs in the CFET serve as the pull-down and pull-up devices, respectively. Unlike conventional ternary logic schemes governed by precise pull-up/pull-down current matching, by explicitly clamping the intermediate state, this architecture structurally prevents variation-induced voltage shifts and suppresses static power dissipation. Consequently, the proposed STI exhibits a narrow middle-state voltage distribution across 25 cells and achieves an I/O swing ratio of 1, with cascaded operation without level-restoring circuitry supported by measurement-calibrated circuit simulations. Ultimately, this vertically integrated ZnO/Te STI offers a compact and variation-tolerant platform for cryogenic logic, while presenting a material-optimization pathway toward room-temperature multivalued systems.

item.title: ACS Nano: Defect-Tolerant Frenkel Exciton Delocalization in Supramolecular Nanotubes
item.description:
Alexey V. Kuevda, Mónica K. Espinoza Cangahuala, Pieter J. Brongers, Sundar Raj Krishnaswamy, Carlo Fasting, Steffen Ernst, Kai Licha, Giuseppe Portale, et al.
Preserving exciton delocalization in the presence of structural and environmental disorder is a central challenge for nanoscale photonic and optoelectronic materials. Here we show that Frenkel excitons in two-dimensional supramolecular nanostructures retain extensive delocalization even in the presence of intentionally incorporated deep-energy traps. Fluorescent trap molecules introduced during the self-assembly of double-walled molecular nanotubes provide a controlled model system in which strong local energetic perturbations are created without significant distortion of the host structure. Increasing the trap concentration shortens the host-exciton PL lifetime from ∼190 ps to ∼15 ps, while polarization-resolved microscopy of individual nanotubes shows that the collective excitonic polarization remains essentially unchanged. Frenkel-exciton calculations based on experimentally established molecular structures reproduce this robustness and reveal that delocalization decreases only weakly because the excitonic wave functions redistribute around the trap sites while remaining extended over large molecular domains. These results demonstrate an intrinsic defect tolerance of delocalized Frenkel excitons in a two-dimensional supramolecular architecture and identify dimensionality as an important design principle for preserving collective excitonic states in structurally imperfect nanomaterials.

item.title: JACS: Solvent Cage Suppresses Dynamically Induced Entropic Pathways to Provide High Selectivity in Intramolecular Fe-Oxo Radical Rebound Reactions
item.description:
Jyothish Joy, Anthony J. Schaefer, Daniel H. Ess
For homogeneous transition metal reactions, it is generally assumed that when intermediates are formed, they are sufficiently long-lived for the surrounding solvent cage to fully equilibrate prior to product formation. However, some transition metal reactions generate a highly reactive and transient intermediate for which product selectivity is not governed by subsequent competing transition states but rather by dynamic effects during descent from the transition state that forms the intermediate. In such reactions, solvent reorganization may be slow relative to product formation, which could significantly impact reaction pathway selectivity. Here, we demonstrate the important role of the solvent cage and explicit solute–solvent interactions in determining pathway selectivity for the ultrafast-evolving radical pair intermediate generated during (PDP)Fe-oxo-catalyzed intramolecular sp3 C–H functionalization. Quasiclassical reactive trajectories showed that with only a continuum solvent model a mixture of oxygen rebound/hydroxylation, desaturation, and direct carboxylate rebound products are formed due to dynamically driven, entropically favored wandering, which is inconsistent with experiments. In contrast, trajectories in explicit solvent reproduced the experimental product selectivity and demonstrated that solvent controls the nonstatistical, motion-driven selectivity by acting as a nonequilibrated solvent cage that restricts access to entropically favorable wandering configurations. The solvent effectively guides the radical pair intermediate toward one dominant product pathway. These results demonstrate the important role of the solvent cage in reactions involving highly transient intermediates where dynamic effects control selectivity.

item.title: JACS: Synergistic Interactions Enable Superior Oxygen Evolution Reaction Activity in Compositionally Complex Nanocrystal–Nanosheet Hybrids
item.description:
Talisi E. Meyer, Cheng-Yin Lin, Andrew Zhao, Yiguo Ma, Zixiao Shi, Reilly P. Lynch, Ching Chun Peng, David A. Muller, et al.
Thiospinel nanoparticles are promising catalytic materials due to their compositional tunability, electronic conductivity, and structural stability. While significant gains in catalysis have been made through material engineering, one continuously developing route is through the use of support materials to enhance performance. Here, we report a simple, scalable, low-temperature method to coproduce colloidal multimetal nanocrystals (<20 nm in diameter) and In2S3-based nanosheets (<1 nm thick), forming compositionally complex hybrid nanocrystal–nanosheet heterostructures in situ. The in situ-formed heterostructures demonstrate enhanced catalytic activity in the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in alkaline conditions; peak performance was achieved in heterostructures formed between (Ni,Co,Fe)3S4 nanocrystals and (In,Fe,Mn)2S3 nanosheets with overpotentials as low as 283 mV at 10 mA/cm2. Heterostructures can also be produced ex situ by introducing nanosheets, postsynthetically, to the nanocrystals, reducing the overpotential of (Ni,Co,Fe)3S4 nanocrystals from 362 mV to 312 mV with only a 5 wt % addition. This improvement highlights synergistic interactions in the heterostructures. These results suggest that an optimum nanosheet loading that maximizes effective nanocrystal–nanosheet interfacial coupling while preserving access to the Ni/Co-rich catalytic domains is the relevant design parameter. Our findings provide a low-temperature, colloidal route for synthesizing compositionally complex and highly uniform (<15% dispersity) sulfide nanocrystals, nanosheets, or heterostructures of the two with tunable structures and enhanced electrocatalytic performance. To our knowledge, this is the first report of a compositionally complex hybrid material that is able to enhance performance when formed both in situ or ex situ and the use of In2S3 as a scaffold for a support material for enhancing OER performance.

item.title: JACS: Magneto-Optical Studies on the Orbital Angular Momenta and Spin–Orbit Coupling in the Excited Triplet States of Octahedral Mo6 Clusters: Magnetic Circular Dichroism and Magnetic Circularly Polarized Luminescence
item.description:
Hirohisa Yanagikawa, Toranosuke Tomikawa, Yuichi Kitagawa, Yasuchika Hasegawa, Kaplan Kirakci, Kamil Lang, Kazuyuki Ishii
The magneto-optical properties─magnetic circular dichroism (MCD) and magnetic circularly polarized luminescence (MCPL)─of octahedral hexanuclear [Mo6I8Y6]2– clusters (1, 2, and 3, possessing OPOPh2, N3, and CF3COO as the terminal Y ligands, respectively) were studied. In their MCD spectra, negative Faraday A terms corresponding to the S0 → Sn transitions were observed at ∼400 nm, reflecting the orbital angular momentum (OAM) and high symmetry of the molecular orbitals (MOs). In their highly concentrated solutions, positive Faraday A terms corresponding to the spin-forbidden S0 → Tn transitions were observed at ∼600 nm due to large spin–orbit coupling (SOC). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first direct observation of the spin-forbidden S0 → Tn transition in metal clusters by MCD. In their MCPL spectra, negative, strong phosphorescent MCPL signals (g ≈ 1.0 × 10–2 at 1.6 T) were observed at ∼690 nm, indicating that these Mo clusters are promising candidates for novel CPL materials. Time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) calculations performed for the model cluster [Mo6I8Cl6]2– could reproduce UV–vis absorption and MCD spectroscopic properties. Especially, the MCD signals were evaluated by analyzing the SOC and the Zeeman effects of the OAM and spin angular momentum in the excited triplet state. TD-DFT gradient calculations indicated the geometrical distortion and stabilization of the lowest excited triplet [Mo6I8Cl6]2– and the destabilization of its Franck–Condon ground state, which explain the large red shift of phosphorescence. These results open new possibilities for understanding and functionalizing metal clusters.

item.title: JACS: Enantioselective Three-Component Reductive Coupling of Aldehydes, Amines, and Alkynes via Ligand-Enabled Cobalt/Photoredox Dual Catalysis for Modular Synthesis of Allylic Amines
item.description:
Hengrui Zhou, Fang Zhang, Yongxian Huang, Daping Jin, He Huang, Genglin Wu, Linna Guo, Cheng-Yong Su, et al.
Here, we disclose a catalytic strategy that merges visible-light photoredox with cobalt catalysis to realize a previously elusive three-component enantioselective reductive coupling of readily available aldehydes, amines, and alkynes. This transformation provides a direct, step-economical route to high-value chiral allylic amines with broad substrate scope and high chemo-, regio-, and enantioselectivity, while overcoming long-standing challenges, including parasitic single-electron over-reduction, competitive aldehyde–alkyne coupling, and the inherent regioselectivity issues of unsymmetrical internal alkynes, and circumventing the moisture sensitivity and limited scope of pre-isolated imines. Central to this breakthrough is the rational design of a chiral phosphoramidite ligand featuring a tricyclic tetrahydrobenzoquinoline core, which avoids coordination saturation at cobalt and establishes a unique electronic “push–pull” synergy with a coordinated iodide anion. Mechanistic studies support an anion-promoted, single-ligand catalytic model wherein a high-spin cobaltacyclopentene intermediate serves as the key stereocontrol element. The monodentate, π-accepting phosphoramidite functions as a flexible electronic buffer, mitigating Pauli repulsion and dramatically lowering the oxidative cyclization barrier. The synthetic utility is demonstrated by late-stage functionalization of complex bioactive molecules and a concise synthesis of the antiplatelet drug prasugrel.

item.title: Nano Letters: Measurement of Parity-Dependent Energy-Phase Relations in a Potential Artificial Kitaev Chain Utilizing a Transmon Qubit
item.description:
Enna Zhuo, Xiaozhou Yang, Yuyang Huang, Zhaozheng Lyu, Ang Li, Bing Li, Yunxiao Zhang, Xiang Wang, et al.
Artificial Kitaev chains have emerged as a promising platform for realizing topological quantum computing. Once the chains are formed and Majorana zero modes are braided/fused, reading out the parity of the chains is essential for verifying the non-Abelian property of Majorana zero modes. Here, we demonstrate a transmon-based microwave probe for a four-site quantum dot–superconductor chain based on a Ge/Si nanowire. One end of the chain is incorporated into a superconducting transmon circuit, enabling spectroscopic identification of the chain’s singlet/doublet ground state and thereby inference of its total Fermion parity. We also demonstrate that, for multiple-dot chains, there are two types of 0−π transitions between different charging states: the parity-flip 0−π transition and the parity-preserved 0−π transition. Furthermore, we demonstrate electrostatic tunability of the interdot coupling. This phase-sensitive microwave platform provides a tool for studying complex hybrid superconducting quantum dot systems and for future extended artificial Kitaev chains.

item.title: ACS Nano: Full-Length Protein Classification through Sequence Reading by Solid-State Subnanopores
item.description:
Bin Meng, Ziyan Zhang, Jindong Li, Yong Xie, Yilong He, Kexin Meng, Chenxi Li, Shuaijian Dai, et al.
Nanopore sequencing for full-length proteins is daunting due to inaccuracy of fingerprinting amino acids with ionic current and lack of theoretical models. Here, we demonstrate that nanopores drilled in 5 nm-thick membranes with constriction diameter <1 nm, i.e., subnanopores, can site-specifically read the primary structure of amyloid-β (Aβ) isoforms after 50-fold coverage. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that charged side chains near the constriction swing and modulate the volume exclusion of neighboring residues, resulting in a sequence context-dependent signal altered between translocation orientations. Orientation of individual label-free molecules is inferred by clustering, which yields high-fidelity empirical consensus that strongly correlates with computational trajectories (PCC = 0.78 ± 0.03). A homemade self-supervised learning method categorizes Aβ42 and Aβ40 at the single-molecule level (AUC = 0.88 ± 0.02) and predicts the mole fraction in agreement with actual ratios. Solid-state subnanopores offer a straightforward strategy for proteoform single-molecule classification and sequence extraction in mixtures.

item.title: JACS: Mechanism-Guided Development of Thioacetylene Probes for Chemoproteomic Profiling of Cellular Protein Thiyl Radicals
item.description:
Seungmin Ahn, Jung-Min Kee
Protein thiyl radicals are transient reactive intermediates involved in oxidative stress and enzymatic catalysis. However, their proteome-wide, site-resolved profiling in living cells remains challenging due to the lack of suitable tools. Here, we report chemoproteomic probes enabling covalent capture and site-resolved identification of protein thiyl radicals in living cells. Designed to leverage sulfur-mediated stabilization of a vinyl radical intermediate, our thioacetylene-based probes selectively capture cysteine thiyl radicals while minimizing cross-reactivity with nucleophilic thiolates and nonradical amino acid residues. In vitro validation and live-cell chemoproteomic analysis established radical-dependent labeling and site-resolved detection of protein thiyl radicals. Notably, the probes enabled site-specific mapping of thiyl radical-associated cysteine residues in live E. coli, including Cys439 of ribonucleotide reductase A (NrdA), a canonical enzymatic thiyl radical site. Expanded residue profiling further confirmed cysteine-predominant labeling and detected probe modification at established and putative glycyl radical residues in PflB, NrdD, and YjjI, suggesting that the platform may extend beyond thiyl radicals to other protein-centered radicals. Application of the probe under oxidative and nitrosative stress revealed condition-dependent changes in cellular protein radical-associated labeling, including decreased labeling at established glycyl radical residues and bidirectional changes in cysteine radical-associated labeling. Together, these findings establish thioacetylene probes as a platform for site-resolved mapping and comparative monitoring of endogenous protein-centered radicals in living cells.

item.title: JACS: Evolution of Interfacial States Induced by Hydronium–Water Ordering on Au(111)
item.description:
Zhengcong Yan, Xia Sun, Yichen Qiu, Ziyang Guo, Xiaochuan Ma, Tongzheng Ji, Xuefeng Cui, Jin Zhao, et al.
Structured interfacial water can substantially modify charge transfer at solid–liquid interfaces, yet direct spectroscopic evidence for how water ordering reshapes interfacial electronic states remains scarce. Herein, using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), we identify parabolic interfacial states (IFSs) arising with the ordered water structures on Au(111), in striking contrast to the insulating nature of disordered water multilayers. Light exposure induces partial dissociation of H2O, and the resulting hydrated protons combine with residual H2O molecules to form ordered Eigen/Zundel-type hexagonal hydronium-water monolayers on Au(111) at 120–140 K. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations based on Eigen/Zundel-type motifs reproduce the experimentally observed IFSs and indicate that the states derive from the renormalized Au(111) Shockley surface state with a reduced effective mass at the water/gold interface. Annealing-driven transition from the Eigen-type to Zundel-type monolayers is evidenced by the distinct changes in the dispersions of the IFSs. These results establish a band-structure perspective for ordered water/metal interfaces and show that hydrated-proton-introduced excess electrons, when confined at a two-dimensional interface, can reshape the interfacial electronic landscape and charge transport.

item.title: JACS: Effect of Water on Elementary Reactions in Solid-Acid Catalyzed Reactions: Thermodynamics of Acid–Base Interactions in H-ZSM-5
item.description:
Yanyu Mu, Jeonghwan Lee, William A. Elliott, Robert M. Rioux
The influence of water on acid–base interactions in zeolites was quantified by measuring the enthalpy of pyridine adsorption on H-ZSM-5 with three Si/Al ratios (11.5, 40, and 140) in water using isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC). This calorimetric study reconciles the liquid- and gas-phase energetics of acid–base interactions in a solvated, pore-filled zeolite through a Born–Haber cycle analysis. In water, the apparent adsorption enthalpy is about 150 kJ/mol less exothermic than the gas-phase value and becomes more exothermic as the Si/Al ratio increases, whereas the gas-phase enthalpy is near −200 kJ/mol and independent of the Si/Al ratio. Since the intrinsic acid strength of the framework does not vary with Si/Al ratio, this increasing apparent adsorption energy trend with increasing Si/Al ratio reflects the influence of solvation rather than acidity. Water stabilizes both the acidic proton and the pyridinium ion, and a fraction of this stabilization is lost when adsorbed pyridine displaces water from the acid site. By combining ITC data with vapor-phase water adsorption isotherms and differential scanning calorimetry to construct a Born–Haber cycle for each zeolite, the aqueous-phase enthalpies are quantitatively reconciled with their gas-phase counterparts, and their dependence on Si/Al ratio is traced to the different extents to which the initial and final states are solvated.

item.title: Nano Letters: Ultralow Electron Temperature Plasma for Damage-Reduced Processing of High-k/Metal Gate Films toward Vertically Stacked Nanosheet Devices
item.description:
Hyung-dong Kim, Hyeonho Nahm, Seokhyeon Ha, Youngdon Kim, Min-seok Kim, Chin-Wook Chung
In vertically stacked nanosheet devices, repeated plasma-processing steps are required to realize multiple threshold voltages (Vth), but such repeated exposure can accumulate plasma-induced damage (PID) in ultrathin high-k/metal gate (HKMG) stacks. Here, we demonstrate that ultralow electron temperature (ULET, Te < 1 eV) plasma generated using a DC-biased grid suppresses PID by controlling the electron temperature and ion energy distribution function (IEDF). Compared with conventional inductively coupled plasma processing at the same substrate bias (−100 V), ULET plasma reduces the mean ion energy from 131 to 101 eV and reduces the IEDF standard deviation by 44% (from 37.4 to 20.9 eV). Consequently, surface roughness decreases by up to 58%, fluorine incorporation decreases by up to 58%, and HfO2 Raman-band intensities are 1.32–1.81 times those under conventional ICP processing. These results establish electron-temperature control as a key parameter for minimizing PID in HKMG films relevant to vertically stacked nanosheet devices.

item.title: JACS: Electronic Dynamics in Long Linear and Cyclic Polyynes
item.description:
Soumyadip Bhunia, Yueze Gao, Jack Woolley, Ross Milverton, Harry L. Anderson, Raj Pandya
Carbyne─the one-dimensional sp-hybridized allotrope of carbon─has long been predicted to exhibit unique properties, yet its synthesis remains elusive. To probe its behavior, finite sp-carbon chains such as cumulenes and polyynes have been studied. While much has been established about the ground-state properties of cumulenes and polyynes, our understanding of their photophysical dynamics, which gives critical insight into how electronic relaxation, structural reorganization, and spin formation evolve, has focused almost exclusively on short, linear systems, with little consideration of topology. Here, we investigate long 48-carbon linear and cyclic polyynes in the liquid phase using steady-state and ultrafast, temperature- and polarization-resolved optical and vibrational spectroscopy. We find highly delocalized ground states in both topologies, with softened Peierls distortion and reduced bond-length alternation relative to shorter chains. In contrast, the excited state singlet dipole depolarization mechanism and subsequent intersystem crossing are strongly dependent on chain length and topology. As in shorter polyynes, transient infrared spectroscopy shows that photoexcitation of long linear polyynes induces a cumulene-like excited-state geometry; however, this structural rearrangement is weaker and shorter-lived than in shorter analogues. Comparison with shorter-chain trends and theoretical predictions shows that the Huang–Rhys factor remains far below the ideal infinite-chain value at 48 carbons, suggesting that vibronic coupling grows more slowly at long chain length than expected from simple extrapolation. Our results reveal how topology influences the largely backbone-dominated electronic dynamics of long polyynes and refine our understanding of finite sp-carbon systems at longer chain lengths than previously accessible with such time-resolved methods.

item.title: JACS: Dynamic Nonlinear Effects in the Asymmetric Kinetic Resolution Polymerization of Racemic Diazoacetates to One-Handed Helical Polycarbenes
item.description:
Xun-Hui Xu, Shu-Ming Kang, Jiaqi Yu, Jie Zhang, Xinhua Wan
The asymmetric kinetic resolution polymerization (AKRP) of racemic diazoacetates mediated by a [Rh(cod)Cl]2/chiral amine dual catalyst system exhibits dynamic nonlinear effects (DNLEs) in the relative rate constant (Krel). The overall Krel increases nonlinearly with the monomer conversion during polymer chain propagation and reaches a plateau at a medium conversion. These DNLEs originate from synergistic chirality amplification between the catalytic chain end and the evolving helical conformation of the growing polymer chain. Under optimized conditions, Krel increases from 15 at 3% monomer conversion to ∼ 138 at 33% conversion, and then reaches a plateau. The steric bulk of both the pendant groups of monomers and the chiral amine ligand critically regulates the magnitude and evolution of DNLEs, and reducing this bulk leads to a pronounced decrease in Krel. Chain extension experiments using the preformed helical macroinitiators exhibited a constant Krel, confirming that a well-formed helical conformation maintains stable enantioselectivity for AKRP. Computational studies further revealed that, during chain propagation, decameric species with well-developed helical conformations exhibit more pronounced energy differences between the R- and S-enantiomers than the corresponding initial monomer-inserted species. These results suggest that the one-handed helical conformation is associated with the enhanced enantiomer recognition at the catalytic center. This study reveals DNLEs in AKRP in which enantioselectivity evolves nonlinearly during polymer chain propagation, highlighting a dynamic chiral amplification mechanism that can surpass the intrinsic selectivity of a static catalyst through the cooperative action of chiral chain ends and helical conformation.

item.title: ACS Nano: Deciphering Charge Delocalization across Mercaptobenzonitrile Ligand Terminals and Inner Hydrides in Atomically Precise Cu14H10 Nanoclusters for Electrocatalytic CO2 Reduction
item.description:
Anik Sarkar, Sarah Elhajj, Zhicheng Yang, Manju P. Maman, Zhenming Du, Ryan T. VanderLinden, Guoxiang Hu, Tianquan Lian, et al.
Cu hydride nanoclusters with atomic precision in composition and structure offer exciting catalytic activities and opportunities for rigorous structure–function correlations. Determination of their atomic structures, especially the hydride locations, hinges on the availability of high-quality single crystals and neutron beams, while their relatively weak UV–visible absorption and electrochemical instability challenge the analysis of their electronic properties. Herein, we synthesize a Cu14H10 nanocluster coordinated by three 4-mercaptobenzonitrile (MBN) and eight triphenylphosphine ligands. Two-dimensional NMR analyses combined with single crystal X-ray diffraction reveal unequivocally the locations of the ten hydrides in four groups (stoichiometry ratio of 1:3:3:3) with drastically different environments (chemical shifts 11–3 ppm): one H at the inversion center and three triangular layers along the C3 axial bridging together the Cu core. MBN serves two additional purposes besides stabilizing ligands: its electron-withdrawing nature and a highly sensitive vibrational reporter of its local charge density. The first property gives rise to a low-lying Cu-core-to-MBN metal-to-ligand charge transfer (MLCT) excited state, and the second property enables direct spectroscopic probing of both the charge transfer nature and dynamics of the MLCT excited state through the dynamic spectral shift of the MBN CN stretching mode. Through combined transient IR absorption spectroscopy and time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) calculations, we obtained the complete atomic and electronic structure, revealing core-to-ligand charge transfers in these nanoclusters. Computed under identical conditions using an iso-structure with a mildly electron-donating ligand, the Cu14H10 featuring charge delocalization toward the electron-withdrawing MBN has a smaller HOMO–LUMO gap, which is deemed favorable for electrocatalytic CO2 reduction. The preferential formation of complex multielectron-hydrogenation products (8–12 e–, C1 hydrocarbons, and C2+ products) over two-electron pathways such as CO formation or the competing hydrogen evolution reaction highlights their promise as atomically precise catalysts for deep CO2 reduction.

item.title: ACS Nano: Tunable Gaussian Random Number Generator from a Nanoscopic Domain-Wall-Based Spintronic Device
item.description:
Simon Arnold, Yung-Cheng Li, Renata Lei, Lukas Fischer, Andrea Migliorini, Jiho Yoon, Kerem Y. Çamsarı, Jae-Chun Jeon, et al.
Existing hardware implementations of Gaussian random number generators (RNGs) rely on large arrays of binary devices, resulting in substantial hardware footprints or sampling-time overheads. Here, we present a racetrack memory-based random number generator (RTM-RNG) that directly generates analog Gaussian random number streams from a single domain-wall-based nanoscale racetrack. A geometrically engineered racetrack tip creates a localized current-density gradient, enabling field-free stochastic domain-wall nucleation driven by nanosecond current pulses. The domain-wall nucleation probability is continuously tunable via an electrically generated Oersted field or an external magnetic field, providing direct control over the mean of the output distribution. We demonstrate more than 256 distinguishable states from a single nanoscopic RTM-RNG device, thus making a Gaussian RNG with more than 8-bit resolution possible. Compared with conventional binary random bitstreams, the RTM-RNG achieves high-quality Gaussian distributions up to 83 times faster.

item.title: JACS: Zeolite-Confined Triatomic Cu Oxides at Silanol Nests as Hydrogen Transport Channels for H2 Production from Methanol Steam Reforming
item.description:
Yongbin Yao, Maoshuai Jiang, Fan Wang, Ligang Zhang, Rudong Liu, Shihao Wang, Kuo Liu, Tao Zhang
Cu-based catalysts offer high methanol steam reforming (MSR) activity but are limited by unstable Cu+–Cu0 interconversions due to the redox and sintering labilities of Cu. Herein, we developed a universal amino-functionalized “gripper” strategy for firmly and precisely anchoring atomically dispersed metals (e.g., Cu, Co, Ni) within Beta-zeolite. Triatomic Cu oxide (Cu3Ox) sites lower the methanol dehydrogenation activation barrier, and the synergistic interplay with adjacent OH groups from silanol nests accelerates H2 evolution and the MSR reaction. Spatially decoupling Cu-mediated methanol activation from silanol-driven H2 evolution at silanol nests as proton transport channels within the confining zeolite framework also effectively protected Cu from sintering, achieving a high specific activity of 951 molH2·molCu–1·h–1 and over 600 h of stability under continuous regeneration. This work provides a universal strategy for synthesizing atomically dispersed metal catalysts and a new design principle for maintaining the Cu structure during MSR.

item.title: Nano Letters: Single-Twinned Seed-Mediated Synthesis of Au Right Bipyramids for Uniform Near-Field Focusing
item.description:
Hao Zhang, Chenyang Luo, Yu Lan, Bin Dong, Xiang Lin, Shunping Zhang, Hongxing Xu
Noble metal nanoparticles with sharp edges and corners, such as triangles, tetrahedrons, bipyramids, etc., support superior plasmonic field enhancement for enhanced spectroscopy. However, high-yield synthesis of gold right bipyramids (Au RBPs) with sharp tips has remained limited because they have a single-twinned (ST) crystal structure whose growth pathway is hard to control. Here, we report the seed-mediated growth of Au RBPs using ST seeds, achieving a yield exceeding 70% by moderately increasing the size of these seeds. Au RBPs with sizes from 34 to 94 nm and controlled corner sharpness are achieved through the regulation of seed and bromide amounts. Uniform and strong near-field enhancement is generated in the Au RBPs-on-mirror configuration, which outperforms the well-established nanocube-on-mirror configuration in Raman enhancement. This work highlights the merits of ST seed-mediated growth for anisotropic nanocrystals and their potentials in plasmonic near-field focusing.

item.title: JACS: Design and Evolution of an Orthogonal HaloTag for Multiplexed Labeling in Cells
item.description:
Benjamin J. Goldberg, Bryan J. Lampkin, Alexander T. Stead, Siena L. Stanten, Patrick Rabe, Joshua A. Kritzer
The self-labeling protein HaloTag is used to install a wide variety of functional small molecules in cells and living organisms with exquisite specificity with respect to cell type and subcellular localization. HaloTag is a core part of many biotechnology-based tools for sensing, tracking, and manipulating biological systems with a high degree of spatial and temporal control. Due to the limitations of fluorescent proteins and other self-labeling proteins, most of these tools have historically been restricted to a single channel. In this work, we used structure-guided rational design and directed evolution to produce an orthogonal HaloTag protein called OrthoTag which reacts selectively with a modified chloroalkane substrate. OrthoTag retains many of HaloTag’s superior properties, and reaction rate measurements with purified proteins show OrthoTag and its substrate have 109-fold mutual orthogonality to HaloTag with respect to substrate concentration. We demonstrate the application of OrthoTag for multiplexed labeling experiments in mammalian cells with minimal optimization. Going forward, OrthoTag should be straightforward to incorporate into HaloTag-based systems to allow simultaneous measurement or manipulation of two biological targets or processes. The availability of multiple high-performance self-labeling proteins will enable the continued development of new multiplexed biotechnology methods.

item.title: Nano Letters: Gold Nanoclusters with Wavelike Chiral Lattices Interact with Outer Membrane Protein BamA to Kill Gram-Negative Bacteria through the Screw-in Effect
item.description:
Jinghua Hao, Chuyan Zhao, Bingjie Zhi, Xun Wang, Zhigang Li, Nali Zhu, Lingxiangyu Li, Yawei Wang, et al.
Resistance threatens to render antibiotics ineffective, which is posing a threat to global public health. Innovative strategies against drug-resistant bacteria are urgent. The outer membrane protein BamA, a hollow barrel with a pore of 2–4 nm, is a unique and essential structure in Gram-negative bacteria. We prepared chiral 3 nm gold nanoclusters (AuNCs) targeting BamA, exhibiting enantiomer-dependent antibacterial activity against drug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The AuNCs with right-handed wavelike lattices (D-AuNCs) preferentially interacted with BamA through the screw-in effect, creating pores in the cell wall and resulting in bacterial death. P. aeruginosa was still susceptible to D-AuNCs due to their excellent antibiofilm activity even after 20 successive passages. D-AuNCs were applied to P. aeruginosa-infected skin wounds in mice, achieving superior wound healing compared to levofloxacin. Our work documented that chiral nanoclusters targeting BamA can efficiently kill P. aeruginosa through the screw-in effect, providing an innovative strategy to combat Gram-negative bacteria.

item.title: Nano Letters: Optical Resonance Tuning of Single Polystyrene Microspheres Using the Phase-Change Material In3SbTe2 as a Switchable Mirror
item.description:
Rebecca Rahmel, Hristiyana Kyoseva, Lukas Conrads, Matthias Wuttig, Gero von Plessen, Thomas Taubner
Dielectric nanoparticles and microparticles show rich optical responses due to their electric and magnetic multipolar Mie modes and low losses. These optical resonances can be modified via the particle size, shape, and dielectric environment. Here we tune the infrared multipolar Mie resonances of dielectric polystyrene microspheres using the plasmonic phase-change material In3SbTe2 (IST). IST exhibits a phase change between a dielectric amorphous phase and a crystalline phase that is metallic in the infrared. We show that a reversibly switchable particle-on-mirror geometry can be created by locally switching the IST under the polystyrene microspheres. Measuring the light-scattering spectra of single polystyrene microspheres before and after crystallization and reamorphization, we observe huge shifts of the resonance wavelength, e.g., from 5.2 to 8.9 μm and back for 6 μm diameter spheres. Our work is a first step toward a controlled tuning of multipolar Mie modes of various particles using reprogrammable IST mirror structures.

item.title: ACS Nano: Addressable Control of Hybrid Spin Qubit in Single-Atom Copper-Modified Fullerene
item.description:
Bingcai Chen, Jiahao Chen, Pengxiang Fu, Di Zhang, Hao Li, Jiayue Yuan, Jianyu Liu, Dahui Zhao, et al.
Developing high-dimensional solid-state quantum technologies requires overcoming the trade-off between spin dimensionality and quantum coherence. Hybrid spin architectures offer a promising solution to expand the quantum state space bottom-up by combining rapid electronic manipulation with robust nuclear phase memory. However, solid-state hybrid spin materials capable of simultaneously supporting both electron and nuclear spin manipulations remain exceedingly rare. Here, we report a Cu2+ (S = 1/2, I = 3/2) hybrid spin system dispersed in a magnetically silent C60 matrix, in which we not only demonstrate comprehensive coherent control over both electron and nuclear spin degrees of freedom but also strike a balance between spin dimensionality and coherence time. The pristine carbon environment suppresses surrounding magnetic noise, acting in tandem with dynamical decoupling to prolong the electron spin coherence time to 16.16 μs. Simultaneously, the nuclear quadrupole interaction of Cu2+ breaks the degeneracy of the nuclear spin manifold, enabling precise addressability of an eight-dimensional Hilbert space. Furthermore, strong electron–nuclear hyperfine coupling acts as a powerful lever, accelerating the nuclear spin Rabi frequency by a factor of 17. By achieving the coexistence of a large manifold of addressable levels and long-lived quantum coherence, Cu/C60 provides a high-dimensional hybrid spin node and a compelling bottom-up approach to expanding the quantum state space.

item.title: JACS: Efficient Long-Wavelength Through-Space Charge-Transfer Thermally Activated Delayed Fluorescence in Conformationally Adaptive Emitters without Conformational Locking
item.description:
Nae Aota, Jaijanarthanan Lingagouder, Nuno Gandum, Leonardo Evaristo de Sousa, Lucy A. Weatherill, Marc K. Etherington, Norimitsu Tohnai, Satoshi Minakata, et al.
Through-space charge-transfer thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TSCT-TADF) emitters often employ conformationally constrained donor–acceptor architectures to control through-space electronic coupling, particularly for long-wavelength emission. Here, we report conformationally adaptive orange-to-red TSCT-TADF emitters based on an S-shaped donor−π–acceptor−π–donor framework composed of phenoxazine donors, xanthene linkers, and a dibenzo[a,j]phenazine acceptor. Structural and NMR analyses reveal substantial conformational mobility, while systematic conformational searches and excited-state calculations identify thermally accessible conformers with distinct donor–acceptor geometries and excited-state characteristics. Comparative studies with reference compounds and fragment-resolved transition-density analysis show that the xanthene linker primarily acts as a conformational regulator and that the low-energy CT states have predominant TSCT character with only minor linker involvement. Temperature-dependent early-time photoluminescence measurements reveal continuous spectral relaxation in fluid toluene that slows upon cooling and is absent in rigid Zeonex and mCBP hosts, providing strong evidence for structural relaxation following photoexcitation within a pre-existing conformational ensemble. The emitters exhibit orange-to-red TADF with reverse intersystem crossing rates on the order of 105–106 s–1. Organic light-emitting diodes employing these emitters show electroluminescence at 598–624 nm, external quantum efficiencies up to 14.9%, and limited efficiency roll-off over a broad luminance range. These results demonstrate that efficient long-wavelength TSCT-TADF can be realized without permanent conformational locking and establish a framework for understanding the interplay between ground-state conformational heterogeneity and excited-state structural relaxation.

item.title: ACS Nano: Data-Driven Atomic Interplay Modulation Enables Dual-Functional High-Entropy Alloy Mediator for Li–S Batteries
item.description:
Jianshuang Wei, Xin Guo, Jingkun Wu, Xia Li, Miaoyu Lu, Yunfeng Zhang, Yao Tang, Yiming Shi, et al.
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have emerged as appealing candidates to achieve performance regulation in Li–S batteries. Nevertheless, the design principles and working mechanisms of HEAs for dual electrodes remain elusive because of their structural disorder and chemical complexity. Herein, we propose a data-driven maneuver to enable rapid and precise screening of a customized HEA nanocatalyst (FeCoNiCuVMn, 6E-HEAs) via a performance-oriented theoretical criterion in the realm of Li–S electrochemistry. The delicate modulation of atomic interplay in 6E-HEAs simultaneously accelerates sulfur redox kinetics and stabilizes lithium metal deposition. Consequently, Li–S batteries sustain favorable cycling performance at 1.0 C over 1000 cycles while affording a capacity decay rate of merely 0.067% per cycle. The pouch cell harvests a specific capacity of 884.8 mAh g–1 at 0.5 C with steady cyclic operation. Our study elucidates crucial roles of effective compositional gain in boosting bidirectional Li–S electrocatalysis, offering atomic-level insights into HEA design for electrocatalytic reactions.

item.title: ACS Nano: Biomimetic Nanozyme-Decoys Reprogram Immune Niches to Intercept Colitis-Carcinoma Transition
item.description:
Qi Sun, Wanling Liu, Sijie Li, Xiwen Chen, Hanjie Zhang, Dongze Mo, Pinwen Zhou, Xiaomiao Cui, et al.
Colitis-associated colorectal cancer (CAC) arises from chronic inflammatory niches characterized by persistent oxidative stress and dysregulated immune cell recruitment. Current anti-inflammatory therapies provide only transient symptom relief and fail to prevent malignant progression due to their inability to simultaneously mitigate oxidative injury and immune chemotaxis. Our analysis of clinical samples revealed markedly elevated C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 2 (CXCL2) in intestinal tissues from patients with inflammatory bowel disease and CAC, implicating the CXCL2-CXCR2 (C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 2) axis in driving excessive neutrophil and macrophage infiltration and fostering tumorigenesis. Herein, we report a biomimetic nanozyme (PB@ECM) that reprograms inflammatory immune niches to intercept CAC progression. PB@ECM integrates a Prussian blue nanozyme core with genetically engineered macrophage membranes, enabling concurrent scavenging of reactive oxygen species through superoxide dismutase- and catalase-like activities and sequestration of CXCL2 via membrane-displayed CXCR2 receptors. In murine models of colitis and CAC, PB@ECM significantly alleviated intestinal inflammation, suppressed neutrophil and macrophage infiltration, and effectively inhibited colitis-carcinoma transition. Notably, treatment with PB@ECM significantly prolonged survival compared with other groups. By disrupting the pathological crosstalk between oxidative stress and immune chemotaxis, this work establishes a biomimetic nanozyme strategy for preventing inflammation-driven carcinogenesis.

item.title: Nano Letters: Tungsten–Carbon Nanohelix Arrays by Helium-Ion Direct Writing: Geometry-Dependent Circular-Polarization Response in the Visible
item.description:
Alba Arroyo-Fructuoso, Gianluca Balestra, Marco Esposito, René Hübner, Gregor Hlawacek, Rosa Córdoba
3D nanohelices provide a direct route to control light–matter interactions with circular polarization at the nanoscale. Here, we report periodic arrays of W–C nanohelices fabricated by He+ focused-ion-beam-induced deposition (FIBID), combining direct-write 3D growth with high spatial resolution and W-rich deposits (∼65 at. % W). Two arrays with the same lateral geometry were fabricated while varying only the vertical pitch, corresponding to helical ratios HR ≈ 1 and HR ≈ 2. Transmittance measurements under circularly polarized light reveal a clear geometry-dependent response. The compact nanohelices (HR ≈ 1) show a larger circular-polarization-dependent transmission contrast (g ≈ 0.17, θ ≈ 2.35°), moderate transmittance (∼30–50%), and a sign inversion near 600 nm. The larger-pitch helices (HR ≈ 2) show higher transmittance (∼35–100%) with a weaker but stable response (g ≈ 0.13, θ ≈ 1.60°). Qualitative simulations reproduce the main spectral trends and support distinct optical responses of the two pitch geometries.

item.title: JACS: Photoresponsive Mechanically Interlocked [ a n]Daisy Chain Network
item.description:
Guoquan Liu, Jingxi Deng, Jun Zhao, Ruixue Bai, Yongming Wang, Shaolei Qu, Yuanhao Wang, Zhiwei Fan, et al.
Muscle integrates molecular-machine motion with hierarchical structural organization, enabling it to sustain large deformations under physiological loads. Mechanically interlocked molecules offer a versatile platform to mimic such molecular-level motion, but efficiently translating it into macroscopic material performance, akin to muscle, remains challenging. Herein, we report a mechanically interlocked network (MIN) with [an]daisy chain backbone which can efficiently scale up the photoresponsive behavior of mechanical bonds, exhibiting intelligently tunable mechanical properties. In specific, photoresponsive unit of arylazopyrazole (AAP) is embedded onto the axis of each mechanical bond in the [an]daisy chain backbone. Ultraviolet light triggers the trans-to-cis (E/Z) isomerization of the AAP moieties, and when amplified through the [an]daisy chain backbone, it brings about significant changes in the material’s properties. On one hand, the E/Z isomerization significantly shortens the dimension of the [an]daisy chain framework, resulting in a notable increase in the material modulus (from 1.6 to 4.0 MPa). On the other hand, the cis configuration of AAP formed after the isomerization restricts the mobility of the mechanical bonds, resulting in a shorter elongation at break (from 343% to 272%). Our work presents an efficient method for amplifying mechanical bond responsiveness, providing a fresh perspective for the development of intelligent materials.

item.title: JACS: Tailoring Solid-State Reaction Pathways for Bulk Fluorination of Mn-Rich Rock-Salt Cathodes
item.description:
Venkata Sai Avvaru, Nathan J. Szymanski, Seonghun Jeong, Meredith Goudreau, Martin Kunz, Mateusz Zuba, Ozgenur Kahvecioglu, Noah Taebin Lee, et al.
Manganese-based cation-disordered rock-salt (DRX) cathodes offer high capacities without relying on cobalt and nickel, but maintaining that capacity over extended cycling often requires bulk fluorination. The challenge is that incorporating fluorine into Mn-rich DRX host structures is hindered by unfavorable thermodynamics and the stability of LiF, often necessitating elevated synthesis temperatures that promote severe lithium and fluorine volatilization. This study overcomes that limitation by manipulating the solid-state reaction pathway using unconventional Li6MnO4 and MnF2 precursors in a challenging Mn-rich model system (Li1.2Mn0.6Ti0.2O2–xFx). This precursor engineering strategy reshapes the thermodynamic landscape. Computational modeling and in situ X-ray diffraction reveal that by using reactive starting materials, we suppress the crystallization of less reactive intermediates, enabling bulk fluorination at a lower temperature. The resulting DRX retains both a high fluorine content and the lithium excess required for three-dimensional percolation, delivering improved electrochemical performance relative to material synthesized from conventional precursors.

item.title: ACS Nano: Overcoming Oral Environmental Barriers: Nanoengineering Strategies for Antimicrobial Peptides in Biofilm-Associated Oral Diseases
item.description:
Jingwen Wu, Yaqi Lin, Fangyuan Shuai, Yaxin Xie, Li Mei, Xianglong Han, Yijia Yin, Hui Xu
Biofilm-associated oral diseases impose a substantial global health burden and are closely linked to systemic inflammation. Although antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) offer a promising alternative to conventional antibiotics, their therapeutic efficacy in the oral cavity is limited by barriers in the oral environment. Free AMPs are rapidly removed by salivary flow, destabilized by local proteases, and impeded by substantial diffusion barriers within mature biofilms. Nanoengineering provides a systematic approach to address these limitations. In this review, we present a barrier-oriented framework for AMP delivery and examine how nanomaterial design addresses the specific constraints of the oral environment. Interfacial engineering prolongs local retention, spatial protection preserves AMP stability, and microenvironment-responsive systems provide on-demand activation for effective biofilm disruption. Alongside these approaches, multifunctional nanosystems combining antimicrobial, immunomodulatory, and regenerative activities are discussed. Finally, key translational challenges, including biosafety, microbiome homeostasis, manufacturing, and regulatory barriers, are critically examined. This review traces the development of AMP nanoengineering from passive delivery vehicles toward precision therapeutic platforms that respond dynamically to the oral microenvironment.

item.title: ACS Nano: Ultrafast High-Photogain UV–Vis-NIR Broadband Photodetection in Parallelly Overlapped Stacking Type-I GaSe/MoTe2 Heterostructure
item.description:
Vijay Laxmi, Yutao Hu, Pushpendra Yadav, Danting Lin, Deepika Tyagi, Yuting Sun, Claudia Draxl, Wenjing Zhang, et al.
Broadband photodetectors are important for next-generation optoelectronic applications, ranging from fundamental science, environmental monitoring, industrial detection to artificial-intelligence-enabled Internet of Things systems, where both high responsivity and fast response are critically demanded. Typically, a trade-off exists between the two in the photogating effect, making it challenging to achieve both simultaneously. This study reports a parallelly overlapped stacking GaSe/MoTe2 heterostructure with type-I band alignment (PSH-GM), which simultaneously realizes an ultrafast photoresponse of 523 ns and a high responsivity of 8.95 × 103 A·W–1, together with a noise equivalent power of ∼0.38 × 10–14 W·Hz–1/2 and a specific detectivity of 8.01 × 1011 Jones. Furthermore, PSH-GM exhibits a responsivity of up to 103 A·W–1 over a broad spectral range of 355–1100 nm, covering the ultraviolet (UV), visible (Vis), and near-infrared (NIR) regions. The underlying photodetection mechanism of the parallelly overlapped stacking type-I heterostructure is clarified using photocurrent mapping, and the origin of the dark current shift at different operation frequencies is elucidated, both of which offer insights into the design principles of two-dimensional heterostructures optimized to simultaneously achieve high responsivity and high response bandwidth. Imaging demonstrations are conducted at 355, 520, and 850 nm, and free-space optical communication is demonstrated at 115.2 kbit·s–1, which highlights the potential of PSH-GM for broadband UV–Vis–NIR photodetection, ultrafast data communication, high-speed imaging, and integration into advanced optoelectronic systems.

item.title: JACS: Multiphase Inorganic-Rich Interphases with Integrated Li-Ion Capture-Transport Ability for High-Rate Lithium Metal Batteries
item.description:
Likun Chen, Tian Gu, Zhuo Han, Wenting Cui, Jinshuo Mi, Xufei An, Ke Yang, Jiabin Ma, et al.
Lithium metal batteries promise high-energy-density storage but are limited by unstable solid–electrolyte interphases, which couple poor passivation, sluggish Li+ transport, dendritic deposition, and safety risks. Herein, we report a multiphase inorganic-rich solid–electrolyte interphase (m-SEI) containing P- and Al-derived species including Li3P, LiAl5O8, Li3PO4, and Li2Al, which is formed from the in situ reaction between a flame-retardant aluminum diethyl hypophosphite (ADP) interlayer and lithium metal. This multicomponent inorganic SEI enables an integrated capture-transport mechanism by combining high Li+ affinity, facilitated desolvation, and low-barrier Li+ migration pathways in individual inorganic phases and their heterophase interfaces, thereby facilitating rapid Li+ interfacial migration. Its chemical inertness and high Young’s modulus of 17.14 GPa further suppress electrolyte decomposition and Li dendrite growth. As a result, the Li-metal batteries with m-SEI deliver an extended lifespan of 1000 h at a high current density of 4 mA cm–2. Li||NCM811 full cells with a high cathode loading (20 mg cm–2) and ultrathin Li foil (50 μm) retain 80% capacity after 250 cycles, while Li||NCM811 pouch cells retain 90% capacity after 500 cycles. This work establishes the capture-transport mechanism as an effective design principle for regulating Li+ interfacial dynamics and offers a practical interphase-engineering strategy for constructing ion-conductive and chemically protective interphases in durable lithium metal batteries.

item.title: JACS: Hydration-Dependent Working-Surface Chemistry in Photocatalytic Methane Coupling
item.description:
Feiyan Xu, Weiyuan Luo, Wantian Mei, Jianjun Zhang, Chuanbiao Bie, Hermenegildo García, Xusheng Zheng, Jiaguo Yu
Selective photocatalytic methane coupling requires directing methane-derived intermediates toward C–C bond formation while limiting their oxidation to CO2, yet how the reaction environment controls this competition through surface chemistry remains unclear. Water is ubiquitous in photocatalytic methane conversion, but its influence is commonly interpreted through specific chemical functions rather than through its broader effects on working-surface chemistry. Here, Au/ZnO is used as a compositionally defined, coupling-competent model catalyst to reveal how hydration regulates carbon transformation pathways by reshaping the working-surface chemistry. Systematic variation of water availability reveals three hydration-dependent catalytic regimes with markedly different product distributions. Moderate hydration increases the ethane production rate from 1590 to 8407 μmol g–1 h–1 and enables ethylene formation, whereas excessive hydration increases CO2 production and lowers C2 selectivity. In situ spectroscopies show that these catalytic regimes are accompanied by hydration-dependent changes in methane adsorption, methane-derived and coupling-related surface intermediates, and oxygen-deficient surface states within a reaction network involving both carbon- and oxygen-centered radical chemistry. Moderate hydration establishes surface conditions that favor C–C coupling and C2 hydrocarbon accumulation, whereas excessive hydration favors oxidized surface species and carbonate formation. These results identify hydration as a key determinant of the steady-state surface chemistry governing carbon partitioning between C–C coupling and oxidation during photocatalytic methane conversion.

item.title: ACS Nano: Bright Alkyl Quantum Defects Govern Early Carbon Nanotube Pharmacokinetics in Mice
item.description:
Han-Sheng Sun, Ai-Phuong Nguyen, Carlos Jose Quiroz Reyes, Ya Chen Li, Joshua M. Lim, Guan-Wan Liu, Rifqi Fajar Maulana, Ngoc-Khanh Tran, et al.
Fluorescent quantum defects in single-wall carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) are a major advance in nanocarbon research, owing to their bright, single-photon emission at telecom wavelengths and versatile conjugation chemistries for biomedical sensing and disease targeting. Here, we introduce an efficient, oxygen-free sonochemical route that generates long-chain alkyl defects, simultaneously shortening nanotubes and producing a bright, homogeneously emissive (6,5) SWCNT ensemble. Among 15 screened reactants, the branched-chain NiaproofⓇ 4, which molecular dynamics simulations show packs more densely and uniformly than linear surfactants, yields a 3.4-fold brightness enhancement and a sharp emission peak near 1108 nm. Single-particle spectroscopy reveals J-aggregate emission redshifts at high defect densities, and fibrinogen titration shows defect chemistry governs protein-driven coating displacement. Using a home-built short-wave infrared imaging system (25 mW cm–2, 989 nm excitation, 1150 nm long-pass collection), we show that these sparse defects (∼9–16 μm–1) drive different pharmacokinetics between NiaproofⓇ 4– and lipid-PEG–functionalized (6,5) at early time points, converging as protein-corona formation masks the underlying chemistry. Histology localizes the nanotubes within macrophages of mononuclear phagocyte system–associated organs. Intravenous administration (∼41 μg kg–1) causes no acute toxicity and a short ∼2-day retention. The NiaproofⓇ 4 group exhibits a reduced circulating myeloid-cell fraction following corona formation, which may reflect organ recruitment and sequestration, while the accompanying increase in CD3+ T cells may partly reflect a proportional shift in leukocyte composition.

item.title: JACS: Porphyrin-Driven Redox Tuning in Structurally Defined De Novo Heme Proteins
item.description:
Cameron Mellor, Christopher Williams, Ethan L. Bungay, Jessica C. Berrones-Reyes, Rob Barringer, Catherine R. Back, Paul Molinaro, Shakir A. Siddiqui, et al.
Designing redox proteins with predictable and tunable electron transfer properties is a major goal in de novo bioenergetics. Here we show that replacing heme B with a series of structurally conservative non-natural metalloporphyrins enables broad modulation of redox potentials over 400 mV in the de novo designed monoheme m4D2 and diheme 4D2 T19D. The non-natural porphyrins bind with high affinity and do not compromise either the heme binding site or global protein structure, as evidenced by X-ray crystallography and NMR spectroscopy. We also report the native-like NMR structure of m4D2 loaded with the non-natural and symmetric iron 2,4-dimethyldeuteroporphyrin IX, confirming our modular approach to tetrahelical redox protein design. This work establishes a versatile platform for constructing tunable electron carriers for engineered bioenergetic pathways and bioelectronic applications.

item.title: JACS: Dynamic Acidic Adsorbates Govern Fast Oxygen Incorporation in Ceria through Interfacial Electrostatics
item.description:
Francesco Chiabrera, Kosova Kreka, Federico Baiutti, Burcu Karagoz, Marlene Anzengruber, Juan Carlos González-Rosillo, Matthijs Van Spronsen, Albert Tarancón
The oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) is a key heterogeneous process underpinning energy conversion, catalytic, and sensing technologies. However, reported ORR kinetics at oxide surfaces often vary widely because surface chemistry evolves under operating conditions. Ceria-based fluorites have been proposed as protective layers to stabilize perovskite electrodes, but ORR kinetics are typically considered sluggish and reported values have large variability. Herein, we demonstrate that cathodic polarization triggers an unexpected activation in Gd-doped ceria (CGO) dense thin films at 500 °C, enabling oxygen incorporation rates that surpass state-of-the-art materials such as La0.5Sr0.5FeO3−δ and approach the performance of La0.6Sr0.4CoO3−δ. Operando near-ambient-pressure X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (NAP-XPS), supported by ex situ surface-sensitive tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (TERS), reveals that CGO surface activation coincides with a reversible, overpotential-dependent modulation of sulfate adsorbates. Integration of these measurements with nondilute space-charge modeling suggests that charged adsorbates dynamically tune the near-surface electrostatic potential and electron concentration, thereby controlling oxygen incorporation kinetics. These results support adsorbate-induced electrostatic effects as a key mechanism in ceria and show that ORR kinetics are dynamically set by surface chemistry under operation, rather than by intrinsic bulk defect chemistry alone.

item.title: ACS Nano: An Optoelectronic SnP2S6 Memristive Neuron for Biologically Inspired Multimodal Neuromorphic Information Processing
item.description:
Thaw Tint Te Tun, Jiali Huo, Kah-Wee Ang
Neuromorphic systems capable of integrating multiple sensory modalities offer a promising route toward energy-efficient information processing that more closely emulates biological neural networks. Here, we demonstrate a multifunctional ITO/SnP2S6/Ti memristive neuron that combines reproducible volatile resistive switching and integrate-and-fire dynamics under electrical-pulse stimulation with wavelength-selective photoresponses and short-term optoelectronic synaptic plasticity. Leveraging these experimentally measured device characteristics, we construct a multimodal neuromorphic recognition framework that integrates volatile memristive neurons with programmable memristive synapses. Inspired by the parallel processing of visual features in the primate visual system, structural and color information are independently encoded and processed through separate electrical and optical pathways before being integrated for classification. Importantly, inference is implemented using experimentally measured neuronal firing statistics and programmed synaptic conductance states, rather than idealized device models, thereby establishing a direct link between device characteristics and system-level functionality. As a proof-of-concept, the framework is evaluated on a fruit-recognition task using a subset of the Fruits-360 image data set, achieving a classification accuracy of 94.9% through multimodal fusion and substantially outperforming recognition based on either modality alone. These results establish SnP2S6 memristive devices as a versatile platform for integrating electrical and optical neuronal functionalities and highlight their potential for hardware-realistic multimodal in-sensor neuromorphic computing.

item.title: JACS: Synthesis and Crystal Structure of Bulk Methanetetrol C(OH)4
item.description:
Dominik Spahr, Lkhamsuren Bayarjargal, Lukas Brüning, Valentin Kovalev, Pascal L. Jurzick, Maxim Bykov, Victor Milman, Björn Winkler, et al.
Methanetetrol, C(OH)4 (orthocarbonic acid), is an elusive tethrahydroxymethane that, due to its rapid dissociation under ambient conditions, has never been synthesized in bulk. A recent study detected the formation of C(OH)4 molecules in the gas phase. Here, we show that C(OH)4 can be synthesized in a diamond anvil cell through the reaction between H2O and CO2 at 45(3) GPa and 50(3) GPa and temperatures <1200(200) K. The crystal structure of C(OH)4 was determined by single-crystal X-ray diffraction and corroborated by density-functional theory calculations together with Raman spectroscopy. It is composed of isolated [C(OH)4]-molecules linked by strong hydrogen bonds. Under high-pressure conditions, orthocarbonic and carbonic acids are denser than coexisting water ice phases, allowing them to segregate gravitationally and form stable reservoirs of oxidized carbon. These phases incorporate large amounts of carbon into their crystal structures as part of [CO4]4–- or [CO3]2–-building blocks. Because the amount of carbon that can be stored as CO2 in clathrates or filled-ices is significantly smaller, orthocarbonic and carbonic acids may provide a host mechanism for sequestering large carbon inventories in the icy mantles of water-rich exoplanets.

item.title: Nano Letters: Intrinsically Moiré-Patterned Two-Dimensional Polymorphic Networks for Modulated Charge Order and Proximity Superconductivity
item.description:
Yanhao Shi, Hui Chen, Qian Fang, Jingyi Duan, Zhongyi Cao, Yikai Chen, Haitao Yang, Wei Jiang, et al.
Moiré superlattices provide a versatile route to engineering correlated electronic and topological states in van der Waals heterostructures, yet their use to organize structural polymorphism and phase-selective charge, magnetic, and superconducting states within a single two-dimensional material remains elusive. Here, we report modulated charge order and proximity superconductivity in an intrinsically moiré-patterned 1T/1T′ polymorphic network of monolayer VTe2 grown epitaxially on superconducting NbSe2. Scanning tunneling microscopy/spectroscopy and first-principles calculations show that in situ annealing of twist-moiré VTe2/NbSe2 creates alternating 1T and 1T′ domains. The origin of the selective 1T-to-1T′ conversion is due to the moiré-induced anisotropic strain. This moiré-registered network hosts phase-specific short-range charge orders: 4 × 4 in 1T and 3 × 3 in 1T′. In the proximity-superconducting regime, spatially modulated in-gap bound states and suppressed coherence peaks reveal phase-dependent magnetic pair breaking. This work establishes intrinsically moiré-patterned polymorphism as a route to programmable two-dimensional quantum materials.

item.title: ACS Nano: Breaking the Capacity–Stability Trade-Off in High-Voltage LiCoO2 via Opposite Co/O Redox Activity
item.description:
Mengjie Zhang, Yulin Cao, Lingfeng Shi, Ruichen Zhu, Yehang Dou, Fangchang Zhang, Yanfang Wang, Ke Li, et al.
LiCoO2 (LCO) suffers from daunting capacity–stability trade-off due to deeper Co oxidation and ensuing O oxidation (O2– → Co4+ electron transfer) at high-voltage (≥4.5 V). Aggressive Co4+ and O2/On– (0 < n < 2) species result in pronounced mechanical/chemical failure and fast capacity decay. Most of the state-of-the-art solutions partially resolve these problems yet sacrificing capacity. Herein, facilitated Co3+/4+ redox and effectively restrained O redox are simultaneously achieved by amplifying Co t2g electron density of states (DOS) near the Fermi level while reducing O 2p electron DOS. Consequently, the engineered cathode harvests a remarkable initial capacity of 212.1 mAh g–1 at 4.6 V (vs 212.9 mAh g–1 of bare LCO). Moreover, advanced multiscale X-ray/electron spectroscopy and imaging techniques reveal that mitigated O redox prevents irreversible phase transitions, lattice O loss, and undesirable surface parasitic reactions. As a result, the cathode has reinforced electrochemical (capacity retention of 88.4% within 330 cycles at 5C) and thermal stability thanks to fatigue-free (de)lithiation channels, less new-generated Co3O4 layer, and inorganic-rich cathode/electrolyte interphase (CEI) film. This work provides a valuable inspiration for the electronic structure engineer of robust LCO cathode toward high operation voltages.

item.title: ACS Nano: Truly Asynchronous and One-Hot Constraint Probabilistic Potts Computing with Floating-Body Metal–Oxide–Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistors
item.description:
Sunwoo Cheong, Jun-Young Park, Janguk Han, Cheol Seong Hwang, Joon-Kyu Han
This work presents a truly asynchronous physical Potts node (TAPPN) using floating-body metal–oxide–semiconductor field-effect transistors (FB-MOSFETs) to overcome the scalability and encoding overhead limitations of binary Ising-based probabilistic computing. The TAPPN enables native multistate representation without external random-number generators (RNGs) or complex digital arbitration by the intrinsic stochastic single-transistor latch (STL) effect and a drain-sharing configuration. The stochastic source and the one-hot constraint are realized by three transistors, and the node requires 25 transistors and 220 nW including the readout, compared with 2160 transistors and 52 μW for a self-contained digital node evaluated at the same boundary. Its truly asynchronous operation allows efficient exploration of the problem space in large-scale graph-coloring benchmarks. In simulations of the update rule, the Potts-based system achieves a higher success probability than simulated annealing (SA) and parallel tempering (PT) on graph-coloring benchmarks. For an integrated array assumed to operate at 5 MHz, the architecture is projected to reach a time-to-solution (TTS) of 3.4 μs and an energy-to-solution (ETS) of 504 nJ. This platform establishes a complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS)-compatible pathway toward large-scale, multistate combinatorial optimization.

item.title: JACS: Programming Oxygen Reduction Selectivity via Peroxo Basicity: Acid-Controlled 2e–/4e– Reduction Switching at a Dicobalt Platform
item.description:
Kai Hua, Yu-Hua Guo, Ming-Tian Zhang
Achieving switchable 2e–/4e– oxygen reduction selectivity within a single molecular catalyst remains an unmet challenge because the key metal–oxygen intermediate typically commits to one pathway. Herein, we demonstrate that this limitation can be overcome by elevating the basicity of the peroxo intermediate to a level where both proton-transfer (PT) and proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) manifolds become accessible, with the dominant pathway dictated solely by the external acid strength. A dicobalt μ-1,2-peroxo complex supported by an electron-rich macrocyclic poly-NHC ligand exhibits a computed pKa1 of ∼8.8, placing it in a unique thermodynamic window. Stoichiometric protonation bifurcates cleanly: strong acids (HClO4) trigger rapid diprotonation to release H2O2, whereas weak acids (Et3NHOTf) promote O–O bond cleavage to afford a μ-hydroxo complex. Under catalytic conditions, this dichotomy translates into complete selectivity switching─100% H2O2 with HClO4 versus 90% H2O with Et3NHOTf, accompanied by a switch in the rate-determining step from O2 binding to PCET (KIE = 1.60). Crucially, a structurally analogous but less basic peroxo complex predictably inverts the selectivity to H2O under identical conditions, providing a closed-loop validation of the basicity-selectivity relationship. These results establish intermediate basicity as a general, tunable design parameter for programming product selectivity in multielectron catalysis.

item.title: Nano Letters: Machine-Learning-Accelerated Metallene Stabilization from High-Throughput Sandwich Modeling
item.description:
Mohammad Bagheri, Pekka Koskinen
Metallenes have appealing properties, but stabilizing them in a monolayer phase poses synthesis challenges. A recent experiment showed that the van der Waals squeezing method can stabilize certain metallenes in a MoS2 sandwich. This pioneering work motivates systematic studies, but such studies are experimentally impractical, while first-principles modeling remains prohibitive. Here, using universal machine-learning interatomic potentials, we constructed 1620 metallene sandwich heterostructures containing 6 different sandwich layers and 45 metals. We performed phonon calculations, which revealed 1208 dynamically stable structures and narrowed them to 331 after structural filtering. We found that Se-based transition-metal dichalcogenides stabilize metallenes effectively. Specifically, hexagonal and buckled hexagonal crystal lattices exhibit the greatest stability. We further evaluated the thermal stability of selected heterostructures with density-functional-theory molecular dynamics simulations at room temperature. By uncovering the physical and chemical factors that govern metallenes stabilization, our results provide systematic insights to guide and accelerate synthesis for future applications.

item.title: Nano Letters: Highly Reliable Sub-2-nm Hafnia Ferroelectric Tunnel Junction via All-Atomic Layer Deposition Growth
item.description:
Renhao Xue, Yushi Sun, Ruizhan Yan, Zenghui Chang, Mansun Chan, Deep Jariwala, Xiwen Liu
Hafnia-based ferroelectric tunnel junctions (FTJs) are promising for post-Moore memories, offering fast, low-power polarization switching and compatibility with the technological maturity of the hafnia platform. Yet nanometer-scale barrier thinning, while desirable for higher speed and energy efficiency, introduces a critical reliability bottleneck. Here, we develop an all-atomic layer deposition (ALD) process for reliable sub-2 nm hafnia FTJs through precise growth and low-roughness interface formation. The resulting devices combine sub-2-V operation with a high breakdown field of ∼12.1 MV/cm, while maintaining stable ferroelectric switching through 1010 cycles without breakdown. Further interface optimization extends the resistance-state endurance toward 1010 cycles, reconciling aggressive barrier scaling with reliable device operation. We further exploit 4-bit nonvolatile multilevel operation to demonstrate an in-memory computing simulation with 95.78% accuracy. By combining the advantages of scaling with high reliability, this work advances hafnia-based FTJs toward high-speed, energy-efficient, and robust memory applications.

item.title: Nano Letters: Quasi-One-Dimensional Topological Band Structure and Van Hove Singularities in Monolayer TaIrTe4 from Laser μ-ARPES
item.description:
Honey Boban, Tanguy Prongué, Amarjyoti Choudhury, Dario Marchiani, Salony Mandloi, Andrés Bareño, Felix Eder, Enrico Giannini, et al.
Recent transport experiments reported a quantum spin Hall insulator phase in monolayer 1T-TaIrTe4 gated away from charge neutrality. This phase is not predicted by band structure calculations and has been attributed to an electronic instability induced by strong correlations at a putative Van Hove singularity. Here, we investigate the electronic structure of exfoliated monolayer 1T-TaIrTe4 using microfocus laser angle resolved photoemission. We find a strongly anisotropic band structure susceptible to density wave instabilities. Our data further reveal a saddle point singularity in the density of states. However, we find that the saddle point lies at a density for which linear transport experiments found no anomalies. Moreover, the quasiparticle line widths suggest weak electron correlations only. This points to a secondary role of Van Hove singularities and electron correlations in the transport phase diagram of monolayer 1T-TaIrTe4.

item.title: JACS: Dye-Sensitization Enables Visible-Light-Driven N–N Bond Cleavage in a Dinuclear Rhenium Dinitrogen Complex
item.description:
Limei Tian, Zijian Zhao, Tian-Lin Zhang, Yun-Shu Cui, Dan-Dan Zhai, Weijian Yang, Jing-Ao Fan, Pengju Li, et al.
Conversion of μ-N2 complexes into nitrogenous compounds is one of the most important and challenging chemical transformations in N2 fixation. Although photochemical N2 splitting has been demonstrated, existing approaches predominantly rely on high-energy ultraviolet light that generally affords low efficiency and poor selectivity. Herein, we establish a visible-light-driven molecular photosensitization strategy that enables efficient and selective N–N bond cleavage in a dinuclear rhenium dinitrogen complex. Blue light excitation of the organic photosensitizer 4DPAIPN (2,4,5,6-tetrakis(diphenylamino)isophthalonitrile) is shown to initiate N–N scission to afford the corresponding rhenium nitride in 96% yield. Kinetic analysis of nanosecond transient absorption data through the Balzani-Scandola model indicates energy transfer from the photosensitizer to an acceptor state that lies approximately 2.31 eV above the ground state of the μ-N2-bridged dirhenium complex.
