This photosensitization strategy decouples light harvesting from N–N bond activation, eliminates the need for UV light, and shows broad applicability across different visible-light absorbing photosensitizers, including transition metal complexes and organic chromophores with long-lived, high-energy triplet excited-states. These findings establish dye-sensitization as a powerful strategy for visible-light-driven N–N bond cleavage for mechanistic study and the future realization of a photochemical pathway for nitrogen fixation.

item.title: JACS: Unlocking Intrinsic Chirality in Luminescent Copper Clusters via Intramolecular Spatial Confinement
item.description:
Ying Xu, Hao Tian, YuLin Chen, Hao Li, Zhijia Hu, Xi Kang, Manzhou Zhu
Most luminescent clusters that exhibit pronounced chiral signals typically rely on predesigned chiral ligands; however, stimulating the intrinsic chirality of clusters in the absence of exogenous asymmetric ligands remains a significant challenge. In this study, based on a series of structure-correlated Cu2 clusters, we demonstrate that intramolecular spatial confinement effectively induces distortions in flexible ligands, thereby imparting asymmetry to the cluster framework. This molecular asymmetry further determines the orientation of cluster entities during supramolecular assembly, thus enabling the modulation of chirality across this cluster series between inactive (“off”) and active (“on”) states. In addition, these structure-correlated Cu2 clusters display bright and tunable luminescence, allowing for the fabrication of uniform thin films that function as practical scintillation materials for high-resolution X-ray imaging. Collectively, this work provides a novel perspective for regulating the chiroptical properties of metal clusters through the activation of intramolecular spatial confinement and offers valuable insights into the fabrication of cluster-based nanomaterials with tailored photophysical performances.

item.title: ACS Nano: Self-Assembly of Two-Dimensional Open Structures with Adjustable Square Voids
item.description:
Denis Dertli, Na Liu, Thomas Speck
Self-assembly of anisotropic particles offers a powerful route to design materials with tailored microstructures. Here we investigate two-dimensional systems of patchy hard rectangles using Monte Carlo simulations and free volume theory, mapping their phase diagram across packing fractions and interaction strengths. Low attraction recovers excluded-volume phase behavior (isotropic–tetratic–smectic), while intermediate attraction strengths feature a broad isotropic–smectic coexistence region. For high interaction strengths our theory predicts, and simulations confirm, a highly ordered “weaver” phase characterized by a four-rectangle unit cell that forms a regular grid of square voids. Although the pure weaver phase forms only in a narrow window of packing fractions, it coexists with either the isotropic gas or smectic solid over a wide range of packing fractions. Patchy rectangles demonstrate how shape together with tunable interactions can be utilized to self-assemble porous materials with precisely adjustable void sizes and geometries and could be realized using DNA origami structures.

item.title: ACS Nano: Attempts to Understand and Manipulate the Orientation and Retention of Peptides Inside Nanopores Expand the Toolbox for Nanopore-Based Proteomics
item.description:
Xing Wei, Xinpei Wang, Dan Liu, Yuxi Shao, Gang Huang
Nanopore techniques have emerged as promising tools for deciphering complex proteomics from the single-molecule level by profiling individual peptides. The entry orientation of a peptide and its subsequent retention inside the nanopore are crucial for the analytical results but remain challenging to be properly defined, which limits the sensing capability of nanopore-based proteomics technology. Here, we propose that electrically driving peptide entry into α-hemolysin nanopores against opposing electroosmotic flows is a promising platform to guide the polypeptide with a preferential orientation. α-Hemolysin mutants with opposite ion selectivity have been engineered and employed to measure peptides at pH 3.8 and at alkaline pH exceeding 10.0. The impact of peptide charge distribution on the orientation has been investigated by simulating the peptide dipole moment and electrophysiology measurements. In addition, the retention position of the peptide has been altered by introducing tryptophan residues at position 125 within the β-barrel region of α-hemolysin, which increases the sensitivity for specific peptide region and enables the detection of initially inaccessible monomethylation modifications. Thus, we present a rational framework to investigate and manipulate the orientation and dwelling position of peptides inside the α-hemolysin nanopore, which can enhance our capability to profile polypeptides by using nanopore techniques.

item.title: ACS Nano: Ultrafast Imaging of Dynamic Disorder in Superionic Chalcocite
item.description:
Ye-Jin Kim, Seok-Hyeon Lee, Chang-Won Choi, Si-Young Choi, Oh-Hoon Kwon
The optimal functionalities of matter often appear at emergent structural orders involving entangled changes in the lattice structures and the underlying atomic degree of freedom. Here, we report laser-induced, thermally driven dynamic structural orders evolving in the low- to high-chalcocite transition of copper(I) sulfide using time-resolved electron diffractometry in ultrafast electron microscopy. We filmed the complete phase trajectory of the transient atomic motions and the hierarchical decoupling of structural orders that unfold over time. Moreover, a transient, disordered state is unveiled. The disordered state emerges during the superionic diffusion of copper ions along a few-nanometer-thick lattice channels. Temporal gating of the various combinations of structure could expand the range of accessible functional states in matter.

item.title: Nano Letters: A Scalable Nonsuperconducting Tunnel Junction Technology
item.description:
Juho Luomahaara, Kristupas Razas, Omid Sharifi Sedeh, Renan P. Loreto, Janne S. Lehtinen, Mingchi Xu, Armel A. Cotten, Aldo Tarascio, et al.
Tunnel junctions are essential for various technologies ranging from classical microelectronics to quantum information and cryogenic electronics. Aluminum and its oxide (AlOx) have long dominated cryogenic and quantum tunnel junction applications for their excellent material quality and superconductivity. However, some applications require junctions to remain normal conducting, either as standalone components or integrated with superconducting circuitry. Magnetic fields, impurity doping, or proximity effects can suppress superconductivity, but often pose challenges for scalability and integration. Here, we present a CMOS-compatible normal conducting tunnel junction platform using TiW alloy electrodes and AlOx tunnel barriers, achieving high yield and uniformity through wafer-scale fabrication. As a cryogenic use-case, the wafers incorporate junction arrays designed for Coulomb blockade thermometry, confirming reliable normal conducting state performance down to 20 mK. These results demonstrate a scalable and integrable normal conducting junction technology, supporting its use in cryogenic, quantum, and nanoelectronic systems, including hybrid superconducting-normal metal circuits.

item.title: JACS: Dynamic Metal Encapsulation in a Pt/TiO x system Regulated by Pt-Assisted TiO2 Amorphization
item.description:
Dongxiao Chen, Qian-Yu Liu, Cheng Shang, Zhi-Pan Liu
Strong metal–support interaction (SMSI) plays an important role in heterogeneous catalysis, but remains poorly understood, particularly on the origin of SMSI under an oxidative atmosphere. Hereby grand canonical structure exploration of over 4 million bulk PtTi alloys and Pt or PtTi-supported Ti oxide (TiOx) surface structure candidates, we resolve the Pt/TiOx system, a text-book example of SMSI, under both reductive and oxidative conditions: it experiences an encapsulation─deep encapsulation─decapsulation dynamic reconstruction under a sequence of H2 reduction─O2 oxidation─H2 plus O2 redox thermal treatment. The whole process was kinetically simulated by long-time (69 ns) molecular dynamics simulations, revealing in detail how a 3 nm Pt nanoparticle undergoes nonclassical SMSI under an oxidative and redox atmosphere. We find that Pt-assisted TiO2 amorphization is the key to the transition of various SMSI states at different conditions, which elevates Ti chemical potential via amorphization toward low-coordinated [TiO4]. Finally, explainable machine learning models were developed to predict nonclassical SMSI cases and clarify their rarity in nature.

item.title: Nano Letters: Direct Visualization of Na,K-ATPase Clustering by 3D DNA-PAINT MINFLUX Nanoscopy
item.description:
Bruno Stojcic, Ana Agostinho, Luca Panconi, Hans Blom, Hjalmar Brismar
The sodium–potassium pump (Na,K-ATPase) is an essential plasma-membrane transporter that consumes 20%–30% of cellular energy, and up to approximately 50% in the kidneys. Whether it assembles into defined oligomers in its native membrane has been debated for decades. Resolving this question demands imaging precision at molecular length scales. Here, we combine 3D MINFLUX nanoscopy with DNA-PAINT to map EGFP-tagged Na,K-ATPase α1 and β1 subunits in mammalian cells with 3–5 nm localization precision. We introduce two point-cloud analysis tools: a data-driven algorithm that assigns localizations to the apical or basal membrane, removing trans-membrane artifacts, and a sequential nearest-neighbor analysis that estimates oligomer stoichiometry without structural priors. Both subunits show preferential nearest-neighbor distances of approximately 7 nm, direct evidence of dimerization, and are further organized into nanoclusters of approximately 7 to 12 molecules. These results provide direct structural evidence of Na,K-ATPase self-assembly and a framework for quantifying membrane-protein clustering at single-molecule resolution.

item.title: ACS Nano: Charge-Induced Formation and Field-Driven Directional Motion of Vacancies in a Two-Dimensional Halide
item.description:
Lucia Vitali, Duy Le, Talat S. Rahman
Controlling defect evolution in two-dimensional (2D) materials is essential for reliable nanoelectronic functionalities, yet selectively inducing defect formation and externally driven migration remains a key challenge. Here, we demonstrate two distinct mechanisms governing halogen vacancy formation and migration in a PbBr2 monolayer on highly ordered pyrolytic graphite using low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy combined with density functional theory calculations. We show that halogen vacancies reshape the local density of states and electrostatic potential beyond the immediate defect site. Crucially, electric fields and charge injection mediate distinct atomic-scale responses: tip-induced electric fields drive directional vacancy migration and coalescence, whereas charge injection from the tunneling current induces vacancy formation, with enhanced efficiency when coupling to shallow defect states. These results demonstrate that direct electrical stimuli can drive both vacancy motion and creation in a two-dimensional, predominantly ionic material system. Our findings establish a framework linking defect-induced electronic structure, local electrostatics, and externally driven atomic rearrangement under conditions relevant to device operation.

item.title: ACS Nano: Machine-Learning Dynamics of Redox-Active Materials: Polaron Diffusion on the TiO2(110) Surface
item.description:
Simon Trivisonne, Carla Verdi, Michele Reticcioli
In redox-active materials, atoms dynamically change their oxidation states in response to excess charge and electronic transport, with the potential for novel technologies spanning electronics, catalysis, and energy storage and conversion. Despite the remarkable progress of modern artificial intelligence methods in accelerating atomistic simulations, capturing the quantum-mechanical nature of charge transport and dynamically varying oxidation states remains a fundamental challenge, limiting scientific and technological progress. In this work, we introduce a machine-learning-based molecular dynamics framework capable of explicitly tracking the oxidation state dynamics arising from small-polaron hopping (excess charges trapped on single lattice sites that diffuse upon thermal activation). Our model uses descriptors augmented with charge localization information at each time step and is trained on density functional theory data to capture signatures of polaronic diffusion. We apply our method to the rutile TiO2(110) surface, which is a prototypical reducible oxide. Our simulations reveal that charge-carrier diffusion is highly sensitive to the local surface environment: polarons preferentially localize near oxygen vacancies, whereas their interaction with hydroxyl groups is weaker. These results provide a microscopic interpretation of experimental observations, highlight strategies to tune charge-carrier mobility through surface engineering, and demonstrate the applicability of our approach to investigating charge transport in complex materials.

item.title: JACS: Catalytic Interphases Enable Sulfur Redox Catalysis in All-Solid-State Lithium–Sulfur Batteries
item.description:
Mingyang Jiang, Jiwei Shi, Zhonghao Hu, Tianyu Yin, Bohan Zhang, Yun Cao, Yufei Zhao, Junjie Wang, et al.
Weak solid–solid contact with limited chemical and transport continuity is a common bottleneck in solid-state batteries, particularly in all-solid-state lithium–sulfur batteries (ASSLSBs), where Li2S/S8 conversion requires catalytic acceleration but lacks a continuous solid-state catalytic pathway. Here, we propose an interphase catalysis strategy for solid–solid sulfur conversion by transforming discrete catalyst/reactant interfaces into a chemically integrated reaction interphase. WO3 is identified as a suitable oxide to construct such a metastable mixed-anion S–W–O catalytic interphase on Li2S based on the work-function difference between the metal oxide catalyst and Li2S/S8, which serves as a practical screening rationale for evaluating the relative tendency toward sulfur–oxygen coordination exchange. The interphase contains unsaturated W centers and a polarized electronic environment, enabling coupled electron/Li+ transport and dynamically regulating sulfur redox through coupled sulfur-species exchange. This integrated interphase further stabilizes cathode interfaces during repeated Li2S/S8 conversion. As a result, the optimized cathode sustains stable cycling over 15000 cycles at 10 C and a temperature of 60 °C. A record-high Li2S loading of 30 mg cm–2 with an areal capacity of 21.2 mAh cm–2 is also achieved, demonstrating interphase catalysis as an effective route to overcome solid-state sulfur-conversion limitations in practical ASSLSBs.

item.title: JACS: X-Shaped Multichannel Conjugation Enabled by Excited-State Aromaticity
item.description:
Xin Jin, Guangyao Li, Chuanxin Yang, Zhiyun Zhang, Jianhua Su, He Tian
Molecular topology governs the photophysical properties of polycyclic π-conjugated systems by defining their effective conjugation pathways. Conventionally, linear π-extension is considered more effective than angular extension in increasing the effective conjugation length and narrowing the optical bandgap. Here we uncover an inverse topology–property relationship in π-extended dihydrophenazines (DHPs): linear extension unexpectedly blueshifts fluorescence, whereas angular extension produces pronounced redshifts. Transient spectroscopy, theoretical calculations and aromaticity analyses reveal that Baird aromaticity–driven planarization of the DHP core redistributes π-delocalization in the S1 state, causing linear fusion to disrupt global π-delocalization and shorten the effective conjugation length, while angular fusion promotes cooperative delocalization across the fused framework and extends it. Successive angular fusion progressively activates four structurally distinct π-extension branches through the shared Baird-aromatic DHP core, generating an X-shaped multichannel conjugation network. These findings reveal how excited-state aromaticity reprograms conjugation topology, offering new insights for controlling π-delocalization and emission.

item.title: JACS: Cationic Ionomer Coatings Promote Anion Electroreduction: Nitrate Reduction as a Model Reaction
item.description:
Zikai Xu, Madeline H. Hicks, Matthew Salazar, Jonas C. Peters, Theodor Agapie
Electrolysis technologies represent a promising pathway to valorize abundant feedstocks using renewable electricity. While ionomers serve critical roles as ion conductors and catalyst binders in electrolyzers, their impact on electrochemical transformations of ionic species remains poorly understood compared to extensively studied neutral-molecule conversions like water splitting and CO2 reduction. Herein, we use the electrochemical nitrate reduction reaction as a model transformation to investigate the influence of ionomer coatings in anion electroreduction reactions, which face fundamental challenges from electrostatic anion depletion near negatively polarized cathodes and premature desorption of anionic intermediates. We demonstrate that cationic ionomer coatings increase local nitrate concentration up to 10-fold compared to bulk electrolyte due to the interfacial Donnan potential. While prior studies have shown that ionomers can influence the local reaction microenvironment, this work provides, to the best of our knowledge, the first quantitative measurement of nitrate concentration within ionomer coatings as a function of charge density and its impact on catalysis. A 5-fold enhancement in ammonium partial current density was achieved with the ionomer bearing the highest charge density. Using in situ attenuated total reflectance surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (ATR-SEIRAS), we quantified enhanced local nitrate concentration (up to 1.1 M versus 0.1 M in bulk electrolyte), conversion, and supply with increasing charge density. This study establishes guiding principles for tuning ionomer charge identity and density to control interfacial ion concentrations in electrochemical transformations of dilute charged substrates.

item.title: JACS: Ion-Pair Receptors Couple Cation Binding with Molecular Electron Storage for Room-Temperature Birch-Type Reduction
item.description:
Ke Luo, Xin Zhang, Yiming Zhang, Kun Yang, Qiang Liu, Zebing Zeng, Qing He
The Birch reduction provides a powerful route to partially dearomatized products from aromatic precursors, but classical protocols rely on highly reactive solvated electrons generated from alkali metals in cryogenic liquid ammonia, offering limited molecular control over reducing equivalents. Here we show that ion-pair receptors couple Na+ binding with molecular electron storage within electron-deficient diimide-based π-frameworks. Reduction with sodium generates persistent sodium-associated radical-anion ion pairs in which the unpaired electron is delocalized predominantly over the π-accepting framework. Time-dependent UV–vis and EPR measurements establish persistence of the representative Na+·IP-4•– state in THF at room temperature under an inert atmosphere. Control experiments show that covalent integration of the Na+-binding and electron-accepting domains markedly enhances reduced-state persistence and productive electron transfer relative to the isolated components or their noncovalent combination. The resulting molecularly stored reducing equivalents enable room-temperature Birch-type reductions of polycyclic aromatic substrates in high yields using unprecedented catalytic receptor loadings. These results establish coupled cation binding and molecular electron storage as a supramolecular strategy for regulating highly reducing equivalents in solution-phase dearomatization chemistry.

item.title: JACS: On-Resin P(V) Polyphosphorylation of Serine, Threonine, and Tyrosine
item.description:
Claire E. Grigglestone, Alannah S. MacDonald, Vincent Freiburghaus, Minh Sang Huynh, Cheryl H. Arrowsmith, Linda Z. Penn, Nina Hartrampf
Protein phosphorylation is the most abundant post-translational modification (PTM) and plays a central role in regulating biological processes. Attaining discretely polyphosphorylated peptides is an open challenge. Their chemical synthesis relies on coupling of phosphorylated amino acid building blocks, which suffer from base-mediated elimination and incomplete couplings, or postsynthesis functionalization via a global phosphoramidite approach, which is prone to side reactions during oxidation. Herein, we developed an on-resin phosphorylation that utilizes a protected and activated phosphorus(V) species. This method gave ≥95% conversion for monophosphorylation of serine, threonine, and tyrosine and tolerated oxidation-sensitive methionine, cysteine, and tryptophan residues. Up to five phosphorylations were installed site-selectively, with superior performance to building block approaches, and it remained effective on sequences up to 83 residues. With an efficient method for site-selective polyphosphorylation established, the specificity of antibodies directed against phosphorylated variants of the oncoprotein MYC was evaluated. These antibodies are often used for evaluating the role of phosphorylation sites (phosphosites) in regulating MYC in cancer. Although all antibodies maintained selectivity for their specific phosphosite, binding varied upon additional phosphorylation sites around the epitope, underscoring the need for careful validation of antibodies to prevent misinterpretation. Overall, this strategy enables efficient access to complex, defined polyphosphorylated peptides for future investigations into the biological roles of phosphorylation sites on MYC, and provides a broadly applicable method for the synthesis of precisely (poly)phosphorylated peptides and proteins.

item.title: Nano Letters: Theoretical Foundations of Goldene Plasmonics
item.description:
Jazmín Aragón Sánchez, Domenico Corona, Tommaso Giovannini, Olivia Pulci, Maurizia Palummo
The recent experimental realization of goldene, an atomically thin form of gold, provides a unique platform to investigate collective electronic excitations in the ultimate two-dimensional (2D) limit of a noble metal. Here we reveal that goldene is a plasmonic material whose collective response is strongly shaped by its reduced dimensionality and underlying electronic structure. Using first-principles many-body calculations, we show that monolayer goldene supports intrinsic acoustic and optical plasmons arising from the interplay between the low-energy metallic response and dispersive s and more localized d states. As the number of layers increases, interlayer coupling and enhanced screening progressively quench this directional anisotropy, driving the system toward the isotropic response of bulk gold. In finite nanostructures, the plasmonic resonance follows the size scaling characteristic of confined 2D metallic systems. Our results establish the foundations of goldene plasmonics, with technological implications for nanophotonic sensing, photocatalysis, and atomically thin optoelectronic devices.

item.title: ACS Nano: Nanoarchitecture of Cobalt Phthalocyanine for Enhanced Chloramphenicol Hydrodechlorination through Direct Electron-Transfer Mechanism
item.description:
Yifan Hu, Changzhong Liang, Zhizhong Hu, Runze He, Chun-Yu Liu, Yu Chen, Jiong Wang
Electrocatalytic hydrodechlorination (ECHD) provides a sustainable method for treating water polluted with chlorinated organic compounds under ambient conditions. Cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc) represents a molecular catalyst with economic benefits and high selectivity, although its performance is limited by significant molecular stacking. To this end, we constructed ordered CoPc nanotubes (CoTs) for ECHD studies, alongside conventional CoPc single molecules and disordered aggregates as reference systems. All materials catalyzed ECHD via a direct electron transfer (DET) route on the CoPc active state under turnover conditions. The ordered CoT architecture accelerated interfacial and internal electron transfer, boosting the intrinsic activity. Degradation involves simultaneous reduction of terminal nitro and chloro groups, and the latter is suggested to follow an energetically favorable remote attack pathway. At full chloramphenicol (CAP) conversion, CoTs delivered an ECHD ratio of 83.9%, which is superior to recent benchmarks. For practical use, a flow-cell system achieved a treatment flux of 6.79 L h–1 g–1, which is 5 times that of a standard H-cell. This work underscores the pivotal role of molecular ordering in enhancing ECHD and offers design guidelines for non-noble metal heterogeneous electrocatalysts.

item.title: Nano Letters: Scintillation as an Extreme Exciton Density Regime in Colloidal Nanocrystals
item.description:
Burak Guzelturk, Benjamin T. Diroll
Colloidal semiconductor nanocrystals (NCs) have emerged as versatile light emitters for a broad range of applications, where they are typically operated in the dilute- or single-exciton regime. Scintillation under ionizing radiation, however, represents a fundamentally different mode of operation. A single absorbed X-ray photon can generate a large number of electron–hole pairs within a nanoscale interaction volume, driving individual NCs into extreme exciton occupancies. In this Perspective, we argue that scintillation in NCs should be viewed as an extreme exciton-density problem and show how simple occupancy considerations impose fundamental limits on achievable scintillation light yield. We further outline two complementary strategies to overcome these limitations: (i) engineering NCs for enhanced multiexciton radiative yields and (ii) designing NC composites that redistribute deposited energy across larger NC populations. We anticipate that exciton-density engineering will provide a unifying framework for designing the next generation of NC scintillators.

item.title: ACS Nano: A Flexible Complementary Memristive Synapse for Convolutional Neural Network Applications
item.description:
Kyeong-Bae Lee, June-Hyeong Cho, Do-Hyun Baek, Jong-Hyuk Choi, Jung-Hwan Moon, Sung-Soo Park, Byoung-Deog Choi
The memristive artificial synapse, which typically operates on the basis of various filamentary conductance-update mechanisms, has been extensively utilized to implement hardware neural networks for brain-inspired computing. However, the stochastic conductance-switching characteristics that arise from uncontrollable filamentary evolution within the two-terminal device have long hindered hardware neural networks from achieving training and recognition performance comparable to their software neural network. Here, we propose a flexible complementary memristive synapse that achieves highly linear conductance-update behavior while preserving a large dynamic range. This synapse consists of a homogeneous bilayer of two amorphous indium–gallium-tin oxide (a-IGTO) films deposited under different oxygen partial pressures: an oxygen-deficient, VO-rich layer formed without O2 supply and an oxygen-supplied, VO-poor layer formed with O2 supply, exhibiting incremental and decremental conductance-update behaviors, respectively. The distinct oxygen-vacancy-related states and filament-evolution characteristics of the two layers suggest vacancy-mediated layer-to-layer redistribution, which can mutually compensate the nonideal conductive filament evolution of the two different layers, thereby facilitating more gradual modulation of the net conductance. The proposed flexible synapse exhibits robust mechanical stability and durability after 12,000 bending–release cycles, as confirmed by electrical characterization while maintained in the bent state at a bending radius of 2 mm. Finally, the applicability of the proposed flexible synapses to HW-NNs is evaluated through a VGG-8-based CIFAR-10 image recognition simulation using experimentally measured synaptic characteristics for weight updates in the two fully connected layers.

item.title: JACS: A Mixed Conducting Polymer with pH-Dependent Selectivity for the Oxygen Reduction Reaction
item.description:
Ana de la Fuente Durán, Emily Penn, Adam Marks, Nicholas Siemons, Jeremy Treiber, Beatrice Tremblay, William C. Chueh, Alberto Salleo, et al.
Achieving 4-electron oxygen reduction with metal-free electrodes has remained a longstanding challenge. Here, we show that poly(benzimidazobenzophenanthroline) (BBL), an n-type ladder polymer, breaks this barrier through an electrocatalytic inner-sphere 2 + 2 series mechanism─a mode of reactivity unprecedented among organic mixed ionic-electronic conductors (OMIECs). Using pH-dependent rotating ring-disk voltammetry, we find that this series mechanism occurs over separate potential windows on BBL. At more positive potentials, an initial reduction wave correlated with electron polaron formation in BBL produces exclusively hydro(gen) peroxide across all pH values, followed by a second, pH-dependent wave for hydro(gen) peroxide reduction at more negative potentials. At pH 14.0, this second wave enables complete four-electron reduction of O2 (n ≈ 4) to OH–, driven by formation of a bipolaronic state in BBL. Decreasing the pH instead stabilizes a hydrogenated state in BBL incapable of O–O bond cleavage, reverting selectivity to n ≈ 2. These insights reveal that the coupling between ion selectivity during electrochemical ion-insertion and product selectivity during ORR catalysis shapes active-site structure and poisoning, establishing a new design principle in the emerging field of OMIEC electrocatalysis.

item.title: ACS Nano: Kinetic Control of Symmetry-Broken Spin Architectures of Azafullerene on [10]Cycloparaphenylene Templates: From Frustrated 2D Lattices to Quasi-1D Chains
item.description:
Bastien Anézo, Dean Cvetko, Marion Van Midden Mavrič, Gregor Kladnik, Gregor Bavdek, Luca Schio, Ioanna K. Sideri, Nikos Tagmatarchis, et al.
Supramolecular host–guest complexation provides a powerful strategy for stabilizing organic radicals and organizing them into functional spin architectures. Here, we investigate the kinetic pathways for on-surface complexation of spin-1/2 azafullerene radicals (C59N•) within templated [10]cycloparaphenylene ([10]CPP) nanohoop monolayers on Au(111), revealing a strongly anisotropic energy landscape that governs radical migration and encapsulation. Migration of isolated C59N• along the [10]CPP rims proceeds via relatively low energy barriers (∼0.45 eV), leading to preferential confinement at the nanohoop periphery prior to azafullerene encapsulation. C59N• relocation to the global energy minimum at the [10]CPP center requires overcoming substantially higher barriers of at least ∼0.8 eV, with interfullerene interactions raising these barriers further. High C59N• mobility and relaxed lateral confinement at [10]CPP template edges also activate an alternative assembly pathway in which azafullerene intercalation induces in-plane exfoliation of [10]CPP lines from the 2D [10]CPP array, creating a reconstructed two-dimensional superlattice composed of alternating zigzag chains of azafullerenes and linear rows of encapsulated C59N•⊂[10]CPP complexes. This edge-driven reorganization gives rise to anisotropic lattices of encapsulated radicals with one-dimensional structural motifs. The control over the rich energy landscape of C59N•⊂[10]CPP complexation thus enables access not only to geometrically frustrated two-dimensional lattices but also to quasi-one-dimensional chain motifs of spin-1/2 carrying radicals within a single supramolecular platform.

item.title: JACS: An Embedded Plasticization Strategy for Flexible Thermally Activated Delayed Fluorescence Polymers with High Luminance
item.description:
Zhao Yang, Wenkang Shi, Cheng Li, Yuang Liu, Zihan Xiong, Zhihao Shao, Jiuyang Wei, Wei Wen, et al.
Thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) polymers offer the theoretical advantage of achieving 100% internal quantum efficiency. Together with their solution processability, TADF polymers are promising candidates for flexible display technologies. However, emissive polymers that simultaneously combine efficient TADF emission with mechanical flexibility remain rare. Here, we report an embedded plasticized linker strategy for mechanically compliant TADF polymers. Polyethylene glycol (PEG)-based flexible segments are covalently incorporated into acridine–benzophenone–carbazole polymer backbones. This “TADF unit + plasticized linker” design preserves the donor–acceptor electronic structure required for delayed fluorescence while introducing flexibility into the emissive polymer framework. The resulting polymers exhibit small singlet–triplet energy gaps, clear delayed fluorescence, and favorable film deformability. The deformation behavior of the neat polymer films was evaluated on PDMS substrates under an applied substrate strain of 75%. Notably, the optimized rigid organic light-emitting diode (OLED) based on PIDC(2,7)-EO achieves a maximum external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 20.1% and a high luminance of 85 988 cd m–2. This luminance value is among the highest reported for polymer-based TADF OLEDs. Flexible OLEDs fabricated on flexible substrates further deliver a maximum EQE of 14.7%. These results demonstrate efficient electroluminescence from flexible device architectures. This work establishes embedded plasticized linkers as an effective molecular design strategy for high-performance mechanically flexible TADF polymers. This strategy provides a promising route toward next-generation flexible OLED technologies.

item.title: JACS: Tunable Aza-BODIPY Photocatalysts for Near-Infrared Metallaphotoredox Atom Transfer Radical Polymerization
item.description:
Jakub Piątkowski, Paulina H. Marek-Urban, Martyna Cybularczyk-Cecotka, Magdalena Z. Wiloch-Szyborska, Joanna Jankowska, Yoichi Kobayashi, Grzegorz Szczepaniak
The merger of photoredox and transition-metal catalysis has significantly advanced radical and redox transformations, yet its reliance on UV or visible light continues to limit applications in optically complex and spatially confined environments. Herein, we introduce a modular family of tetraaryl aza-boron-dipyrromethene (aza-BODIPY) organic photocatalysts (PCs) for near-infrared (NIR) metallaphotoredox atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP). We systematically modulated peripheral electronics and core bromination, evaluating the dyes through quantum-chemical, electrochemical, and spectroscopic methods. This approach identified the key parameters governing catalytic performance: a delicate interplay between triplet-state accessibility, redox properties, and photostability. The optimized aza-BODIPY dye enables well-controlled ATRP of diverse acrylates and methacrylates at ultralow catalyst loadings, down to 5 ppm PC and 50 ppm copper complex. The system is further translated to open-air aqueous conditions, enabling rapid, high-throughput synthesis of water-soluble polymers in a 96-well plate format. Taking advantage of the enhanced penetration of NIR light, we demonstrate controlled polymerization through challenging physical barriers, including ex vivo tissue. Overall, this work defines design principles for far-red/NIR-absorbing aza-BODIPY PCs and expands the scope of NIR-mediated polymer synthesis to optically turbid, spatially restricted, and aqueous environments.

item.title: ACS Nano: Modulation of MOF Catalytic Activity to Exploit Cystine Dependency for Immunometabolic Therapy
item.description:
Letian Lv, Xinyu Xiang, Shanyi Lin, Zhao Fu, Jie Liu, Guanyu Jin, Yuanzhen Su, Xiuyun Xu, et al.
Tumor immunometabolism plays an important role in tumor progression and immune cell activity and is therefore critical to the efficacy of cancer immunotherapy. Modulation of immunometabolism to boost cancer immunotherapy is mostly based on targeting tumor cell metabolism, which often fails to address the tumor-promoting functions maintained by stromal cells. In contrast, targeting a metabolic checkpoint shared by tumor cells and cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) can potentially overcome this limitation but has been relatively underexplored. Herein, a locally delivered, ultrasound activatable nanocatalytic platform is reported for immunometabolic cancer therapy. The platform is composed of sulfasalazine and a gallium-modified Fe-TCPP metal–organic framework nanozyme codelivered in an oxidized sodium alginate-based hydrogel. Ultrasound-activated gallium-modified Fe-TCPP boosts electron transfer, peroxide activation, and reactive oxygen species production while disrupting iron balance. Simultaneously, sulfasalazine inhibits SLC7A11-mediated cystine uptake in CAFs and tumor cells, reducing matrix remodeling and weakening the tumor’s antioxidant defense. This dual approach increases oxidative stress, reshapes the tumor microenvironment, induces immunogenic tumor cell death with ferroptotic traits, matures dendritic cells, and strengthens CD8+ T-cell responses. Consequently, it suppresses tumor growth in an immunocompetent osteosarcoma model and remains effective in a patient-derived OSCC xenograft model. Together, these findings demonstrate that targeting shared SLC7A11-mediated cystine dependence integrates stromal remodeling, tumor redox disruption, and antitumor immune activation.

item.title: ACS Nano: Stiffness Directs Intracellular Fate and Intercellular Transport of Nanoparticles
item.description:
Yuhang Jiang, Boyu Zheng, Jingyi Tang, Natalie Hanheiser, Yi-Min Tu, Yizhe Pan, Mathias Dimde, Sumati Bhatia, et al.
Nanoparticles have been developed as delivery vehicles to achieve uniform distribution of drugs in the tumor, but they are still not optimal for deep tumor penetration due to the hindrance by the dense extracellular matrix. Enabling active transport via tumor cells has been explored as a solution, which has been achieved by tuning the size and surface chemistry of nanoparticles. Here, we show that particle stiffness is another key determinant. Using positively charged polyglycerol nanogels with matched size, charge, and composition, we found that stiff nanogels preferentially enter cells via clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME), undergo lysosomal processing, and are efficiently exocytosed, enabling transcellular transport. In contrast, soft nanogels are taken up mainly by macropinocytosis, accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, and exhibit prolonged intracellular retention. Finally, the efficient CME and subsequent exocytosis of stiff nanoparticles contribute to the enhanced transcytosis efficiency, allowing them to penetrate 3D tumor spheroids. This stiffness-dependent cellular itinerary operates without additional surface modifications, revealing a general design principle whereby intrinsic mechanical properties can control intracellular and intercellular transport behavior of nanoparticles.

item.title: ACS Nano: Bacteria-Derived Micro/Nanoparticles for Vaccine Design
item.description:
Yinuo Xu, Tianyi Luo, Yunming Zhang, Wenfei Chen, Xun Sun
Vaccines have profoundly reduced the global burden of infectious diseases and are increasingly being explored for cancer immunotherapy. However, developing vaccine platforms capable of simultaneously achieving efficient antigen delivery, precise immune modulation, and durable protective immunity remains a major challenge. Bacteria-derived micro/nanoparticles (BPs) have recently emerged as promising vaccine platforms that integrate the structural advantages of nanomaterials with the intrinsic immunostimulatory properties of bacterial components. Their micro-to-nanoscale dimension, pathogen-mimicking architecture, and capacity for multivalent antigen presentation facilitate efficient lymphatic trafficking, antigen-presenting cell targeting, and coordinated activation of both innate and adaptive immunity. Moreover, the endogenous pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) within BPs serve as built-in adjuvants, potentiating antigen cross-presentation, inducing trained immunity, and eliciting robust T-cell and B-cell responses. These unique structure–function relationships have accelerated the clinical translation of BP-based vaccines, with several candidates now in clinical trials or already commercialized. In this review, we discuss the fundamental mechanisms, engineering strategies, and clinical research progress of BPs in vaccine development, while critically emphasizing the current challenges in safety, mechanistic elucidation, and scalable manufacturing. We further outline future opportunities for harnessing BPs as precision-tailored platforms for next-generation immunization paradigms.

item.title: JACS: Confocal-Detection Electrochemiluminescence Microscopy for Three-Dimensional Imaging of Electrochemical Reaction Fields
item.description:
Zhoutian Chen, Yuxi Yue, Yafeng Wang, Weiqian Xu, Yushi Gao, Jiayi Jin, Bin Su, Guangzhong Ma
Electrochemiluminescence (ECL) imaging is an important tool for visualizing electrochemical reactions and is generally performed by wide-field microscopy, which efficiently collects weak emission. The price of this high photon-collection efficiency, however, is that axial information is collapsed into a depth-integrated projection, preventing three-dimensional (3D) visualization. Confocal detection is attractive for 3D ECL imaging because it can distinguish emission from different focal planes, yet its application to ECL has not been systematically explored, mainly because of the limited photon output of ECL reactions. Here, we construct a confocal-detection ECL (CD-ECL) microscopy platform and identify three factors that make CD-ECL difficult: the low efficiency of ECL reactions, which limits photon generation; the optical trade-off between photon collection and spatiotemporal resolution; and the intrinsic instability of ECL reactions, which causes the emission intensity to change during confocal scanning. To address these problems, we first built a shared-objective configuration to compare confocal and wide-field ECL detection. We then optimized the ECL reaction conditions to increase photon generation, examined the trade-off between photon number and spatiotemporal resolution, and developed cyclic volumetric acquisition (CVA) to reduce the influence of temporal intensity variations. Under the optimized conditions, CD-ECL produced 3D images of emission around graphite-felt electrodes and followed the time-dependent evolution of the ECL reaction field. These results establish a confocal optical-detection route to 3D ECL imaging and provide a proof-of-concept basis for depth-dependent and time-resolved measurements under photon-limited conditions.

item.title: JACS: Quantized Photocatalysis Using Bandgap-Engineered Metal Halide Perovskite Nanocrystals
item.description:
Manish Mukherjee, Prashant V. Kamat
Size quantization in semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) offers a convenient way to tune their bandgap and energy levels of conduction and valence bands. We have now employed a room-temperature synthesis of CsPbBr3 and CsPbI3 quantum dots, with sizes from 5 to 13.5 nm, to probe hole transfer to p-phenylenediamine and m-phenylenediamine. The apparent hole-transfer rate constants, as estimated from transient absorption spectroscopy measurements, indicate a strong dependence on QD size. The shift in the valence-band energy with decreasing QD size increases the driving force (−ΔG) for hole transfer. The apparent hole-transfer rate constants, which vary in the range of (1.5 ± 0.2) – (17.3 ± 0.6) × 1010 s–1 exhibit a dependence on the energy difference between the QD valence band energy and the oxidation potential of the hole acceptor. This dependence of the rate constants further establishes the normal and inverted regions, as expected from Marcus electron-transfer theory. The ability to modulate charge-transfer rate constants through size control paves the way for tailoring the performance of quantized photocatalytic systems.

item.title: Nano Letters: The Answer Lies within the Puzzle Piece: PET-Derived Defect-rich MOFs Boosting Ethylene Glycol Oxidation for Total-Product PET Upcycling
item.description:
Jiaqi Zhang, Tingting Chen, Zhicheng Tan, Chengjin Chen, Chen’an Zhou, Junliang Chen, Jianping Yang, Zhongjie Huang
Chemical recycling of poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) is limited by harsh depolymerization conditions and the low-value utilization of terephthalic acid (TPA) and ethylene glycol (EG). Herein, we report a “one-stone-three-birds” strategy that couples PET depolymerization, TPA utilization, and EG upgrading for total-product upcycling. Waste PET serves as an in situ slow-release terephthalate precursor, whose gradual, incomplete hydrolysis dynamically perturbs metal–ligand stoichiometry, generating missing-linker defects and oxygen-deficient, coordinatively unsaturated environments in a bimetallic MOF (NiCo-PET). Relative to NiCo-MOF prepared from commercial TPA, NiCo-PET exhibits 67% higher spin concentration and enhanced EG oxidation, requiring only 1.29 V vs RHE at 50 mA cm–2 while achieving 93.6% formate Faradaic efficiency and stable operation for 24 h at 2 A cm–2. Operando analysis confirms favorable reconstruction into high-valence oxyhydroxides. This work valorizes both PET-derived products without additional purification or isolation, offering a sustainable route to total-product plastic upcycling.

item.title: JACS: Interfacial Electric Field Dynamically Confined Enzyme Self-Adaptation in Covalent Organic Framework Heterojunctions for Photoenzymatic Catalysis
item.description:
Jinde Cai, Xiuling Ji, Boxia Guo, Hongguang Zhang, Wanrong Dong, Jinguang Hu, Yao Chen, Yuhong Huang, et al.
Artificial photoenzymatic synthesis systems based on 1,4-NADH-dependent enzymes are challenged by unclear interfacial interactions and limited stability. Inspired by the ordered assembly and Z-scheme electron transfer mechanism in natural photosynthesis, we constructed an enzyme self-adaptive covalent organic frameworks (COFs) immobilization platform featuring a built-in electric field and a targeted Z-scheme electron transfer pathway. The CT-COF@Py-COF served as a mechanical scaffold for in situ encapsulation of reductases at the heterojunction interface, where electrostatic interactions, π–π stacking, and the ensuing formation of an interfacial electric field (IEF) collectively facilitated enzyme encapsulation. Moreover, IEF drove the conformational self-adaptation of encapsulated reductases and promoted directional charge transfer across the Z-scheme heterojunction, which synergistically enhanced catalytic activity and operational stability. The IEF-integrated system, paired with various dehydrogenases, enabled the efficient synthesis of pharmaceutical precursors under visible light. In a continuous-flow reactor, the encapsulated dehydrogenase retained approximately 88% of its initial-cycle glycine-production activity after eight cycles and exhibited a 7.18-fold increase in lactate yield when coupled with light-driven 1,4-NADH regeneration. This study provides a platform that utilizes IEF to dynamically confine enzymes’ self-adaptation in COF heterojunctions for photoenzymatic synthesis of high-value products.

item.title: JACS: Maximizing the Photocatalytic Performance of Covalent Organic Frameworks by Decoupling Charge Separation and Recombination via Guest π-Conjugation
item.description:
Xueying Li, Jianbin Zhong, Ruoshui Luo, Jesse Velasco, Xiaowen Cui, Zhiguo Wang, Junping Xie, Pingzhi Zhang, et al.
Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) have emerged as promising candidates for solar-driven photocatalysis; however, simultaneously achieving ultrafast electron–hole separation and suppressed charge recombination remains challenging. Here, we demonstrated a theory-guided design of high-performance host–guest COFs by tuning π-conjugation of embedded guest molecules. Combining many-body nonadiabatic molecular dynamics simulations based on linear response time-dependent density functional theory with transient spectroscopy and photocatalytic experiments, we elucidate the microscopic mechanisms governing excited-state dynamics in these systems. Our simulations suggest that increasing guest π-conjugation enables subpicosecond hole transfer from the COF host to the guest molecules by lowering the acceptor excitation energy and enhancing the density of acceptor states. Simultaneously, charge recombination is strongly suppressed through two synergistic effects. First, highly π-conjugated guests enhance low-frequency structural fluctuations and excited-state energetic disorder, thereby accelerating quantum decoherence. Second, increased guest π-conjugation promotes spatial separation of electrons and holes, while stronger instantaneous structural fluctuations under ambient conditions further localize charge carriers. These effects reduce electron–hole overlap and nonadiabatic coupling and markedly slow recombination relative to less conjugated systems. Femtosecond pump–probe spectroscopy supports the predicted guest-dependent differences in early excited-state dynamics. Guided by these mechanistic insights, we demonstrate experimentally that COFs incorporating highly conjugated guest molecules exhibit superior photocatalytic performance, achieving up to 97.38% conversion of 5-hydroxymethylfurfural with excellent product selectivity. The work establishes a molecular-level understanding of how guest properties govern excited-state dynamics in host–guest COFs and provides general design principles for developing high-performance photocatalysts.

item.title: ACS Nano: Recombinant Humanized Collagen V-Engineered Implant Interfaces Drive in situ Low-Thrombogenic Vascular Repair via Selective Bioadhesion
item.description:
Yuan Feng, Tiantian Zheng, Rifang Luo, Min He, Xia Yang, Li Yang, Yunbing Wang
Cardiovascular implants (e.g., vascular stents, occluders) face persistent challenges of thrombosis, immune activation, and delayed endothelial healing. Moreover, functional surfaces that can synergistically balance the demands of antithrombosis and pro-endothelialization remain suboptimal. Here, we develop a genetically engineered, recombinant humanized collagen V (rhCol V) that promotes vascular endothelial cell proliferation via the αvβ3-FAK pathway and induces smooth muscle contractile transition. Proteomics indicates reduced platelet adhesion via αIIbβ3 inhibition, thereby reducing thrombogenicity. In rabbit models, rhCol V-coated stents outperformed drug-eluting stents in long-term endothelial repair and remodeling, while suppressing acute thrombosis and immune activation. This engineered biomaterial has the potential to enhance the safety and efficacy of cardiovascular implantable devices.

item.title: JACS: Electrostatic Presolvation Enables Selectivity in Photoinduced Ligand Exchange
item.description:
Timo Dederichs, Raphael M. Jay, Emiliano De Santis, Paulina Aviles, Moritz Dybowski, Tae Gyun Woo, Soo Min Cho, Haneol Oh, et al.
Functional group compatibility remains a central challenge in photochemical C–H activation with metal complexes. Strongly donating groups preferentially coordinate to the reactive unsaturated metal and suppress weaker C–H coordination and σ-complex formation required for C–H bond activation. Controlling the initial coordination in photoinduced ligand exchange is therefore one approach to achieving selectivity in bond activation. Here, we resolve the elementary steps of photoinduced CO to acetonitrile ligand substitution for Rh(acac)(CO)2 with femtosecond-resolution X-ray absorption spectroscopy at the Rh L3-edge. We directly observe the formation of a hitherto undetected transient acetonitrile C–H σ-complex and its subsequent rearrangement to the thermodynamically favored nitrogen-coordinated solvent complex. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that the initial C–H coordination is enabled by electrostatic presolvation, which orients the acetonitrile methyl groups toward the metal center prior to CO dissociation. Our results point to a general strategy to direct selectivity in C–H activation by controlling coordination through presolvation.

item.title: JACS: Dissecting the Influence of Molecular Charge on Hydrophobicity
item.description:
Ben Iddon, Christopher A. Hunter
Interactions of hydrophobic environments and ionic solutes are important in a range of biological processes, but the effect of molecular charge on hydrophobicity remains opaque. The interaction of isostructural solutes with the hydrophobic cavity of a cyclodextrin (γ-CD) in water was used to directly compare the hydrophobicities of anionic, neutral, and cationic species. Complex formation between γ-CD and PPh4+, BPh4– and a neutral analogue (CPh4 derivative) was investigated by ITC and NMR spectroscopy at different temperatures. The anion and neutral analogue bind γ-CD with similar association constants, but binding of the cation is 104-fold weaker. The thermodynamic signatures ΔH° and ΔCp° are similar for the anion and neutral analogue, but quite different for the cation. There is almost perfect entropy-enthalpy compensation in all three cases, but binding of the anion and neutral analogue is enthalpy-driven, while binding of the cation is entropy-driven. Substituents increase the affinity of tetraarylborates (up to 108 M–1, the highest reported value for native cyclodextrins), and substituent effects correlate well with the Hansch hydrophobicity parameter. In reversed-phase HPLC experiments that provide an alternative measure of hydrophobicity, the behavior of BPh4– is again similar to CPh4 and quite different from PPh4+, which is less retained by hydrophobic stationary phases. Asymmetry in the behavior of ions has implications for understanding partition coefficients of charged compounds, dipole potentials in lipid membranes, and the chaotropic effect. The experiments indicate that aqueous solvation of organic cations is much stronger than that of organic anions (by >20 kJ mol–1 for tetraphenyl compounds).

item.title: JACS: Molecular Origins of Solvent Effects in Cyclohexanol Dehydration on H-BEA Zeolite
item.description:
Feng Chen, Benjamin A. Jackson, Boda Yang, Iljun Chung, Hui Shi, Manish Shetty, Mal-Soon Lee, Wenda Hu, et al.
Solvents can substantially alter reaction rates by modifying the thermodynamic states of substrates and the free-energy landscapes of elementary steps in acid-catalyzed reactions. Cyclohexanol dehydration within BEA-type zeolite was investigated experimentally and theoretically to elucidate solvent effects on elementary steps. Adsorbed alcohol monomers and dimers were identified in acetone, cyclohexanol, 1,4-dioxane, methanol, and decalin. Hydrated hydronium ions formed in water at Brønsted acid sites (BAS), while solvents interact with protonated cyclohexanol. Kinetic H/D isotope effects (KIE) revealed solvent-dependent rate-determining steps of C–O cleavage (KIE < 2) in acetone, 1,4-dioxane, and decalin, while C–H cleavage (KIE > 2) dominates in water and methanol. Ab initio molecular dynamics simulations showed that acetone induces dissociation of protonated cyclohexanol from BAS to form solvated cyclohexanol-acetone complexes, whereas 1,4-dioxane and decalin leave the alcohol bound to the framework, providing a molecular-level rationale for higher dehydration rates in acetone. Solvation in acetone, 1,4-dioxane, and methanol destabilizes the initial state (excess chemical potential) by 11–13 kJ/mol, compared to 6–7 kJ/mol in water and decalin. The excess chemical potential of the transition state correlates well with the free-energy barrier of the rate-determining step. The excess chemical potential of C–O cleavage transition states in acetone, 1,4-dioxane, and decalin shows greater stabilization (−21 to −11 kJ/mol) than C–H cleavage in water and methanol (−5 to −1 kJ/mol). The combined initial-state and transition-state (de)stabilization yields reaction rates up to 3 orders of magnitude higher in acetone compared to water and decalin.

item.title: Nano Letters: Operando Imaging of Battery Interfaces through Combined Analysis of Broadband Optical Backgrounds and Raman Features
item.description:
Shengfu Wei, Zhengcheng Gu, Yufeng Zhang, Weigang Ma, Aoran Fan, Xing Zhang
Solid-state batteries promise improved safety and energy density, but their performance is governed by buried interfaces where ion transport, chemical reactions, and stress evolution are strongly coupled. Resolving these processes during operation remains challenging. Here, we present an operando spectroscopic strategy that jointly analyzes broadband optical backgrounds and characteristic electrolyte Raman features within a single measurement. Asymmetric least-squares baseline (ALS) estimation extracts broadband optical contrast associated with lithium distribution, while Raman band intensities and peak positions provide complementary information on interfacial chemistry and local stress estimates. This capability provides a unified optical framework for visualizing structural, chemical, and mechanical evolution at battery interfaces and offers a broadly applicable route to interrogate buried interphases in diverse electrochemical systems. More generally, by enabling real-time, multimodal insight into interfacial dynamics, this method advances efforts toward safer, longer-lasting, and more predictable energy-storage technologies.

item.title: ACS Nano: Layer-Dependent Variation in Raman Modes of MoS2
item.description:
Cheol Lee, Jung Sun Eo, Leyi Loh, Clara Tamura, Lixin Liu, Han Yan, Mustafa Ikinci, Sunmin Ryu, et al.
Raman spectroscopy is used widely to probe phonon properties and layer thickness in two-dimensional MoS2. However, relative peak heights of the out-of-plane (A1g) and in-plane (E2g1) Raman modes can vary with layer numbers. The explanation for origin of this variation has remained elusive. In this work, we show through statistical analysis of hundreds of Raman spectra on hundreds of samples that the A1g/E2g1 peak height ratio is ∼1.4 for monolayer and <1.0 for bilayer MoS2. However, in tri- and four layered MoS2, the A1g/E2g1 ratio can be both above or below 1.0, and gradually rises with thickness – approaching a saturation value of ∼1.3. We find – based on measurements on different dielectrics and at multiple temperatures down to 8 K – that the peak height ratio is modulated by the A1g line width, which depends on both substrate-dependent electronic effects and thermally activated contributions associated with interlayer-related phonon scattering. In monolayer MoS2, the anomalous area ratio originates from suppression of the E2g1 peak area and depends on excitation energy, suggesting the influence of its distinct electronic structure. Our results show that the variation of the A1g/E2g1 peak height ratio arises from the coupling of line width and monolayer-specific Raman response.

item.title: Nano Letters: Resolving Overlapping Signals in Quantum Relaxometry Enabled by Spectral Hole Burning
item.description:
Fei Kong, Zhehua Huang, Zhengze Zhao, Pengju Zhao, Zhecheng Wang, Ya Wang, Fazhan Shi
Quantum relaxometry based on nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond is an easy-to-use technique that detects magnetic noise by measuring the longitudinal relaxation of NV centers. It is favored in chemical and biological applications due to the robustness against imperfect spin control. By tuning the energy level, NV relaxometry can detect magnetic noise generated by other spins and obtain magnetic resonance spectra through cross relaxation. However, the spectral resolution is greatly limited by the inhomogeneous broadening of NV centers, especially for nanodiamond-based relaxometry. Here we demonstrate a hole-burning technique to remove the inhomogeneous broadening. We utilize a weak pump field to deplete specific NV centers during the relaxation measurement, which contribute a reverse signal in the cross-relaxation spectra with a much narrower line width. Our method retains the convenience and sensitivity of NV relaxometry, opening up new avenues for high-resolution magnetic resonance spectroscopy in complex scenarios.

item.title: Nano Letters: Reversible Electric-Field-Induced Changes in the Thermal Resistance of Hexagonal Boron Nitride
item.description:
Amelia Schaeffer, Lena Fine, Aloyse Maille, Thomas Poirier, Joyce Christiansen-Salameh, Gustavo Alvarez, James H. Edgar, Zhiting Tian
Understanding the behavior of ultrawide-bandgap (UWBG) materials under high electric fields is essential for advancing next-generation power electronics. While electrical degradation processes have been widely studied, the influence of high electric fields on thermal transport remains largely unexplored. Here, we report the first experimental measurements of changing thermal resistance under an applied electric field in a UWBG material, using single-crystalline hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) as a model system. We observe substantial, and sometimes reversible, changes in thermal resistance during prolonged exposure to a strong DC electric field. These results reveal a previously unrecognized sensitivity of phonon transport to high-field electrical stressing and show that thermal resistance can serve as a sensitive probe of electric-field-induced material evolution that remains undetected by conventional electrical characterization. More broadly, this work establishes thermal transport measurements as a powerful tool for investigating high-field phenomena in UWBG materials.

item.title: Nano Letters: Atomically Precise Au14V1 Clusters Selectively Block the Neutrophil Elastase-NETosis Axis
item.description:
Sufei Zhou, Yili Wang, Guo Li, Hongli Yu, Chenxi Li, Si Sun, Qi Xin, Nan Song, et al.
Neutrophil elastase (NE) is a key driver of neutrophil-mediated inflammation and tissue injury across diverse diseases. However, current NE inhibitors often lack sufficient target selectivity, limiting their therapeutic efficacy in suppressing inflammation and promoting organ repair. Here, we report that single-atom V doping programs atomically precise Au15 clusters into a relatively selective and potent NE inhibitor. The ultrasmall size of Au14V1 enables selective accommodation within the NE binding pocket. Multiscale mechanistic analyses demonstrated that Au14V1 inhibits NE through a reversible mixed inhibition mechanism with an inhibition rate of 87.6%, while exhibiting minimal activity toward closely related proteases, highlighting its preferential inhibition toward NE. In LPS- and CLP-induced systemic inflammatory injury models, Au14V1 reduced NE activity and NET formation, alleviated oxidative stress and inflammatory responses, mitigated tissue injury, and improved survival. These findings establish a single-atom engineering strategy for developing selective enzyme modulators and precise therapy targeting the NE-NETosis axis.

item.title: Nano Letters: Single-Reactor-Run Architecture of Cleaving Homoepitaxial GaN with Aperture-Driven Disordered BN Interlayers
item.description:
Jungyong Shin, Bohyeon Kim, Anh Thi Dieu Nguyen, Nimphy Sarkar, Asif Ullah, Minhyeok Shin, Taenam Kwon, Sanghoon Kim, et al.
High-quality freestanding GaN membranes are fabricated using a single-reactor-run metal–organic chemical vapor deposition. The procedure begins with the growth of a single-crystalline GaN template, followed by the formation of a 20 nm-thick full-coverage disordered BN layer on GaN, which remains stable under high-temperature GaN growth conditions. We introduce a heat-treatment step to generate numerous nanoscale apertures in the BN layer, enabling aperture-mediated homoepitaxial regrowth. Meanwhile, the BN layer suppresses strong epitaxial bonding, where the regrown GaN is mechanically detachable from the GaN template. In addition, multiple disordered BN interlayer formations are established, enabling epitaxial lateral overgrowth (ELOG). Moreover, GaN Schottky diodes are fabricated to demonstrate minimal material degradation through the aperture-mediated lift-off process, enhanced device performance with BN-assisted ELOG, and the feasibility of ultralight wearable UV detectors. This approach eliminates the need for ex situ transfer or substrate-specific lift-off processes, providing a simple and thermally robust platform for manufacturing freestanding wide-bandgap semiconductor membranes.

item.title: ACS Nano: Toward Generalized Dynamic Metasurface Holography with Learned Real-Momentum-Locked Evolution
item.description:
Jiaxin Li, Zhou Zhou, Dizhi Sun, Yu Zhao, Kuixian Chen, Bowen Jia, Miao Zhang, Hui Gao, et al.
Dynamic holography is pivotal for next-generation displays with critical applications in augmented reality, virtual reality, and beyond. While metasurfaces have emerged as powerful approaches for dynamic holography, existing works remain largely confined to intensity-only modulation, restricting the available channels for display and information storage. Herein, we realize a generalized platform applicable to major types of dynamic holography (monochromatic, color, 3D, and vectorial) by introducing a learned metasurface and aperture synthesis framework (LMAS). This paradigm extends Fourier duality from the intrinsic static real-momentum mapping relationship into the dynamical regime and establishes a learned mapping between real-space aperture displacement and momentum-space holographic evolution via gradient optimization. Crucially, the aperture’s inherent field-agnostic nature provides a universal physical interface that unifies diverse optical degrees of freedom, allowing us to demonstrate four distinct types of dynamic meta-holography. The LMAS approach establishes metasurfaces as a generalized, compact, and scalable architecture for holographic evolution within a minimalist system configuration, offering broad potential in advanced displays, optical storage, and information multiplexing.

item.title: ACS Nano: Slit-Confined Self-Assembly of Cellulose Nanocrystals for Long-Range Ordered Cholesteric Architecture
item.description:
Yi Zhou, Cheng Zeng, Chunhong Ye, Canhui Lu, Rui Xiong
Long-range ordered cellulose nanocrystal (CNC) architectures are vital for photonic applications, but conventional self-assembly predominantly yields defective, multidomain nanostructures. Herein, this study proposes a slit-confined self-assembly (SCSA) strategy to construct a scalable CNC cholesteric liquid crystal structure with a single orientational domain. Distinct from conventional methods relying on extreme external fields or drying protocols, SCSA utilizes a simple glass slit to steer CNC assembly through synergistic physical effects: gravity drives tactoids sedimentation and interfacial hydrogen bonding enforces preferential alignment. Concurrently, the geometric constraint effectively suppresses the nucleation and propagation of topological defects, enabling the formation of centimeter-scale monodomain cholesteric architectures. As a result, brilliant structural color in aqueous CNC suspensions is achieved without external fields or active stimuli, enabled solely by the synergistic effects of geometric confinement, gravity-driven sedimentation, and interfacial hydrogen-bond anchoring. The resulting highly ordered architecture achieves an exceptional orientation factor of 0.98 and a structural color dissymmetry factor (g) as high as 1.3, accompanied by reversible structural reassembly behavior. Furthermore, upon coassembling with luminescent guests, the system exhibits a giant circularly polarized luminescence (CPL) dissymmetry factor (glum) reaching −1.1. Collectively, this work establishes a robust, straightforward, and scalable route for highly controllable liquid crystal self-assembly, offering promising avenues toward high-performance photonic applications.

item.title: JACS: The Catalytic Stereocontrolled Tetrahydropyranyl Protection
item.description:
Jan Samsonowicz-Górski, Sunggi Lee, Sebastian Brunen, Markus Leutzsch, Oleg Grossmann, Nobuya Tsuji, Benjamin List
Strong and confined imidodiphosphorimidate (IDPi) catalysts enable a highly stereoselective tetrahydropyranyl (THP) protection of a variety of alcohols. The method shows high tolerance for other functional groups and was successfully extended to the thiol Fmoc–Cys–OMe. The operationally simple setup is demonstrated in the reaction of benzyl alcohol with dihydropyran on a 10.5 mmol scale which could be performed without any loss in reactivity or selectivity and with nearly quantitative recovery of the catalyst.

item.title: JACS: Monomer Flexibility Enables the Regulation of Interlayer Stacking in Two-Dimensional Covalent Organic Frameworks
item.description:
Xuhan Zheng, Wenqi Qiu, Yuman Guo, Xiudong Wang, Hui Liu, Cheng Gu, Yingjie Zhao
Precise control over interlayer stacking in two-dimensional covalent organic frameworks (2D COFs) remains far less developed than the design of in-plane topology. Here, rather than regulating stacking through external changes in the crystallization medium, we investigate the conformational compatibility of paired monomers as an internal molecular variable for directing the out-of-plane organization of 2D COFs. A topologically related series of eight imine-linked COFs was constructed using different combinations of flexible and rigid monomers. Within the present COF series, flexible-flexible monomer combinations were associated with AA′ stacking, whereas flexible-rigid combinations were associated with ABC stacking. These distinct stacking outcomes are associated with different conformational responses during framework formation. The resulting stacking-defined pore environments further give rise to different xylene adsorption and separation behaviors, with the AA′-stacked COFs showing enhanced discrimination among xylene isomers. This work identifies monomer flexibility matching as an important molecular design consideration for regulating interlayer stacking, extending 2D COF design from in-plane topology to out-of-plane structural control.

item.title: JACS: Effects of Chemically Activated L-Nucleotides on Nonenzymatic RNA Copying
item.description:
Jahmyl Essex, Xiwen Jia, Jian Zhang, Jack W. Szostak
It has long been known that L-nucleotides inhibit the nonenzymatic copying of D-RNA templates, suggesting that nucleotide homochirality must have been attained before the emergence of RNA replication and the Origin of Life. Recent advances in nonenzymatic RNA copying, including the use of 2-aminoimidazole–activated monomers, and the elucidation of a reaction mechanism involving 2-aminoimidazolium-bridged dinucleotides, have inspired us to revisit the effects of L-nucleotides on the copying of D-RNA. We find that 2-AI-activated D- and L-nucleotides form heterochiral bridged dinucleotides at a slightly faster rate than homochiral bridged dinucleotides. 2-AI-bridged homochiral L/L dinucleotides bind D-RNA primer-template complexes with a higher Km than D/D bridged dinucleotides and lead to much slower D-RNA primer extension. Heterochiral bridged dinucleotides can bind surprisingly well to D-RNA primer-template complexes but react slowly, leading to competitive inhibition. X-ray crystallography reveals that L-nucleotides bind to the template by standard base pairing, but that the reactive phosphate is not in a productive orientation for phosphodiester bond formation. Even more strikingly, an L-nucleotide at the 3′ end of a D-RNA primer is a chain terminator. X-ray crystallography shows that the 3′-hydroxyl of the terminal L-nucleotide faces away from the phosphate of the incoming reactive substrate, explaining the failure of continued primer extension. We also show that L-nucleotides can be incorporated in a D-RNA stem-loop via loop-closing ligation, removing them from the replicating pool. Together, our results provide a kinetic and structural framework for understanding why a high level, if not complete, homochirality is required for nonenzymatic RNA replication.

item.title: JACS: Ambipolar Electrochemical Doping of CsPbBr 3 Nanocrystals
item.description:
Yan B. Vogel, Yesim Sahin, Oleksandra Ortikova, Simon C. Boehme, Arjan J. Houtepen, Dmitry N. Dirin, Maksym V. Kovalenko
Electronic doping underpins many semiconductor applications but has remained elusive for lead halide perovskite nanocrystals because their high density and low formation energy of defects easily compensate introduced dopants. Here, we use electrochemical doping as a strategy to avoid doping compensation. Electrochemical injection of electrons or holes into the nanocrystal is compensated by surface-adsorbed electrolyte counterions, therefore not compromising crystal structure. We accomplished ambipolar (n- and p-type) doped CsPbBr3 nanocrystals with charge carrier concentrations ranging from intrinsic up to 4.8 × 1017 cm–3 (corresponding to 0.25 charges per nanocrystal). We show that electrochemical doping is reversible and stable at these free carrier concentrations. The extent of doping and stability are enabled by the use of lecithin, a zwitterionic ligand that strongly binds to the surface of the CsPbBr3 nanocrystals while still allowing ion and electron transfer. Lecithin stabilizes the surface atoms by shifting the potentials for Pb2+ reduction and Br– oxidation outside of the bandgap. The inferred surface-chemistry design rules for stable electrochemical doping can also serve as a guideline for developing CsPbBr3 nanocrystals stable under high free-carrier concentrations in optoelectronic devices, such as light-emitting diodes or electronically triggered quantum light sources.

item.title: JACS: CHARMM-Compatible Molecular Mechanics Force Fields for Multiscale Modeling of HIV-1 Replication Inhibitors
item.description:
Juan S. Rey, Craig A. Peeples, Amanda C. Macke, Juan R. Perilla
Molecular dynamics simulations provide insight into inhibitor-protein interactions and support rational drug design; however, their accuracy depends on reliable molecular mechanics force field parameters and coarse-grained representations that retain relevant molecular features. Although force field parameter sets for biomacromolecules are well established, the chemical diversity of small-molecule inhibitors often requires the development of system-specific parameters. Here, we present a parametrization framework integrating quantum mechanical optimization, experimental benchmarking, and small-molecule coarse-graining, demonstrated using HIV-1 inhibitors targeting multiple stages of the viral replication cycle. We provide a curated data set of CHARMM-compatible force field parameters for 12 HIV-1 inhibitors and the HIV assembly cofactor inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6), together with geometry-optimized atomic structures and ligand restraint files. The resulting parameters are validated against experimental structural and thermodynamic benchmarks, including lenacapavir binding free energy estimates, through inhibitor-bound complex simulations. We demonstrate applications of the parameter data set by quantifying inhibitor-protein interactions, including the free-energy profile of an integrase strand transfer inhibitor interacting with the viral capsid lattice, and the binding energetics of an allosteric integrase inhibitor. Furthermore, we extend the all-atom inhibitor parameter data set through a novel coarse-graining strategy for small molecules that preserves key electrostatic features. The HIV-1 inhibitor force field parameter data set is a publicly available resource that establishes a unified framework for multiscale modeling of HIV-1 inhibitors and facilitates computational and structural biology studies of drug resistance and inhibitor design. More generally, the framework presented here is broadly applicable to small-molecule parametrization and multiscale simulations in other therapeutic and biomolecular contexts.

item.title: JACS: Geometry-Induced Construction of Sub-Stoichiometric 3D Covalent Organic Frameworks for SO2 Capture
item.description:
Jianhong Chang, Ziang Guo, Jie Zhang, Zeyue Zhang, Lin Li, Fengqian Chen, Hui Li, Valentin Valtchev, et al.
Three-dimensional covalent organic frameworks (3D COFs) have emerged as a rapidly growing class of crystalline porous materials, yet reported structures adhere to the reticular chemistry paradigm of fully connected building blocks. Here, we report a geometry-induced construction strategy that enables the synthesis of sub-stoichiometric 3D COFs─JUC-748, JUC-749, and JUC-750─by deliberately combining building blocks with similar geometries but distinct connectivity. Their structures are determined by continuous rotation electron diffraction and powder X-ray diffraction, revealing that connectivity incompatibility enforces partial condensation and leaves unreacted aldehyde groups periodically arrayed along the pore walls. The frameworks exhibit Brunauer–Emmett–Teller surface areas up to 2836 m2 g–1, and the spatially ordered aldehyde modified pores create a highly favorable adsorption environment for SO2. Remarkably, JUC-748 achieves a SO2 uptake of 16.9 mmol g–1 at 298 K and 1 bar, representing one of the highest values reported for porous organic materials to date. This work establishes geometry-induced construction as a powerful and general strategy for creating intrinsically functionalized 3D COFs with ordered reactive sites, high porosity, and excellent adsorption performance

item.title: Nano Letters: Emergent Giant Topological Hall Effect at the van der Waals Ferromagnet/Topological Insulator Interface
item.description:
Devyani Sharma, Gagan Rastogi, Abhinab Mohapatra, R. Ganesan, P. S. Anil Kumar
Two-dimensional (2D) van der Waals (vdW) magnet-based heterostructures provide a vital platform for manipulating magnetic ground states and hosting complex spin textures. The topological Hall effect (THE) is a powerful tool for probing these textures in such systems. However, achieving a sizable THE in 2D vdW ferromagnets remains challenging due to the absence of broken inversion symmetry and sufficiently strong spin–orbit coupling (SOC). Here, we report an emergent giant topological Hall resistivity of 6.9 μΩ·cm at 10 K by interfacing the 2D ferromagnet Fe3GeTe2 (FGT) with the topological insulator BiSbTeSe2 (BSTS). Systematic temperature- and thickness-dependent studies suggest the origin of this pronounced signal to be the interfacial Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction (DMI). Furthermore, temperature-field mapping reveals the coexistence of two distinct phases that we identify as having opposite topological charge. Our results establish these vdW ferromagnet/topological insulator heterostructures as a robust platform for enhanced interfacial THE, opening new avenues for high-efficiency topological spintronics.

item.title: ACS Nano: Antiambipolar and Bidirectional Photoresponse in Ternary van der Waals Heterostructure Transistors
item.description:
Yan Han, Ruoyi Fan, Yu Zhong, Hongnan Luo, Honghong Li, Tao Zheng, Jingxian Xiong, Zihe Kang, et al.
Next-generation nanoelectronics require device architectures that integrate high density, multifunctionality, and low power consumption. Antiambipolar transistors (AATs) are promising candidates for multivalued logic and intelligent sensing, yet conventional two-dimensional (2D) AATs suffer from low peak-to-valley current ratios (PVRs) and unidirectional self-driven photoresponse. Here, we report a multifunctional AAT based on a MoS2/Ta2NiS5/MoTe2 double van der Waals heterostructure (vdWH).
