Jeong Ung Ahn, Junyeong Choi, Minseong Kwon, Won-Young Choi, Ki Hyuk Han, Cheol Jun Kim, Chaun Jang, Dong-Soo Han, et al.
We report a nonlinear Hall effect in a high-mobility InAs quantum-well two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) with coexisting Rashba and Dresselhaus spin–orbit interactions. Under zero magnetic field, a second-harmonic transverse electric field emerges that scales quadratically with current density and is significantly larger than the second-harmonic longitudinal response. Angle-dependent measurements reveal a pronounced 2-fold anisotropy that follows the combined spin–orbit field. This 2-fold symmetry reflects the anisotropic spin–orbit field generated by coexisting Rashba and Dresselhaus interactions rather than crystal symmetry. The normalized signal reaches ∼10–9 V–1 m and persists up to room temperature. Conductivity scaling shows a quadratic dependence consistent with skew-scattering-dominated transport. These results establish conventional semiconductor 2DEGs as a promising platform for spin-orbit-driven nonlinear transport and rectification functionalities.

item.title: Nano Letters: Hydrogen-Bonded Organic Framework-Confined Carbon Dots toward Efficient Red Room-Temperature Phosphorescence via Resonance Energy Transfer
item.description:
Zhenti Xu, Wenjie Xu, Jiurong Li, Wenxuan Sun, Xiao Gong
Room-temperature phosphorescence (RTP) materials are promising for information encryption and anticounterfeiting. However, realizing long-wavelength RTP of carbon dots (CDs) is challenging owing to unstable triplet states and strong nonradiative decay. Herein, we construct a hydrogen-bonded organic framework (HOF) through molecular self-assembly and realize the in situ generation of CDs within the HOF matrix. By further incorporating Rhodamine B (RhB) into the HOF, a donor–acceptor resonance energy transfer (RET) system is established, enabling efficient red RTP emission. In this system, the HOF matrix provides a confined environment for the CDs and RhB. Meanwhile, the hydrogen-bonded network restricts excited-state molecular motions and suppresses nonradiative relaxation. The optimized CDs-RhB@HOF composite exhibits outstanding red phosphorescence centered at 600 nm, achieving a high PLQY of 34.20% (versus 0.71% for CDs@HOF) and a prolonged lifetime of 458 ms. The composite material has been successfully applied to multilevel anticounterfeiting encryption.

item.title: JACS: A Biodegradable Metal–Organic Framework/Oligomer Composite for Sustainable Gold Recovery and Circular Water Management
item.description:
Tianwei Xue, Yanyin Wu, Longzhao Xu, Hongmei Qiao, Jinlong Wan, Shanshan Shi, Shimiao Cheng, Yupeng Chen, et al.
The rapid growth of artificial intelligence and digital technologies is generating unprecedented e-waste streams rich in secondary gold resources, yet sustainable recovery strategies remain scarce. Here, we report a bioderived, environmentally degradable metal–organic framework (MOF)/oligomer composite (SU-102/pGSH) constructed via host–guest self-assembly of glutathione (GSH) within a Zr-ellagate framework. The composite integrates abundant electron-rich functional groups into a robust porous architecture, achieving a remarkable gold uptake capacity of 4385 mg·g–1, the highest reported for MOF-based adsorbents. It also exhibits outstanding selectivity in complex e-waste leachates. Mechanistic investigations reveal synergistic coordination with abundant electron-rich groups, followed by electron-transfer reduction of Au(III) to Au(0). Importantly, the spent adsorbent could degrade into benign mineral phases and natural metabolites with negligible phytotoxicity, ensuring a safe end-of-life pathway. Preliminary techno-economic analysis indicates favorable economic potential for practical implementation. By integrating efficient gold recovery with sustainable material design and end-of-life management, this work provides a viable strategy for circular water treatment.

item.title: Nano Letters: Minerals Modulate Lithium Ion Sieve for Efficient Lithium Extraction
item.description:
Cheng Zhang, Runqin Gao, Kun Yu, Qian Wang, Xiongbo Dong, Huaming Yang
Efficient lithium recovery from salt-lake brines is vital for lithium-resource supply. Nevertheless, practical application of titanium-based H2TiO3 (HTO) ion sieves is limited by insufficient adsorption performance. Herein, a high-performance HTO adsorbent (HTO-VMT) was fabricated using vermiculite to regulate the spatial coordination environment and surface hydrophilicity of HTO. Theoretical calculations and experimental analysis reveal that vermiculite, as a Si source and support for HTO, enables interfacial Si migration through isovalent substitution of Ti atoms, leading to atomic-level integration into the HTO crystal lattice. The Si substitution results in an upward shift of the p-band center of O of HTO, which enhanced hybridizations between Li 2s and O 2p orbitals, thus accelerating lithium adsorption rates in the surface diffusion phase. Thanks to an optimal coordination structure and surface hydrophilicity, HTO-VMT exhibits exceptional lithium extraction performance, surpassing state-of-the-art counterparts. This work provides design insights for Li-selective adsorbents via mineral-mediated atomic-scale coordination modulation.

item.title: JACS: Tumor-Specific Gene Editing Enhances Cancer Immunogenicity through Succinate Metabolism-Mediated MHC-I Reprogramming
item.description:
He Yang, Haoyu Zhang, Ziyin Zhao, Yuxuan Ren, Yanhan Xu, Kaimin Cai, Jianjun Cheng, Xun Liu, et al.
Impaired expression of major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) greatly compromises cytotoxic T-cell-mediated anticancer immunotherapy. Existing MHC-I activation strategies are greatly challenged by poor tumor specificity and off-target toxicity. Herein, we report a dual tumor-specific CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing system that can precisely knock out succinate dehydrogenase subunit C (Sdhc) to activate the MHC-I pathway via epigenetic and transcriptional regulation. A tumor-specific gene editor is first engineered via reversible shielding of sgRNA using an apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease 1 (APE1)-responsive, complementary ssDNA, yielding AP-sgRNA with blocked editing activity in normal cells yet completely restored activity in APE1-overexpressing tumor cells. Subsequently, tumor-targeted delivery of AP-sgRNA and Cas9 mRNA (mCas9) is achieved using dibenzocyclooctyne-decorated lipid nanoparticle (DLNP), which upon bioorthogonal click reaction can anchor cancer cells that are prelabeled with azido groups using the unnatural sugar DCL-AAM. Thus, AP-sgSdhc/mCas9@DLNP enables efficient and selective Sdhc editing in tumor cells, leading to epigenetic and transcriptional activation of MHC-antigen processing and presentation genes and thereby provoking robust antitumor efficacy in the B16-OVA melanoma model through enhanced, T cell-mediated immune responses. Moreover, it completely suppressed pulmonary metastasis after combination with aPD-L1 in the 4T1 lung metastasis model. This study provides an enlightened paradigm for precision gene editing and renders a promising mechanism for potentiating cancer immunotherapy.

item.title: JACS: Stereodivergent Synthesis of γ-Functionalized Primary Alcohols via Relay-Synergistic Ir/Amine/Ni Catalysis
item.description:
Rui Ding, Guanlin Li, Ziyun Lai, Haoyang Wang, Xinxin Yuan, Wanbin Zhang, Xiaohong Huo
Primary alcohols bearing chiral motifs constitute a class of highly valuable organic compounds that are widely prevalent in natural products and pharmaceutical molecules. Although impressive progress has been made in α- and β-functionalization of primary alcohols, the development of efficient methods for the synthesis of the γ-functionalized primary alcohols─particularly in an asymmetric fashion─remains a significant challenge. Here we report a relay-synergistic Ir/amine/Ni catalytic manifold that converts primary allylic alcohols into γ-functionalized primary alcohols bearing adjacent γ,δ-stereocenters with full catalyst-controlled stereodivergence. The reaction proceeds sequentially through iridium-catalyzed borrowing hydrogen to oxidize the primary allylic alcohol, followed by a stereodetermining Michael addition cooperatively catalyzed by a chiral amine and a chiral nickel catalyst, and concludes with iridium-hydride-mediated reduction. A series of primary alcohols bearing adjacent γ,δ-stereocenters could be easily synthesized in moderate to excellent yields and with good to excellent stereoselectivities (up to 94% yield, >20:1 dr, >99% ee). By permuting the configurations of the amine and nickel catalysts, all four stereoisomers can be accessed. Remarkably, control experiments indicate that the relay-synergistic strategy suppresses retro-Michael addition by rapidly reducing the unstable Michael adduct, thereby maintaining high diastereoselectivity. Kinetic isotope experiments identify the borrowing-hydrogen oxidation of the primary allylic alcohol as the rate-determining step.

item.title: Nano Letters: Finite-Depth Interfacial Coupling in Metal/Topological Insulator van der Waals Heterostructures
item.description:
Yin-Song Liao, Hsin-Hsien Chan, Ruei-Yu Wang, Han-Wei Tsai, Hsun-Ting Hsieh, Cheng-Maw Cheng, Jyh-Pin Chou, Meng-Kai Lin
Metal/topological insulator van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures offer a platform for engineering emergent quantum states beyond isolated layers. While proximity effects in covalently bonded systems are well studied, coupling depth across vdW interfaces remains unclear. Using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy and first-principles calculations, we investigate the thickness dependence of TiTe2/Bi2Te3 electronic states. Despite nominally weak vdW bonding, the buried interface induces emergent bands and splitting near a band crossing, consistent with hybridization. Interface-induced features persist in the bilayer, while band evolution nearly saturates in thicker films. Even at four layers, the electronic structure does not simply recover to the intrinsic TiTe2 limit, consistent with finite-depth coupling that substantially reshapes the overlayer bands. Charge redistribution and a moiré-modulated interfacial potential contribute to this reconstruction. Finite-depth coupling may be a hallmark of strongly coupled vdW heterostructures and guide topological and quantum electronic device design.

item.title: ACS Nano: Turning Insulators into Accelerators: Deciphering the Interfacial Ionic Conductivity Boost in Composite Solid-State Electrolytes through Machine Learning Molecular Dynamics Simulations
item.description:
Boyuan Xu, Cheng Qian, Liyi Bai, Chenlu Wang, Feng Ding, Qisheng Wu
Halide solid-state electrolytes have emerged as promising candidates for all-solid-state lithium batteries due to their high oxidative stability and deformability, yet their moderate ionic conductivity remains a bottleneck. While incorporating ionically insulating ZrO2 nanoparticles has been experimentally shown to enhance the ionic conductivity of Li2ZrCl6, the atomistic origin governing this interfacial phenomenon remains unclear. Here, we bridge the spatiotemporal gap in modeling complex heterostructures by developing an accurate machine-learned force field based on the neuroevolution potential, enabling large-scale molecular dynamics simulations of ZrO2/Li2ZrCl6 heterostructures. By systematically investigating four representative low-lattice-mismatch ZrO2/Li2ZrCl6 interfaces, we identify spontaneous interfacial amorphization driven by space-charge effects upon surface cleavage, trapping Li+ and leading to under-coordinated Li+ polyhedra with pronounced geometric distortion. These distorted amorphous interfacial regions exhibit markedly enhanced Li+ hopping activity, significantly outperforming the bulk lattice, provided that the local mobile Li+ density is not depleted by surface charge redistribution. This work establishes a computational framework for training validated machine-learned force fields for interfaces and provides one plausible origin for the experimentally observed conductivity boost in the insulator-conductor composites, guiding the rational design of electrolytes toward next-generation solid-state batteries.

item.title: ACS Nano: Early Pathway Selection Precedes Conformational Locking in Protein Self-Assembly
item.description:
Ruoxuan Peng, Lele Zhou, Runnan Bai, Yunhao Yang, Yi Zhou, Hao Zhang, Xinyan Wang, Jing Ren, et al.
When early intermediates begin to bias subsequent pathways during protein self-assembly remains difficult to resolve experimentally because early-stage processes are transient and poorly accessible. Here, using regenerated silk fibroin as a model system, we experimentally capture and analyze an early nucleation window in which assembly pathways begin to diverge before conformational locking occurs. By combining controlled electric-field perturbation with multiscale structural characterization and coarse-grained simulations, we identify reproducible nanoscale intermediates that mediate pathway selection. Within this window, electric fields bias early assembly kinetics in a nonmonotonic manner, modulating the formation, elongation, and competition of intermediates rather than directly enforcing structure or orientation. Time-resolved measurements show that subsequent growth proceeds primarily through elongation and fusion of existing intermediates, while β-sheet formation and crystallization emerge only at later stages and serve to stabilize pathways that were biased at earlier stages. Together, we locate the emergence of detectable pathway biasing within the nucleation stage and provide a framework for understanding and guiding protein self-assembly under nonequilibrium conditions.

item.title: ACS Nano: Cation-Intercalated Mott Insulator α-RuCl3 Superlattice for Actively Tuned Optoelectronics
item.description:
Ran Tang, Daozhi Shen, Linglan Guo, Qiaolin Gu, Xinyue Li, Dingyun Zhang, Yufan Mao, Feifan Wang, et al.
Active tuning of the spectral response within sensing materials is critical for application-specific optoelectronics. However, current approaches typically suffer from limited tunability, complex architectures, or sacrificed stability. Here we report an on-chip cation intercalation strategy that transforms the Kitaev-candidate Mott insulator α-ruthenium chloride (α-RuCl3) into a tetramethylammonium (TMA+)-intercalated RuCl3 layered superlattice. The intercalation-induced reconstruction of the Mott-derived electronic states substantially narrows the optical gap from ∼1.1 eV to ∼0.6 eV, extending the spectral response into the short-wave infrared (SWIR) regime. The introduction of an in situ van der Waals tunneling barrier suppresses dark current by >3 orders of magnitude and enhances specific detectivity by 4–6 orders of magnitude. By employing machine learning models, we demonstrate device-response-guided image processing for intelligent recognition under degraded environments. This work establishes a connection between correlated-electron systems and intelligent sensing, stimulating research directions at the intersection of quantum materials, optoelectronics, and intelligent sensing systems.

item.title: ACS Nano: Design of Water-Resistant, Food-Grade Microneedles for Fish Injection and Underwater Cargo Delivery
item.description:
Meng Li, Jad Raad, Yunteng Cao, Yue Hu, Colleen Wolfe, Doyoon Kim, Bradley D. Frank, Gregory D. Wiens, et al.
Aquatic foods provide around 15% of consumed animal-derived protein worldwide and aquaculture now supplies most of it. But the industry faces significant challenges in disease prevention and excessive use of antimicrobials. Vaccination, particularly for juvenile fish, can mitigate these risks, but manual and automated needle-based vaccination methods are costly, stressful, and labor-intensive. Here, a water-resistant, food-grade microneedle platform is designed to deliver cargos underwater. Silk fibroin-based microneedles are engineered to remain water resistant from minutes to hours in order to penetrate fish skin in wet conditions. To meet the requirements of different underwater applications, three microneedle morphologies─shell, solid-tip, and hollow─are developed, and their different combinations of mechanical integrity, water-resistance performance, cargo compatibility, and release kinetics are studied. The microneedles also preserve the supercoiled conformation of ⩾50% of the loaded pIHNVw-G plasmids─developed to protect fish against infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus─outside the cold chain for 4 weeks under dry conditions. In pilot animal studies, injected microneedles remain attached to zebrafish and juvenile rainbow trout while swimming. Using this food-based microneedle platform, we envision the development of tools for underwater vaccination of juvenile fish that increase aquaculture efficiencies and reduce environmental impact.

item.title: ACS Nano: Air-Stable Nickel Oxide Nanosheets as a Model Platform for Decoupling Structure–Activity Relation in Oxygen Evolving Electrocatalysts
item.description:
Harry E. Taylor, Norton G. West, Eleanor Ender, Liam Dwyer, Ramadan Chalil Oglou, Jeppe V. Lauritsen, Alex S. Walton
Nickel oxides are among the most active electrocatalysts for the alkaline oxygen evolution reaction (OER), a key process in green hydrogen production. However, the fundamental reaction mechanism remains unclear, limiting the rational design of electrocatalysts capable of reducing the cost of sustainable hydrogen generation. Herein, we develop an air-stable model electrocatalyst system of submonolayer nickel oxide (NiO) nanosheets with controlled coverages and morphologies on atomically flat Au(111), enabling atomic-scale investigation of structure–activity relationships under ambient conditions. Atomic force microscopy (AFM), scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) in ultrahigh vacuum (UHV), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and electrochemical measurements were combined to correlate nanosheet structure and composition with electrocatalytic performance. We reveal OER activity scales with nanosheet edge density, identifying edge sites as the dominant active sites of the reaction. XPS measurements demonstrate the formation of nickel hydroxide on the nanosheet surfaces and edges following OER testing, consistent with the generation of a catalytically active nickel oxyhydroxide phase during operation. These findings provide insight into the structure–activity relationships governing NiO electrocatalysts and demonstrate a strategy for resolving atomic-scale structure–activity relationships without the need to maintain samples under UHV. We propose that future NiO-based OER electrocatalysts are designed to maximize the number density of accessible edge sites, hence maximizing the electrocatalytic activity.

item.title: ACS Nano: Photodoping-Driven Lattice Expansion Enables Polarization Enhancement in Sliding Ferroelectric MoS2
item.description:
Kun Yang, Jianxin Yu, Jia-Wen Li, Jia Zhang, Sheng Meng, Jin Zhang
Light-matter interactions provide a powerful route to dynamically control ferroelectricity in low-dimensional materials, yet the microscopic mechanisms governing light-induced polarization remain elusive in sliding ferroelectrics. However, the influence of photodoped carriers on the macroscopic polarization and lattice responses remains largely unexplored. In this work, we employ first-principles calculations to demonstrate the microscopic origin of the photostrictive response in rhombohedral bilayer MoS2 under carrier photodoping. The system exhibits a characteristic lattice deformation, including in-plane expansion with the magnitude of 2% under a moderate photodoping density, collectively enhancing electronic hybridization. The coupling gives rise to a substantial interlayer contraction and an increase in out-of-plane spontaneous polarization, accompanied by a softening of the interlayer vibrational mode. These results demonstrate a microscopic, nonthermal pathway for modulating ferroelectric properties and underscore the potential of lattice-engineered polarization control in two-dimensional sliding ferroelectrics for advanced optoelectronic and information storage technologies.

item.title: ACS Nano: Human Urine–Derived Induced Pluripotent Stem Cell Membranes Enable Personalized Transdermal Nanotherapy for Melanoma
item.description:
Dasong Hong, Taihyun Kim, Sung-Eun Heo, Manho Kim, Juhyun Park, Chae-Won Moon, Sang-Jun Ha, Won-Gun Koh, et al.
Melanoma treatment remains limited by drug resistance, immune-related adverse effects, and inadequate tumor-specific drug delivery. Nanoparticle (NP)-based delivery platforms have shown promise, but their clinical translation is hindered by rapid immune clearance and suboptimal biocompatibility. Current membrane-coating strategies often depend on invasive cell sources and lack patient-specific applicability. This study introduces a personalized melanoma therapy platform that integrates MnO2 NPs (MNPs) coated with urine-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) membranes into a hydrogel-based transdermal patch. The patient-derived iPSC membrane enhances tumor targeting and immune evasion through the CXCR4/CXCL12 axis, while the MNPs facilitate pH-responsive release of cytotoxic drugs within the tumor microenvironment, maximizing therapeutic efficacy. The hydrogel transdermal patch enables direct, noninvasive delivery to skin lesions, promoting sustained drug exposure and potentially improving patient compliance. By combining autologous cell membrane coating, pH-responsive nanocarriers, and transdermal administration, this platform addresses key limitations of current melanoma therapies and supports the potential for clinical translation of personalized nanomedicine.

item.title: JACS: Interfacial Kinetic Control Enables Regulated Growth of Functional Metal–Phenolic Network Films
item.description:
Tianzheng Wang, Zhixing Lin, Omid Mazaheri, Chang Liu, Wanjun Xu, Zhaoran Wang, Jingqu Chen, Ben McLean, et al.
Metal–phenolic network (MPN) films are of widespread interest because of their potential application in biotechnology, catalysis, and the environment. Their formation typically involves the supramolecular assembly of phenolic ligands and metal ions from solution onto a solid substrate. Such assembly has been conducted exclusively from a single-phase solution, thus limiting spatiotemporal control over coordination and/or the range of precursors that can be used, and thereby restricting the compositional and structural diversity, as well as functionality, of MPN films. Herein, we report a liquid–liquid interfacial assembly (LLIA) approach, which leverages two immiscible phases, to prepare functional MPN films with specific properties. LLIA enables both the kinetic regulation of film growth (a key parameter in designing films with desired properties) and the use of a broader range of building blocks. The assembled MPN films exhibit controlled thickness (∼30–500 nm) and stiffness (∼2–12 GPa) and distinct structural properties (e.g., crystallinity) relative to other methods, which contribute to their conductivity and molecular selectivity (e.g., H2/CO2 separation performance). Functional MPN films with wettability, conductivity, antibacterial, or fluorescence properties are assembled by integrating various functional components (e.g., polymers, nanoparticles, and dyes), as well as inorganic and metal–organic framework films.

item.title: JACS: Diffusion-Gating Enabled Ternary C2H4 Purification and Inverse C2H2/CO2 Separation in an Adaptive Hopf-Link Metal–Organic Framework
item.description:
Lina Jiang, Zhixuan Liu, Tingting Pan, Zijin Mao, Jiacheng Zhou, Le Shi
The simultaneous purification of polymer-grade ethylene (C2H4) and recovery of high-purity acetylene (C2H2) from complex ternary mixtures with carbon dioxide (CO2) represents a critical industrial challenge. Conventional adsorbents employ thermodynamic selectivity to bind C2H2 and CO2 preferentially over C2H4, enabling one-step C2H4 purification but necessitating an energy-intensive desorption step for C2H2 recovery, as C2H2 typically binds more strongly. Here, we report a fundamentally different approach using diffusion-gating in an adaptive Hopf-link metal–organic framework, ZJNU-600, which replaces thermodynamic control. The framework comprises two orthogonal, interpenetrated sql nets mechanically interlocked as Hopf links, with thiocyanate linkers acting as molecular hinges that modulate the pore aperture. This architecture establishes an ideal kinetic diffusion hierarchy of CO2 > C2H2 > C2H4, completely inverting the elution order compared to equilibrium-based separation. Dynamic breakthrough experiments demonstrate that ZJNU-600 achieves one-step production of C2H4 from ternary mixtures while simultaneously enabling the direct recovery of C2H2 via inverse separation, eliminating the need for energy-intensive desorption. The exceptionally low isosteric heat of CO2 adsorption (24.7 kJ mol–1) further suggests minimal regeneration energy. Computational studies reveal that the diffusion barrier hierarchy arises from the differential chemical compatibility of each gas with the hydroxyl-decorated pore walls. This work establishes kinetic pore-aperture engineering as a generalizable and energy-efficient design principle for multicomponent gas separations, effectively inverting the separation hierarchy dictated by thermodynamic affinity.

item.title: Nano Letters: High-Contrast Broadband Optical Edge Detection by Low-Loss Geometric Phase Gratings
item.description:
Xin Zhang, Yu-Hao Lei, Zi-Ting Liu, Kai-Xin Han, Yan-Hao Yu, Zhen-Ze Li, Junxiao Zhou, Ke-Mi Xu, et al.
Optical edge detection is emerging as a key technique in image processing owing to its merits of large-scale and real-time operation. However, achieving both broadband and high-contrast functionality remains challenging. While broadband optical edge detection has been demonstrated using nanograting-based geometric phase (GP) gratings, the relatively low image contrast limits their effectiveness. Here, we demonstrate high-efficiency nanopore-based GP gratings by ultrafast laser writing in silica glass, enabling high-contrast and broadband edge detection. A maximum contrast of 0.97 is achieved at 515 nm, approaching the theoretical limit of unity. We further show that the edge detection contrast and spatial resolution are influenced by the period of the GP gratings. Moreover, the nanopore-based GP gratings exhibit broadband performance from 450 to 2000 nm and support both one-dimensional and two-dimensional edge detection. Finally, we demonstrate edge detection capability in complex environments, e.g., through water or silicon at appropriate wavelengths.

item.title: JACS: A Stable Terminal Mercury Hydride and Its Reactivity To Form Mercury–Metal Bonds
item.description:
Eric S. Yang, Milan Gembicky, Joshua S. Figueroa
Organomercury hydrides are typically encountered as unstable intermediates in organic transformations. These compounds are conventionally thought to be intrinsically unstable and have eluded isolation in the condensed phase. Here, we report the synthesis, isolation, characterization, and reactivity of an unexpectedly stable arylmercury hydride using a sterically encumbering fluorenyl-hydrindacene scaffold. The arylmercury hydride readily reacts with metalloradicals and metal hydrides to form bimetallic complexes containing unsupported mercury–metal bonds. These results suggest that the instability of mercury hydride compounds is not due to an intrinsic weakness of the mercury–hydrogen bond, but rather their propensity to undergo bimetallic reactions that result in mercury–mercury bond formation.

item.title: JACS: Inverse-IMPRESSION: A Graph-Based Platform for Molecular Structure Elucidation from Experimental NMR Spectroscopic Properties
item.description:
Zheqi Jin, Grace Armitage, Richard Cox, Ben Honoré, Mohammad Golbabaee, Craig Butts
Here, we present a platform built on our inverted graph transformer network, IMPRESSION-G2, which can accurately and rapidly reconstruct molecular bonding directly from experimental nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopic information. It comprises three interconnected stages: a one-shot model that reads in NMR parameters and uses these to predict bond connectivity between atoms; a structure correction stage that corrects the predicted structures by removing uncertain bonds and iteratively reassigning them; and noise-augmented multishot prediction, generating an ensemble of candidate structures, which are ranked to identify the best-fit structure. By integrating a range of 1H and 13C NMR data, including two-dimensional (2D) experiments such as COSY, HSQC, and HMBC, the inverse-IMPRESSION platform correctly identifies the structures of 77.8% of molecules with up to 30 heavy atoms (H, C, N, O, and F) using simulated NMR data, and 11 of 19 (58%) molecules using experimental NMR data. The experimental structures solved are representative of the complex structures in synthetic and natural products that routinely challenge chemists, assessed by high nSPS scores (greater than 40) for successfully elucidated structures and molecular weights of up to 480 Da. The inverse-IMPRESSION framework thus provides a highly effective approach for automated molecular structure elucidation by using graph-based machine learning on experimental data.

item.title: Nano Letters: Atomic Lift-Off of Wafer-Scale Single-Crystalline Gold Membranes Enables Buried-Interface Epitaxy for Flexible Oxide Electronics
item.description:
Yongbin Sun, Hanwen Chi, Ziyue Shen, Kaixin Wang, Fan Zhang, Ni Tu, Tianhao Yang, Wenzhe Niu, et al.
Flexible oxide electronics require inorganic semiconductors that maintain high-performance under bending, yet scalable approaches to wafer-scale single-crystalline (SC) oxide films and, critically, atomically sharp metal/oxide contacts remain limited. Here, we introduce a buried-interface epitaxy strategy based on atomic lift-off of epitaxial metal films to create atomically defined SC metal/oxide heterostructures in flexible architectures. We fabricate 2-in. freestanding SC Au(111) membranes and employ film-flipping to expose the originally buried Au/Si epitaxial interface as an intrinsically atomically flat growth surface. This converts conventional surface deposition into interface deposition, enabling wafer-scale epitaxial Cu2O(111)/Au with a flat interface. The interface-deposited flexible Cu2O exhibits nearly 2-fold higher carrier mobility and photocurrent, while maintaining stable transport under bending. Flexible Cu2O photocathodes further exhibit 1.6 times higher full-angle light harvesting and 5.6 times higher photocurrent-to-mass metrics compared with rigid counterparts. This work establishes freestanding SC metals as transferable epitaxial templates for flexible oxide electronics and energy devices.

item.title: ACS Nano: Third-Eigenmode Atomic Force Microscopy for Resolving Solvation Structures and Structural Defects in Organic Semiconductor Films under Ambient Conditions
item.description:
Georgios Atsas, Alba Cazorla, Félix Devaux, Christian Ruzié, Yves Henri Geerts, Esther Barrena, Daniel Martin-Jimenez
Organic semiconductor molecules are key elements for the development of next-generation flexible and lightweight electronic devices. Their performance is largely governed by molecular arrangement within thin films, whereas environmental sensing is governed by surface functionality and mediated by the interfacial structure at the solid–gas interface. However, experimental tools capable of accessing such information with molecular-scale resolution remain scarce. Here, we employ third-eigenmode atomic force microscopy (AFM) with moderately compliant cantilevers to directly probe the interfacial solvation structure of the liquid layer formed at the interface between small-molecule organic semiconductor thin films and the ambient gas environment. This approach also enables true molecular-resolution imaging across molecular steps, providing detailed insight into interplanar molecular organization and crystal growth mechanisms. Overall, our results establish third-eigenmode AFM as a versatile methodology for high-resolution characterization of molecular packing and for elucidating the relationship between surface functionality and interfacial structure in organic semiconductor materials.

item.title: JACS: Framework Deuteration Regulates Excited-State Dynamics and H2O2 Release in Covalent Organic Framework Photocatalysis
item.description:
Zhengrong Xu, Shihang Yu, Xinxin Chen, Tian Zhang, Dong Lv, Tianqi Liu, Aiguo Kong, Xiaolei Fan, et al.
Hydrogen/deuterium (H/D) substitution provides a unique means of perturbing nuclear motion while largely preserving electronic structure. Here, we investigate isotope-regulated photocatalysis using structurally matched H-TpPa and D-TpPa covalent organic frameworks (COFs) for H2O2 production. Deuteration preserves framework connectivity, crystallinity, porosity, and ground-state electronic structure, yet increases the H2O2 production rate by 1.80-fold in O2-saturated pure water. Spectroscopic and theoretical analyses show that D-TpPa exhibits weaker effective exciton–phonon coupling, a lower apparent exciton-dissociation energy, a longer-lived photoexcited population, and redistributed mode-resolved Huang–Rhys contributions, collectively improving charge utilization. Both isotopologues follow the same coupled two-electron oxygen reduction and four-electron water oxidation pathway. At the catalytic interface, isotope-dependent vibrational free-energy contributions reduce terminal *HOOH stabilization and lower the free-energy requirement for H2O2 release. These results establish framework isotope engineering as a generic strategy for regulating photocatalysis from excited-state evolution to interfacial product release without substantial electronic reconstruction.

item.title: JACS: Contact-Electro-Catalysis Enables Ambient Coupling of CO2 and NH3 for Urea
item.description:
Han Qian, Wenbo You, Ning Wu, Shaoxin Li, Mohsin Shah, Feiyao Yang, Liwu Zhang, Richard N. Zare, et al.
Urea is an essential chemical for agriculture and industry, yet its production remains dominated by energy-intensive thermochemical processes. Here we report a contact-electro-catalysis (CEC) strategy that enables direct urea synthesis from carbon dioxide and aqueous ammonia under ambient conditions. Mechanical contact electrification (CE) continuously generates interfacial charges at dielectric-liquid interfaces, creating a unique reaction microenvironment characterized by a giant interfacial electric field and local pH gradients. This electric-field-engineered microenvironment promotes the formation and stabilization of neutral carbamic acid (NH2COOH), enabling urea synthesis through a pathway distinct from conventional carbamate-mediated mechanisms. Spectroscopic and isotopic-labeling studies further reveal a persistent cyanate intermediate that converts to urea after ultrasonication, supporting a dual-pathway mechanism centered on NH2COOH. Confocal Raman spectroscopy combined with vibrational Stark effect probes directly quantifies an interfacial electric field of up to 1.5 × 1010 V m–1, orders of magnitude higher than those reported at gas–liquid or liquid–liquid interfaces. Importantly, density functional theory calculations further corroborate that the interfacial field modulates reaction free energies and stabilizes key intermediates. These findings establish CEC as an ambient synthetic paradigm in which the interfacial electric field acts as an active driving force for selective C–N coupling and inorganic-to-organic conversion.

item.title: JACS: Synthesis of Medium-Sized Cyclic Ethers via Endo -Selective Pd(0)/B(C6F5)3-Catalyzed Hydroalkoxylation of Enynols and Enynediols
item.description:
Maxwell Eaton, Yuping Dai, Jackson Yates, Bo Li, Karinne Miqueu, Shih-Yuan Liu
Medium-sized cyclic ethers are present in many natural products and therapeutic agents. Herein, we describe a mild catalytic method for the synthesis of 6- to 8-membered oxacycles by endo-selective hydroalkoxylation of enynols and enynediols. The utility of this method is demonstrated through the total synthesis of (±)-corypsoriol D and E. Experimental and computational mechanistic studies revealed an oxidative syn-outer-sphere proton transfer mechanism, followed by a rate-determining reductive elimination via nucleophilic attack of the alkoxide on the resulting Pd-π-allyl.

item.title: JACS: Ligand Field Determines g-Tensor Anisotropy and Radicaloid Character of (L)RuV=O and (L)RuV=N Catalytic Intermediates
item.description:
Hasan Tuncer, Yulia Pushkar, Pavel Pokhilko
High-valent metal-oxo and metal-imido species mediate complex chemical transformations, yet their electronic structures remain difficult to characterize experimentally and computationally because of their short-lived nature and pronounced multiconfigurational character. The RuV (S = 1/2) complexes investigated here promote O–O bond formation in water oxidation and enable C(sp3)–H bond amination. Using multiconfigurational CASSCF/NEVPT2 calculations combined with wave function analyses, we demonstrate that g-tensor anisotropy, accessible via EPR measurements, is governed by spin–orbit coupling to low-lying doublet excited states whose energies are determined by the ligand field. Wave function analyses reveal that these transitions originate from the RuV=X (X=O, N) bonding and reflect varying degrees of RuIV-X• oxyl character. Our calculations reproduce the experimentally observed low g-tensor anisotropy of established RuV=O and RuV=N (S = 1/2) species. However, two previously reported highly anisotropic EPR signals are difficult to reconcile with a RuV assignment and can be more readily explained by proposed alternative RuIII species, which have low-lying spin–orbit-coupled excited states giving rise to the high g-tensor anisotropy. Overall results establish a quantitative relationship between the ligand field, which determines the excited-state electronic structure and radicaloid character of RuV=O and RuV=N fragments. These, in addition, manifest themselves in visualized natural orbitals and via spin–orbit selection rules, in the g-tensor anisotropy, elucidating the origins of EPR spectral features of high-valent transition-metal intermediates. Overall, our quantitative analysis establishes low g-tensor anisotropy in the EPR spectrum as a diagnostic spectroscopic signature of a high-valent RuV intermediate, should such a species be generated.

item.title: JACS: Decoupled Proton and Oxygen Transport at Cathode Triple-Phase Interfaces via Noncovalently Cross-Linked Biomimetic Nanochannels
item.description:
Fantao Kong, Tao Yang, Hao Zhuo, Yifan Huang, Min Li, Qin Li, Xiangzhi Cui, Jianlin Shi
The performance of proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs) is critically governed by the cathodic triple-phase interface, where platinum catalyst poisoning and inefficient proton/oxygen transport severely impede the oxygen reduction reaction. Inspired by the selective transport of biological membranes, we herein develop a porphyrin-based organic network (H-PorBz) as a multifunctional ionomer modifier to reconfigure the catalyst/ionomer/gas triple-phase interface. In situ noncovalent cross-linking between the H-PorBz and Nafion via NH+-H···SO3– interactions forms an interfacial layer that decouples proton and oxygen transport while suppressing sulfonate-induced Pt poisoning. Spectroscopic and computational studies reveal that H-PorBz simultaneously enhances proton conduction and oxygen transport by establishing a low-barrier proton-transfer network and tuning nanopore polarity. This membrane-mimetic design reduces sulfonate coverage on Pt by 28% and oxygen-transport resistance by 39.4%, delivering a mass-specific power density of 15.8 W mgPt–1 under H2/air conditions, 1.7-fold that of a conventional Pt/C@Nafion cathode. The composite ionomer also demonstrates excellent durability (>120 h at 0.6 V), with a voltage decay rate below 50 μV h–1. This work presents a bioinspired interfacial engineering strategy that reconfigures the three-phase region to mitigate catalyst poisoning and transport losses, offering a viable route to high-performance low-Pt PEMFCs.

item.title: JACS: Fine-Tuning Universal Machine Learning Potentials Enables Efficient Computation of Li Electrode Potentials in Battery Electrolytes
item.description:
Feng Wang, Yu-Hang Tang, Yi-Min Wei, Jun Cheng
The electrode potential of Li metal is fundamental to the performance and stability of Li-metal batteries, yet its accurate prediction across diverse electrolyte chemistries remains a challenge. Standard quantum chemistry using cluster models fails to account for explicit bulk solvation, while ab initio molecular dynamics is restricted by the high computational cost of thermodynamic sampling. In this work, we present an integrated framework that combines a universal machine learning potential for electrolytes with a data-efficient fine-tuning strategy to compute Li electrode potentials. This workflow achieves ab initio level accuracy using ∼200 extra density functional theory calculations per electrolyte system. Furthermore, the identified relationship between local Li+ solvation environments and electrode potential shifts provides mechanistic insights into electrolyte-dependent redox behavior and offers guidance for rational electrolyte design.

item.title: JACS: Arene-Perfluoroarene-Enabled Electrostatic Modulation in Organic Porous Photocatalysts for Ni/Photoredox C–N Coupling
item.description:
Wenbo Hu, Zhiye Wang, Zongwei Li, Jiancheng Yang, Yingying Wei, Heng Li, Bingxin Yuan
How molecular connectivity can tune photoresponsive local electrostatics in porous organic photocatalysts lacking long-range order remains unclear. Here, we use arene-perfluoroarene (AP)-based constitutional design to examine this relationship in 4CzIPN-derived porous photoredox polymers. Carbazole and perfluorocarbazole units are connected through ortho-, meta-, and para-linked biphenyl bridges. Kelvin probe force microscopy reveals local light-induced contact potential difference (CPD) shifts of 27.1, 18.3, 5.0, and 4.3 mV for o-CBCP, m-CBCP, p-CBCP, and the AP-free control P(4Cz), respectively. o-CBCP also exhibits a stronger surface photovoltage response than P(4Cz) and the lowest fitted intermediate-frequency resistance under 425 nm blue LED illumination. In a catalyst-discriminating Ni/photoredox C–N coupling reaction, product yields follow the same order as the local CPD shifts. With 0.2 mg of photocatalyst on a 0.2 mmol reaction scale, o-CBCP affords the product in good yield, whereas P(4Cz) gives only trace product. These findings identify linkage geometry as a molecular handle for tuning photoresponsive local electrostatics and catalytic behavior in disordered porous polymer photocatalysts.

item.title: JACS: Operando Imaging of Charge Transfer and Photoelectrochemical Water Oxidation at Defect-Rich Grain Boundaries
item.description:
Wei Nie, Thomas Dittrich, Yuying Gao, Ziyuan Wang, Dongfeng Li, Fusai Sun, Qian Li, Xiuli Wang, et al.
The microstructural properties of grain boundaries (GBs) and defects in semiconductor materials critically influence solar energy conversion. Yet, the precise role of GBs in charge separation and transport remains poorly understood and widely debated, particularly under reaction conditions. A key knowledge gap persists in linking charge separation and transfer to surface reactions at the GB-liquid interface, necessitating detailed operando nanoscale investigations. Here, we establish nanoscale, operando imaging of charge transfer and catalytic activity of a working BiVO4 photoanode using operando atomic force microscopy–scanning electrochemical microscopy (AFM-SECM) under illumination. We found distinct GB behaviors, with defect-rich GBs emerging as locally active regions for charge transfer and O2 generation, whereas other GBs impede charge transfer and serve as recombination sites. Specially for defect-rich GBs, operando electrochemical imaging and transient spectroscopy reveal that oxygen vacancies within GB interiors and on grain surfaces act synergistically on distinct time scales to trap photogenerated electrons and extend hole lifetimes into the millisecond range, thereby enhancing water oxidation activity locally at GBs. These insights underscore the pivotal role of defect-rich GBs in sustaining long-lived charge carriers, thereby highlighting the importance of modulating GB characteristics for efficient solar energy conversion.

item.title: Nano Letters: Voltage–Current-Emission Framework of Time-Resolved Electroluminescence
item.description:
Hui Bao, Longjia Wu, Yanan Guo, Jianchang Yan, Ying Wang, Haizheng Zhong
Time-resolved electroluminescence has been a central methodology for the development of LED devices. However, it still lacks quantitative theoretical descriptions of time-resolved electroluminescence. By combining the equivalent circuit models of semiconductor devices and the carrier dynamics of electroluminescence processes, here we have developed a voltage–current-emission framework to illustrate time-resolved electroluminescence from the pulse voltage as input, to injection current, and finally generate electroluminescence as output. The features of different LED devices can be quantitatively interpreted, confirming their universal applicability across LEDs with different materials and device structures. Importantly, the curves of time-resolved electroluminescence can be simulated to quantitatively describe the dynamics of current and carriers of the LED operation. In all, the voltage–current–emission framework offers theoretical guidance for achieving advanced LED devices for artificial intelligence (AI) technology.

item.title: ACS Nano: X-ray Crystallography of a Nanobody/JAM-1 Complex Informs Barrier Weakening and Enhanced Drug Permeability in a Cellular Blood–Brain Barrier Model
item.description:
Liyu Chen, Michael D. Healy, Haoyue Xi, Esteban Cruz, Mingze Xu, Rainbow Wing Bo Chan, Tishila Palliyaguru, Jonathan L. F. Lee, et al.
For pharmacological treatments of brain disorders, the blood–brain barrier (BBB) poses a formidable obstacle, tightly restricting the cerebral uptake of therapeutic agents. Tight junction (TJ) binders, including peptides, proteins, and monoclonal antibodies, that specifically bind to the extracellular domains (ECDs) of TJ proteins are increasingly being explored as BBB-weakening agents for enhanced drug delivery to the brain. Given that nanobodies (Nbs) can access epitopes that are often inaccessible to conventional antibodies, we obtained 16 Nbs with unique CDRs via immunization of alpaca with the ECD of either human (h) or murine JAM-1 (mJAM-1), a major TJ protein. Twelve Nb candidates exhibited high-affinity binding to mJAM-1, as measured by surface plasmon resonance (SPR), and these interactions were further validated for 9 Nbs by immunostaining of JAM-1-overexpressing cells. Five Nbs were found to weaken the barrier of the eGFP-hCldn5-MDCKII cellular monolayer, as shown by reduced transendothelial electrical resistance (TEER). X-ray crystallography revealed that the lead barrier-weakening Nb, E6, binds to the membrane-proximal nondimeric D2 domain of mJAM-1. Mutating key residues at this interface eliminated the BBB-weakening effect of E6, as evidenced by unaltered sodium fluorescence (NaFI) leakage in both eGFP-hCldn5-MDCKII and mJAM1-mGL-MDCKII cellular monolayers compared with the nontreated control. Our study highlights the potential of JAM-1-targeting Nbs as BBB modulators, offering a promising approach for generating TJ binders to enhance brain drug delivery.

item.title: Nano Letters: SecAntiGami: A Secondary-Antibody-Inspired RNA Origami for Qualitative Aptamer Validation
item.description:
Linus S. Frey, William Verstraeten, Mai P. Tran, Dana Venkert, Luca Monari, Cody Geary, Kerstin Göpfrich
RNA aptamers are short, single-stranded RNA molecules that fold into specific three-dimensional structures and selectively bind molecular targets. Despite applications in therapeutics, diagnostics, and biosensing, tools for aptamer validation remain scarce compared to well-established pipelines for other biomolecular binders such as antibodies. Here, we introduce SecAntiGami─a secondary-antibody-inspired RNA origami─as a modular tool for signal enhancement and aptamer characterization. SecAntiGami binds aptamers of interest through programmable kissing-loop interactions and carries a fluorescent aptamer for visualization. It amplifies aptamer-dependent size increases in dynamic light scattering assays and enables fluorescence-based aptamer localization. We rationally design three different variants of a biotin-binding aptamer and use SecAntiGami to demonstrate that all of them retain their functionality, enabling efficient integration of aptamers into RNA origami structures. SecAntiGami serves as a versatile tool for qualitative aptamer validation for synthetic biology, structural RNA nanotechnology, RNA therapeutics, and diagnostics.

item.title: ACS Nano: One-Dimensional Carbon Nanostructures with Periodic Graphitic Nitrogen Substitution
item.description:
Nicolò Bassi, Shantanu Mishra, Zheng Zhang, Xiao-Ye Wang, Feifei Xiang, Nils Krane, Carlo A. Pignedoli, Klaus Müllen, et al.
Heteroatom substitution is a powerful route to tune the chemical and electronic properties of carbon nanomaterials. In particular, replacement of an sp2-hybridized carbon atom in the graphene lattice with a nitrogen atom (denoted as graphitic nitrogen) induces substantial changes in the electronic properties. These include changes in the band structure that can influence electronic transport and magnetism. A key requirement for applications is both the periodic and precise incorporation of the heteroatoms in extended carbon lattices. Here, we report the on-surface synthesis and characterization of two one-dimensional carbon nanostructures─a polymer and a graphene nanoribbon─consisting of periodically incorporated graphitic nitrogen atoms. The on-surface reactions toward the formation of the nanostructures were monitored by scanning tunneling microscopy. The bond-resolved chemical structures of the reaction intermediates and products were investigated by atomic force microscopy, which enabled atomic-scale visualization of the graphitic nitrogen sites. The electronic properties of the nanostructures were studied by scanning tunneling spectroscopy and density functional theory calculations. Our analyses revealed the presence of localized nitrogen-centered electronic states in the nanostructures. In the gas phase where the nanostructures are in the neutral charge state, these states undergo spin polarization leading to an open-shell ground state. Upon adsorption on Au(111), the nanostructures exhibit electron transfer to the surface, which resulted in a closed-shell ground state. Our results demonstrate a straightforward and generally applicable route to synthesize graphitic nitrogen-substituted carbon nanomaterials with potential applications in spintronics, catalysis, and energy storage.

item.title: JACS: Machine Learning-Guided Precise Electrolyte Engineering Enables Stable Lithium Metal Pouch Cells Exceeding 350 Wh/kg at −40 °C
item.description:
Zichun Xiao, Yong Li, Yankai Zheng, Ruohong Ke, Yangyang Liu, Zhenxin Huang, Xu Zhang, Yu Liu, et al.
High-energy-density lithium metal batteries (LMBs) with wide-temperature adaptability are urgently needed for aerospace and military fields, yet extreme temperature conditions disrupt Li+ transport kinetics and cause failure in solid–electrolyte interphase (SEI) chemistry regulation. To guide molecular selection for wide-temperature electrolyte design, we constructed Electrolyte-65K, a rule-defined library of electrolyte-relevant molecules, and trained D-P Compass using batch-computable molecular descriptors to efficiently predict and rank dipole moment (D) and polarizability (P). Applying the trained models to a literature-derived set of electrolyte molecule candidates, D-P Pareto analysis identified N,N-dimethyltrifluoromethanesulfonamide (DMTMSA) as the candidate at the Pareto knee. The thermally sensitive dipole–dipole interactions between DMTMSA and weakly solvating solvent 1,2-diethoxyethane (DEE) enable a temperature-autoresponsive electrolyte that maintains an anion-dominated solvation structure across a wide temperature range, enabling SEI chemistry engineering regulation from −40 to 60 °C. A 5.8 Ah pouch cell achieves a high energy density of 503.7 Wh kg–1 at 25 °C with a lifespan of 275 cycles and retains 365.5 Wh kg–1 at −40 °C with 99.8% capacity retention over 50 cycles. This work establishes a data-driven molecular screening framework for wide-temperature electrolyte engineering design.

item.title: ACS Nano: Wafer-Scale p-type TeSeO x for Complementary Oxide Electronics
item.description:
Ting Liu, Fan Yang, Ziyi Liu, Jianshi Tang, Wen Sun, Zhidong Tang, Bin Gao, He Qian, et al.
The absence of a scalable p-type oxide semiconductor remains a major limitation for complementary oxide electronics, in part because improving hole conduction in amorphous oxide networks often coincides with increased defect-mediated leakage. Here, we report an anneal-free, wafer-scale predominantly amorphous tellurium selenium oxide (TeSeOx) p-type oxide semiconductor that achieves a more favorable balance between leakage suppression and hole conduction. Spectroscopic analysis and first-principles calculations indicate that Se incorporation reconfigures the local coordination environment, weakens the strongly Te–Te-dominated connectivity of Te-rich networks, and retains spatially connected valence-band states consistent with the experimentally observed partial recovery of on-state conduction. Consequently, p-channel field-effect transistors fabricated across 4-in. wafers exhibit a final screened yield of 91.4%, a mean mobility of 4.52 cm2 ·V–1 ·s–1, and wafer-scale uniformity without postdeposition annealing of the TeSeOx channel. Temperature-dependent transport measurements further support leakage suppression in the engineered network, with an on/off ratio exceeding 109 at 77 K. As a device-level proof-of-concept relevant to three-dimensional integration, vertically configured TeSeOx PFETs and IGZO NFETs were assembled into complementary inverters and multi-input logic gates, demonstrating correct functionality under a low thermal budget. Collectively, these results support local coordination engineering as a viable route toward scalable amorphous p-type oxide semiconductors for thermally compatible complementary oxide electronics, with potential relevance to 3D integration.

item.title: ACS Nano: Sweeping Surface Trap States under the Carpet: Cd2+ Inclusion in InAs Quantum Dots
item.description:
Habibul Arfin, Jordi Llusar, Carmelita Rodà, Satyaprakash Panda, Yurii P. Ivanov, Giorgio Divitini, Mirko Prato, Andrea Toma, et al.
We have investigated the effect of CdCl2 as an additive in the colloidal synthesis of amino-As-based InAs quantum dots (QDs). Our results demonstrate that this metal halide promotes the incorporation of Cd into the InAs QDs, leading to the formation of In(Cd)As alloyed QDs featuring a narrower bandgap and enhanced photoluminescence (PL) compared to their undoped InAs counterparts. By varying the relative amount of CdCl2, it was possible to synthesize, in a one-pot process, QDs with PL tunable from ∼1000 to ∼1430 nm with a quantum yield as high as 17% at ∼1430 nm, without requiring any postsynthesis shell growth. These In(Cd)As QDs feature longer exciton lifetimes compared to InAs QDs, due to suppressed ultrafast nonradiative trap pathways, and a fast biexciton lifetime that follows the expected linear scaling with nanocrystal volume. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations revealed that (i) In(Cd)As alloys, which are thermodynamically unfavorable in the bulk phase, are stabilized by finite-size effects; (ii) the bandgap narrowing induced by Cd incorporation arises primarily from a pronounced upward shift of the valence band maximum (VBM); and (iii) this upward shift of the VBM also buries the surface trap states below the valence band edge, thereby accounting for the observed high PL efficiency in In(Cd)As QDs. Overall, this work provides mechanistic insights into defect passivation in InAs QDs and establishes metal-halide-mediated growth as an effective strategy for infrared emitting InAs-based QDs.

item.title: ACS Nano: Capturing the Hidden Short-Range Order in Amorphous Oxide Interfaces That Directs Quasi-Epitaxial Thin-Film Growth
item.description:
Junghwa Kim, SeungGyo Jeong, Whan Kyun Kim, Soo-Yoon Hwang, Kwangrak Kim, Junho Jeong, Hansaem Park, Wookrae Kim, et al.
As solid-state device architectures become increasingly complex, buried interfaces play a critical role in determining thin-film texture, morphology, and defect formation. However, resolving the structural features that control growth on nominally amorphous interlayers remains challenging because it requires three-dimensional sensitivity at high spatial resolution. Here, we combine four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy, fluctuation electron microscopy, and multislice electron ptychography to investigate ruthenium (Ru) thin films grown on an underlying amorphous Ta2O5 layer, a material stack relevant for next-generation electronic and spintronic devices. Although the Ta2O5 layer appears amorphous in conventional imaging, diffraction and depth-resolved ptychographic reconstructions reveal nanoscale β-Ta2O5-like ordered motifs near the Ru/Ta2O5 interface. These locally ordered motifs, together with the interfacial morphology, guide the orientation of the Ru layer and produce a textured, quasi-epitaxial film. The curved and atomically rough interface further induces depth-dependent strain gradients and promotes planar defect formation within the Ru layer. Collectively, these results demonstrate that hidden short-range order within nominally amorphous oxides can direct the growth of metallic thin films, providing a framework for engineering buried interfaces in advanced electronic and spintronic material stacks.

item.title: JACS: Dual Regulation of Electronic Structure and Hydrogen Distribution through Co Single-Atom-Functionalized Supports for Efficient Ru-Catalyzed Ammonia Synthesis
item.description:
Yifan Yan, Zhenjie Sun, Haolong Chang, Zhongliang Cao, Jianjian Yang, Jingnan Wang, Kui Lin, Xiaohu Hu, et al.
Under mild reaction conditions, ammonia synthesis over Ru catalysts is severely constrained by hydrogen poisoning because excessive surface hydrogen blocks the Ru B5 sites required for efficient N2 activation. To overcome this challenge, we design an atomically functionalized support by anchoring isolated Co single atoms at framework sites of K-modified KL zeolite, creating a dual-function support. The Co single atoms serve as hydrogen-accepting sites that continuously remove surface H atoms from Ru via hydrogen spillover, i.e., spatial regulation of surface hydrogen. Moreover, they indirectly strengthen the electron donation from framework K to Ru for N2 activation, without any direct Co → Ru charge transfer, thereby enhancing both the availability and the intrinsic activity of Ru B5 sites for efficient N2 dissociation. This cooperative mechanism is collectively revealed by comprehensive kinetic analyses, operando spectroscopy, isotope-exchange measurements, chemisorption studies, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations. Consequently, Ru/Co1–KL achieves a near-equilibrium ammonia synthesis rate of 65.3 mmol g–1 h–1 at 400 °C and 1 MPa and maintains stable performance for over 1500 h. This work demonstrates that atomic support functionalization can spatially decouple competing adsorption processes at catalytic interfaces, offering an effective strategy for overcoming site-blocking limitations in heterogeneous catalysis.

item.title: JACS: Fast ON/OFF Emission Photoswitching of Turn-On Mode Fluorescent Diarylethenes
item.description:
Masakazu Morimoto, Shinsuke Tojo, Shunsuke Tanaka, Eri Fujisawa, Shoya Takasu, Ryo Nishimura, Kazuki Okazawa, Yasuteru Shigeta, et al.
Fluorescent chromophores having reversible photoswitching ability are applicable for various types of analysis and imaging. 1,2-Bis(2-ethyl-6-phenyl-1-benzothiophene-1,1-dioxide-3-yl)perfluorocyclopentene (1) is known to undergo turn-on mode fluorescent photoswitching. One serious drawback of the chromophore is its very low photocycloreversion (switching off) quantum yield (<10–3). To improve the yield, derivatives bearing various alkyl substituents at 2- and 2′-positions were prepared. It was found that introduction of bulky substituents, such as isobutyl or neopentyl groups, is effective in increasing the yield. The yield increases by almost 3 orders of magnitude from 5.9 × 10–4 to 4.6 × 10–1 by replacing ethyl substituents with neopentyl groups. Theoretical analysis revealed that the energy barrier in the photocycloreversion reaction is inferred from the calculated potential energy difference between 2Ao and 2Ac local minima in the excited-state (S1) potential energy surface, and the decrease in the energy difference by introducing bulky primary alkyl substituents at 2- and 2′-position increases the photocycloreversion quantum yield. Although substitution of primary alkyl groups increases the yield, secondary alkyl substituents are ineffective. 1,2-Bis(2-neopentyl-6-phenyl-1-benzothiophene-1,1-dioxide-3-yl)perfluorocyclopentene (6) undergoes very fast ON/OFF emission photoswitching cycles over 2000 times even in the presence of air without any marked fatigue, and the colored closed-ring isomer is stable at 80 °C for 50 h.

item.title: JACS: Copper-Catalyzed Diastereoselective and Enantioselective α-C–H Allenylation of Alkylamines
item.description:
Dongshun Ni, Yang Yu, Yuming Pan, Zhenghua Li, Li Deng
Herein, we report a diastereoselective and enantioselective α-allenylation of N-α-cyanoarylidene alkylamines with propargylic carbonates via a sequential copper-catalyzed imine propargylation and aza-Cope rearrangement process. This method features broad substrate scope with respect to both reaction partners, thereby establishing an unprecedented protocol for the efficient asymmetric synthesis of chiral amines containing both central and axial chirality from readily accessible alkylamines and propargylic carbonates. Additionally, we demonstrated that these chiral α-allenyl amines could be readily transformed into a diverse range of chiral amine derivatives. Mechanistic studies revealed that the simultaneous coordination and π–π interaction between the cyano group and dicopper-allenylidene complex played decisive roles for the induction of the chemoselectivity, diastereoselectivity, and enantioselectivity during imine propargylation. The subsequent aza-Cope rearrangement proceeded with an efficient central-to-axial chirality transfer to generate the chiral allene motif.

item.title: JACS: Total Synthesis of Damasterpenes II, IV, V, and VII
item.description:
Yutaro Yamada, Haruka Fujino, Masayuki Inoue
Damasterpenes are highly oxygenated, multiply acylated dolabellane diterpenoids with anti-herpes simplex virus type 1 activity. These compounds share an 11/5-trans-fused carboskeleton with three methyl groups and one isopropyl group, but differ in their unsaturation, oxidation, and acylation patterns. Here, we present the first total synthesis of damasterpenes II, IV, V, and VII. In the first stage, a common 11/5-fused intermediate was convergently assembled using radical-polar crossover three-component coupling to install the two carbon branches onto the five-membered ring, followed by ring-closing metathesis to form the medium-sized 11-membered ring. In the second stage, this intermediate was transformed into damasterpenes II, IV, V, and two possible structures of damasterpene VII by tuning the oxidation levels and introducing three to four acyl groups. These architecturally complex molecules bearing 8 to 10 stereocenters were synthesized in 26–29 steps, and the previously unknown stereochemistry of damasterpene VII was elucidated. This work demonstrates the value of radical-polar crossover reactions for the rapid construction of densely substituted molecular frameworks and highlights the importance of controlling the three-dimensional conformations of 5- and 11-membered rings to achieve site- and stereoselective functional group manipulations.

item.title: JACS: Dynamic Site Heterogeneity in Nanoparticle Catalysis from Hierarchical Machine Learning
item.description:
Dongxiao Chen, Qian-Yu Liu, Dongfang Cheng, Philippe Sautet
Identifying the activity of all individual surface sites on catalytic nanoparticles is challenging but critical for heterogeneous catalysts, especially for understanding site heterogeneity. Here, we developed a hierarchical machine learning approach that links the atomic local environment to both energy and reaction barrier predictions with similar computational costs, opening the feasibility of extensive catalytic reactivity exploration on nanoparticle catalysts. Applying the methodology to propane dehydrogenation at a reaction temperature of 973 K on Pt nanoparticles up to a size of 5 nm revealed a highly dynamic and heterogeneous activity with a wide distribution of propane C–H cleavage barriers (0.5–1.3 eV) and rare highly active or inactive sites. Conventional global optimization methods underestimate the catalytic activity, even by considering a large set of metastable structures. Instead, accurate activity and size effect trend emerge by using ensemble-averaged molecular dynamics trajectories, emphasizing the dynamic nature of site activity and heterogeneity. Notably, classical polyhedral models, like those obtained from a Wulff construction, can predict correct trends for larger nanoparticles but do so through error cancellation between missing dynamics and overestimating probabilities of metastable sites. Furthermore, our simulations reveal a fast barrier fluctuation at the reaction temperature for a given surface Pt atom within 100 ps trajectories with a barrier shift by up to 0.8 eV, indicating that individual atoms can switch between active and inactive states on a picosecond time scale. This work provides a feasible approach to shift the views of catalysts from a combination of static active sites to highly heterogeneous and fast dynamically evolving sites.

item.title: JACS: Redox-Active Spin Trapping for the Electrochemical Detection, Quantification, and Kinetic Analysis of Sulfate Radicals in Aqueous Media
item.description:
Seth T. Putnam, Zirui Wang, Collin Reutimann, Joaquín Rodríguez-López
Sulfate radicals (SO4•–) are important intermediates in synthetic and environmental chemistry, yet robust methods for their selective detection and quantification remain underdeveloped. Spin traps such as 5–5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline-N-oxide (DMPO) are used to extend the lifetime of these radicals, but the resulting adduct (DMPO–SO4•–) is unstable in water, undergoing nucleophilic substitution to DMPO–OH•, causing misidentification and mechanistic confusion in aqueous systems. Here, we report an electrochemical approach for the selective and quantitative detection of sulfate radical spin-trap adducts in aqueous conditions. Using electrochemical electron paramagnetic resonance (EC-EPR) spectroscopy, we measured the half-life of DMPO–SO4•- in water to be ∼98 s. This short half-life makes the quantification of SO4•– by traditional EPR methods challenging. To overcome this, we used an approach to electrochemically detect spin-trap adducts and found that DMPO–SO4•– could be electrochemically oxidized at ∼0.75 V vs Ag/AgCl. Coupling this approach to microband interdigitated electrode arrays (IDAs) in generation-collection mode, automated electrochemistry, and finite-element simulations, we leveraged the short detection time (ms) of IDAs to capture DMPO–SO4•– before it decays. Quantitative understanding allowed us to estimate the DMPO spin trapping rate constant for SO4•– (4 × 105 M–1s–1). Finally, changes in the DMPO–SO4•– collection current were used to extract the kinetics of a competing reaction (oxidation of benzyl alcohol) in a radical clock-type approach. These results demonstrate the broad utility of redox-active spin trapping for quantifying electrogenerated radical intermediates such as SO4•– with sufficient versatility to capture their transient processes.

item.title: JACS: Diazo DOC: A Diazomethane Sulfonyl Fluoride Surrogate for Diversity-Oriented Clicking and SuFEx-Driven Protein Labeling
item.description:
Joshua W. Kop, Siyang Ding, Vivian G. Shang, Carol Hua, Daniel L. Priebbenow, Yuning Hong, Christopher J. Smedley
Diversity-oriented clicking (DOC) is a unified click approach for the modular synthesis of lead-like structures through the application of the wider family of click transformations. Here, we present a diazomethane sulfonyl fluoride surrogate, tert-butyl(((diazomethyl)sulfonyl)methoxy)dimethylsilane (tBu-DMSM, a diazo DOC hub), as the latest connective hub in DOC, marking a significant advancement in the field. Through a series of processes that adhere to many of the click chemistry principles, followed by silyl deprotection and electrophilic fluorination, we highlight the potential of this DOC hub in the synthesis of a library of unprecedented clickable heterocycles (tetrazoles, 3,3′-cyclopropyl spirooxindoles, and benzo[d]oxepines). The diversification of these novel cores through sulfur fluoride exchange (SuFEx) click chemistry yields the corresponding sulfonate esters, showcasing the versatility of the DOC strategy. Additionally, simple removal of the silyloxymethane group increases the scope further for the selective synthesis of heterocycles, with tBu-DMSM acting as a diazomethane alternative or a one carbon synthon. Furthermore, the utility of this method is showcased in the synthesis of a novel aggregation-induced emission (AIE) fluorescent tetrazole probe for covalent protein labeling via SuFEx, revealing selective and structure-dependent protein modification.

item.title: JACS: Protein Scaffolds Modulate the Electronic Structure of a Common Ketyl Radical Intermediate in Thiamine Pyrophosphate-Dependent Radical Biocatalysis: Insights from EPR and ENDOR Spectroscopy
item.description:
Guodong Rao, Zheng Zhang, Xin Liu, Angela A. Shiau, R. David Britt, Yang Yang
New-to-nature radical biocatalysis has emerged as a powerful strategy for asymmetric C–C bond formation, yet the enzyme-bound radical intermediates that underpin these transformations have remained largely uncharacterized. Here, we combine photobiocatalytic reaction development with multifrequency electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR), electron–nuclear double resonance (ENDOR) spectroscopy, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations to elucidate the ketyl radical intermediates formed during thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP)-dependent radical biocatalysis. We first develop an oxidative photobiocatalytic cross-coupling of aldehydes with alkyltrifluoroborates catalyzed by engineered benzoylformate decarboxylase (BFD) variants, providing enantioenriched α-chiral ketones through a new oxidative radical manifold inaccessible to benzaldehyde lyases (BALs). Freeze-quench multifrequency EPR and ENDOR spectroscopy directly identify the catalytically generated TPP-bound ketyl radical and reveal that this common radical intermediate adopts distinct electronic structures in BFD and BAL despite their identical chemical composition. Analysis of 1H, 19F, 31P, and 14N hyperfine interactions, together with DFT calculations, demonstrates that enzyme-specific active-site conformations redistribute spin density between the TPP cofactor and substrate fragment. Greater substrate-centered spin delocalization in BFD provides a mechanistic basis for its superior radical C–C coupling activity relative to BAL. These results establish a direct relationship between protein-controlled electronic structure and catalytic function in TPP-dependent radical biocatalysis and demonstrate that engineering the electronic properties of a common radical intermediate represents a useful strategy for controlling enzyme reactivity in radical biocatalysis.

item.title: JACS: Electron–Nuclear Hyperfine Coupling Enables Electron Paramagnetic Resonance Detection of Diamagnetic Cu(I) with Trityl Spin Probes
item.description:
Yan Wang, Xiaoli Tan, Jing Zhao, Qi Chang, Yuqi Hu, Hui Gao, Wenbin Cai, Yafei Wang, et al.
Copper homeostasis is tightly regulated in biological systems, and its dysregulation is implicated in various diseases. In the intracellular reducing environment, Cu(I) is the predominant oxidation state of labile copper; however, its detection remains highly challenging because of strong buffering by endogenous ligands and competition from biologically abundant metal ions. Here, we report an electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR)-based strategy that enables detection of otherwise EPR-silent Cu(I) by converting Cu(I) coordination into a characteristic spectroscopic fingerprint through electron–nuclear hyperfine coupling. A series of Cu(I)-hyperfine spin probes (CHYPs) were developed by tethering stable trityl radicals to Cu(I)-selective ligands through various linkers. Among these probes, CHYP7 formed a 1:1 complex with Cu(I) and displayed a well-resolved four-line EPR signal arising from hyperfine splitting by the copper nucleus (I = 3/2). CHYP7 exhibited high Cu(I) affinity, excellent metal-ion selectivity, and a low detection limit of ∼4 nM (0.2 pmol). A hydrophilic analogue, CHYP8, further enabled quantitative Cu(I) measurement under acidic conditions in the presence of endogenous ligands and competing metal ions. CHYP8 was also applied to measure cellular labile copper pools and monitor copper-level changes following copper supplementation or hypoxia-reoxygenation treatment, as well as to quantify labile copper pools in tissues and serum from mice subjected to ischemia/reperfusion injury. Overall, this work establishes hyperfine-coupling-enabled EPR detection as a new strategy for probing Cu(I) in biological systems and provides a platform for investigating copper homeostasis and copper-associated pathophysiology.

item.title: JACS: Acidity-Driven Spontaneous Degradation of Trifluoroacetic Acid at Droplet Air–Water Interfaces
item.description:
Yunqian Chen, Jingxin Lin, Zhengxiang Sun, Haiping Xiong, Zhongyu Guo, Xinke Wang, Runqi Zhang, Sihan Liu, et al.
Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), an ultrashort-chain per- and polyfluoroalkyl substance, is increasingly detected in the environment and has raised widespread concern because of its negative effects on health and ecosystems. However, whether TFA can degrade naturally in the environment remains unresolved. Here, we report the spontaneous degradation of TFA at the air–water interface of droplets, yielding F– and fluorine-containing transformation products, including CHF3O, CF3O2H, and CH2F2O2. The extent of degradation is strongly dependent on droplet acidity, with the F– yield at pH 10 being 12-fold higher than at pH 5. Density functional theory calculations reveal a mechanism favored by alkaline conditions and oxygen in which interfacial decarboxylation triggers sequential oxidation and defluorination. These findings identify the air–water interface of pH-regulated droplets as a reactive microenvironment for spontaneous TFA degradation, offering new insights into the environmental transformation of ultrashort-chain PFAS.

item.title: ACS Nano: Pressure-Regulated Confined Crystallization Drives Self-Organization of Bioinspired Mineral Architectures
item.description:
Jia-hua Liu, Jie Zhou, Junjie Mao, Qinbo Yang, Zhou Chen, Xi Zhang, Yicheng Han, Jian Lu, et al.
Nature employs amorphous precursors to construct inorganic biominerals with highly ordered patterns within spatially confined environments. However, bottom-up fabrication of bulk materials with well-organized patterns remains challenging. Here, we report a pressure-regulated strategy to fabricate inorganic monoliths featuring periodic motifs via consolidation of hydrated amorphous calcium carbonate (ACC) gels. The applied pressure governs both structural water retention and the degree of confinement, thereby tailoring crystallization kinetics. Confined crystallization induces shrinkage through coupled dehydration and phase transformation, generating contractile stresses within bulk monoliths. These stresses trigger surface buckling and drive the spontaneous formation of long-range concentric patterns. With increasing pressure, these periodic features further evolve into three-dimensional surface relief structures. Finite element analysis simulates this dynamic morphogenesis and supports a chemo-mechanical coupling mechanism. These findings provide a bottom-up route for constructing monoliths with complex morphologies and offer insights into biomineralization.

item.title: JACS: Tuning Superconductivity and Topological Bands in Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–C Medium-Entropy Carbides by Valence Electron Concentration
item.description:
Jingjun Qin, Mingmin Li, Hong-Xue Jiang, Hongyu Liu, Zhen Wang, Lingyong Zeng, Rui Chen, Yucheng Li, et al.
The search for unconventional superconductors is a hot topic in materials science and condensed matter physics, yet remains challenging. Here we report a series of medium-entropy carbides (MECs) within the Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–C system with finely tuned valence electron concentration (VEC). Through VEC engineering, the type-II Dirac points are deliberately shifted from approximately 0.19 eV below the Fermi level in the base composition Ta0.25Nb0.25Hf0.25Zr0.25C to within 6.7–59.1 meV of the Fermi level in the optimal composition Ta0.1875Nb0.1875Hf0.3125Zr0.3125C. All five compositions form single-phase rock-salt structures and exhibit type-II bulk superconductivity with TcMid ranging from 2.2 to 4.9 K. Among these, the equimolar Ta0.25Nb0.25Hf0.25Zr0.25C composition exhibits the highest Tc of 4.9 K, with μ0Hc2GL = 1.16 T, μ0Hc1(0) = 65.9 Oe, and ΔC/γTc = 1.16, alongside excellent stability in acidic/alkaline environments and under pressures up to 52 GPa. Our findings establish VEC engineering as a potentially transferable strategy for bridging topological band physics with superconductivity in medium/high-entropy ceramics, positioning this MEC family as a candidate platform for investigating topological superconductivity in disordered systems.

item.title: JACS: Cooperative Reactivity of Mangano–Germylene and Germylidyne Complexes Featuring a Ge≡Mn Triple Bond
item.description:
Fengming Rong, Siyavash Moradi, Arseni Kostenko, Xufang Liu, John A. Kelly, Tobias Weng, Christopher J. Stein, Shigeyoshi Inoue
Multiple bonding between heavier group 14 elements and transition metals has long fascinated chemists, yet manganese–germanium bonds remain virtually unexplored. We now report a germylidyne-manganese complex featuring a structurally authenticated Ge≡Mn triple bond, supported by detailed electronic structure analysis. The Ge≡Mn triple bond further exhibits pronounced π-reactivity toward Au(I), affording a heterotrinuclear Ge–Au–Mn metallacycle and providing chemical support for its multiple-bond character. In parallel, two monomangano–germylene complexes were isolated. These species display distinctive reactivity in regioselective alkyne carbonylation and nitrene insertion, transformations that are inaccessible to conventional single-site systems.
